items.title: TOTP in Node with no packages: four steps, each checked against RFC 6238
items.summary: When an authenticator code is rejected, the fault sits in one of four steps: decoding the secret, turning the clock into a counter, the HMAC, or the truncation to six digits. Writing those four steps yourself is the quickest way to know which one to look at. Here they are in Node with no packages, each with a known answer to check against. The known answer is the test vector from RFC 6238. Its secret is the ASCII text 12345678901234567890 , which an authenticator app takes in Base32 as GEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQGEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQ . At 59 seconds after 1 January 1970 the 8-digit SHA-1 code is 94287082 , and the 6-digit code is its last six digits, 287082 . A function that prints those two is right. Step 1: the Base32 secret becomes bytes The setup key printed under a QR code is Base32: the letters A to Z and the digits 2 to 7, each character carrying 5 bits. Spaces, padding and lower case do not matter, so strip them first. const ALPHABET = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ234567' ; function base32Decode ( input ) { const clean = input . toUpperCase ( ) . replace ( / [ \ s = ] / g , '' ) ; let bits = 0 , value = 0 ; const out = [ ] ; for ( const ch of clean ) { const idx = ALPHABET . indexOf ( ch ) ; if ( idx === - 1 ) throw new Error ( `not Base32: ${ch}` ) ; value = ( value << 5 ) | idx ; bits += 5 ; if ( bits >= 8 ) { out . push ( ( value >>> ( bits - 8 ) ) & 0xff ) ; bits -= 8 ; } } return Buffer . from ( out ) ; } Check: the Base32 decoder , set to Decode and Base32, turns the test secret into 12345678901234567890 and reports 20 bytes. That size is normal: most services use 20 random bytes, 160 bits, which is 32 Base32 characters. Step 2: the clock becomes a counter Unix time in seconds, divided by the period and rounded down. The period is 30 seconds unless the service says otherwise. The counter is then written as 8 bytes, big-endian. const counter = Math . floor ( time / period ) ; // 59 / 30 -> 1 const msg = Buffer . alloc ( 8 ) ; msg . writeBigUInt64BE ( BigInt ( counter ) ) ; // 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 01 For a real date: at 12:00:10 UTC on 8 November 2026 the counter is 59804640. That step runs from 12:00:00 to 12:00:30, so the code on screen then has 20 seconds left. Step 3: HMAC-SHA1 of those 8 bytes const mac = crypto . createHmac ( 'sha1' , base32Decode ( secret ) ) . update ( msg ) . digest ( ) ; For the test key and counter 1 this is 20 bytes: 75a48a19d4cbe100644e8ac1397eea747a2d33ab You can check this step on its own. The counter bytes are not printable, so a text box cannot hold them, but a file can: printf '\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x01' > counter.bin openssl dgst -sha1 -hmac 12345678901234567890 counter.bin The HMAC generator with SHA-1, the key typed as Text and the message switched to File gives the same hex for counter.bin . If your own value differs here, look at how the counter was encoded: the text "1" and the 8-byte number 1 are different messages. Step 4: truncate to digits The low 4 bits of the last byte pick an offset. The 4 bytes starting there, with the top bit cleared, make a number, and the code is its last 6 or 8 digits. const offset = mac [ mac . length - 1 ] & 0x0f ; // 0xab & 0x0f = 11 const bin = mac . readUInt32BE ( offset ) & 0x7fffffff ; // 0xc1397eea -> 0x41397eea return String ( bin % 10 ** digits ) . padStart ( digits , '0' ) ; 0x41397eea is 1094287082. The last 8 digits are 94287082 and the last 6 are 287082 . Keep the padStart : a code whose number begins with zeros still has to be six characters long. Steps 2 to 4 as one function const crypto = require ( 'node:crypto' ) ; function totp ( secret , { time = Date . now ( ) / 1000 , period = 30 , digits = 6 , algo = 'sha1' } = { } ) { const counter = Math . floor ( time / period ) ; const msg = Buffer . alloc ( 8 ) ; msg . writeBigUInt64BE ( BigInt ( counter ) ) ; const mac = crypto . createHmac ( algo , base32Decode ( secret ) ) . update ( msg ) . digest ( ) ; const offset = mac [ mac . length - 1 ] & 0x0f ; const bin = mac . readUInt32BE ( offset ) & 0x7fffffff ; return String ( bin % 10 ** digits ) . padStart ( digits , '0' ) ; } const secret = 'GEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQGEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQ' ; console . log ( totp ( secret , { time : 59 , digits : 8 } ) ) ; // 94287082 console . log ( totp ( secret , { time : 59 } ) ) ; // 287082 Both lines print the RFC values on Node 24. For a live check I pasted the same secret into a TOTP generator this afternoon. At 14:09 IST it showed step 59856079 with 713 395 as the previous code, 827 335 as the current one and 749 271 as the next; totp() for steps 59856078, 59856079 and 59856080 printed the same three. Checking a code someone typed Servers usually accept a code from one step before or after the current one, so a code typed a few seconds late still works. Returning which step matched also tells you roughly how far off the user's clock is. function verify ( secret , code , { window = 1 , period = 30 , . . . opts } = { } ) { const now = Date . now ( ) / 1000 ; for ( let step = - window ; step <= window ; step ++ ) { const expected = totp ( secret , { . . . opts , period , time : now + step * period } ) ; if ( expected . length === code . length && crypto . timingSafeEqual ( Buffer . from ( expected ) , Buffer . from ( code ) ) ) { return step ; // 0 on time, -1 one step late, +1 one step early } } return null ; } timingSafeEqual is there for a reason: an ordinary string comparison stops at the first different character, so its timing leaks how much of a guess was right. A constant-time comparison checks every byte every time. When the phone and the server still disagree The clock. A code that only works one step early or late means a clock about 30 seconds off. Settings the app ignores. Google Authenticator historically used SHA-1, six digits and 30 seconds whatever the otpauth link asked for. Keep those defaults unless you control both sides. The secret. One wrong character in the Base32 key, or a different algorithm, digit count or period on the server, changes every code. The same example is worked through by hand in the TOTP guide . I wrote this with AI help; the test values come from the linked pages as they read on 26 November 2026, and every output above is from running the code.
items.summary_html:
When an authenticator code is rejected, the fault sits in one of four steps: decoding the secret, turning the clock into a counter, the HMAC, or the truncation to six digits. Writing those four steps yourself is the quickest way to know which one to look at. Here they are in Node with no packages, each with a known answer to check against.

The known answer is the test vector from RFC 6238. Its secret is the ASCII text 12345678901234567890, which an authenticator app takes in Base32 as GEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQGEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQ. At 59 seconds after 1 January 1970 the 8-digit SHA-1 code is 94287082, and the 6-digit code is its last six digits, 287082. A function that prints those two is right.

Step 1: the Base32 secret becomes bytes

The setup key printed under a QR code is Base32: the letters A to Z and the digits 2 to 7, each character carrying 5 bits. Spaces, padding and lower case do not matter, so strip them first.

const ALPHABET = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ234567';

function base32Decode(input) {
  const clean = input.toUpperCase().replace(/[\s=]/g, '');
  let bits = 0, value = 0;
  const out = [];
  for (const ch of clean) {
    const idx = ALPHABET.indexOf(ch);
    if (idx === -1) throw new Error(`not Base32: ${ch}`);
    value = (value << 5) | idx;
    bits += 5;
    if (bits >= 8) {
      out.push((value >>> (bits - 8)) & 0xff);
      bits -= 8;
    }
  }
  return Buffer.from(out);
}

Check: the Base32 decoder, set to Decode and Base32, turns the test secret into 12345678901234567890 and reports 20 bytes. That size is normal: most services use 20 random bytes, 160 bits, which is 32 Base32 characters.

Step 2: the clock becomes a counter

Unix time in seconds, divided by the period and rounded down. The period is 30 seconds unless the service says otherwise. The counter is then written as 8 bytes, big-endian.

const counter = Math.floor(time / period);  // 59 / 30 -> 1
const msg = Buffer.alloc(8);
msg.writeBigUInt64BE(BigInt(counter));      // 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 01

For a real date: at 12:00:10 UTC on 8 November 2026 the counter is 59804640. That step runs from 12:00:00 to 12:00:30, so the code on screen then has 20 seconds left.

Step 3: HMAC-SHA1 of those 8 bytes 
const mac = crypto.createHmac('sha1', base32Decode(secret)).update(msg).digest();

For the test key and counter 1 this is 20 bytes:

75a48a19d4cbe100644e8ac1397eea747a2d33ab

You can check this step on its own. The counter bytes are not printable, so a text box cannot hold them, but a file can:

printf '\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x01' > counter.bin
openssl dgst -sha1 -hmac 12345678901234567890 counter.bin

The HMAC generator with SHA-1, the key typed as Text and the message switched to File gives the same hex for counter.bin. If your own value differs here, look at how the counter was encoded: the text "1" and the 8-byte number 1 are different messages.

Step 4: truncate to digits

The low 4 bits of the last byte pick an offset. The 4 bytes starting there, with the top bit cleared, make a number, and the code is its last 6 or 8 digits.

const offset = mac[mac.length - 1] & 0x0f;          // 0xab & 0x0f = 11
const bin = mac.readUInt32BE(offset) & 0x7fffffff;  // 0xc1397eea -> 0x41397eea
return String(bin % 10 ** digits).padStart(digits, '0');

0x41397eea is 1094287082. The last 8 digits are 94287082 and the last 6 are 287082. Keep the padStart: a code whose number begins with zeros still has to be six characters long.

Steps 2 to 4 as one function 
const crypto = require('node:crypto');

function totp(secret, { time = Date.now() / 1000, period = 30, digits = 6, algo = 'sha1' } = {}) {
  const counter = Math.floor(time / period);
  const msg = Buffer.alloc(8);
  msg.writeBigUInt64BE(BigInt(counter));
  const mac = crypto.createHmac(algo, base32Decode(secret)).update(msg).digest();
  const offset = mac[mac.length - 1] & 0x0f;
  const bin = mac.readUInt32BE(offset) & 0x7fffffff;
  return String(bin % 10 ** digits).padStart(digits, '0');
}

const secret = 'GEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQGEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQ';
console.log(totp(secret, { time: 59, digits: 8 }));  // 94287082
console.log(totp(secret, { time: 59 }));             // 287082

Both lines print the RFC values on Node 24. For a live check I pasted the same secret into a TOTP generator this afternoon. At 14:09 IST it showed step 59856079 with 713 395 as the previous code, 827 335 as the current one and 749 271 as the next; totp() for steps 59856078, 59856079 and 59856080 printed the same three.

Checking a code someone typed

Servers usually accept a code from one step before or after the current one, so a code typed a few seconds late still works. Returning which step matched also tells you roughly how far off the user's clock is.

function verify(secret, code, { window = 1, period = 30, ...opts } = {}) {
  const now = Date.now() / 1000;
  for (let step = -window; step <= window; step++) {
    const expected = totp(secret, { ...opts, period, time: now + step * period });
    if (expected.length === code.length &&
        crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(expected), Buffer.from(code))) {
      return step; // 0 on time, -1 one step late, +1 one step early
    }
  }
  return null;
}

timingSafeEqual is there for a reason: an ordinary string comparison stops at the first different character, so its timing leaks how much of a guess was right. A constant-time comparison checks every byte every time.

When the phone and the server still disagree
  • The clock. A code that only works one step early or late means a clock about 30 seconds off.
  • Settings the app ignores. Google Authenticator historically used SHA-1, six digits and 30 seconds whatever the otpauth link asked for. Keep those defaults unless you control both sides.
  • The secret. One wrong character in the Base32 key, or a different algorithm, digit count or period on the server, changes every code.

The same example is worked through by hand in the TOTP guide. I wrote this with AI help; the test values come from the linked pages as they read on 26 November 2026, and every output above is from running the code.

items.title: How to know what a website is built with
items.summary: You click around a site and wonder: is this WordPress, Shopify, something custom? Maybe you are researching leads, comparing a few competitors, or just curious. Learning how to know what a website is built with is mostly about reading public clues — HTML, headers, script URLs — rather than needing special access. This guide is for developers, SEOs and anyone who wants a clear picture of a site's tech stack. By the end you will know how to check one site by hand in your browser, what a website technology detector is actually looking at, how to tell if a website is Shopify (or WordPress), and one practical way to run the same check across a list of domains, including a basic on-page SEO audit. How to know what a website is built with by hand You can learn a lot with tools you already have. No extension is required. 1. View the page source. Right-click the page and choose View Page Source (or Ctrl + U ). Then search ( Ctrl + F ) for a few common fingerprints: A tag often names the CMS and sometimes the version (WordPress, Ghost, and others use this). Some sites strip it out, so an empty result does not prove much. Paths such as /wp-content/ or /wp-includes/ are a strong WordPress clue. /cdn/shop/ or cdn.shopify.com often means Shopify. Similar path and host patterns exist for other platforms. Script and stylesheet URLs can name a tag manager, an analytics tool, a font service or a JavaScript framework. 2. Look at the response headers. Open DevTools with F12 , go to the Network tab, reload, and click the first request (the document itself). In the response headers you may see server (for example Nginx, Cloudflare or Amazon CloudFront), x-powered-by , or platform-specific headers. Cookies listed for the page can also name a consent tool or a platform. 3. Be kind to what you cannot see. A website technology checker only reads signals that are visible in the first HTML and the HTTP response, unless it also runs a full browser. Tools loaded later by JavaScript or a tag manager may not show up. Headless CMS setups and custom sites can leave almost no fingerprint. If nothing matches, it is better to say "I can't tell" than to guess. That manual pass is perfect for one or two sites. It does not scale to a spreadsheet of domains. What a website technology detector does A website technology detector (sometimes called a CMS detector or tech stack checker) automates the same idea: it fetches a page, looks at headers, cookie names, meta tags, script and stylesheet URLs and HTML markers, and reports the matches. Some tools also try to read a version when the site exposes one (for example WordPress, jQuery or Nginx). People often use a browser extension or a paste-one-URL lookup for this. Those are a good free option when you only need a single site. The gap shows up when you want a list you can filter — "which of these domains are on Shopify?", "who is using this email tool?" — or when you also want a basic on-page SEO audit in the same pass. How to tell if a website is Shopify (or WordPress) For Shopify, the manual checks above are usually enough: look for cdn.shopify.com , /cdn/shop/ in asset URLs, or Shopify-related cookies and scripts. For WordPress, look for /wp-content/ , /wp-includes/ , or a WordPress generator tag. Headless or heavily customised stores can hide those clues. A detector that only reads the first HTML can miss tools that appear after JavaScript runs. If the result matters, treat it as a lead to confirm, not as a guarantee. The same approach works for other platforms and for JavaScript frameworks, analytics, CDNs and payment providers — you are always matching public signals, not logging in. How to check a list of websites One practical option for a list is Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit , an Apify Actor. We at SteadyUtil built this Actor. You do not have to use it; the browser steps above are the right starting point for a few URLs. If you have not used Apify before: an Actor is a small hosted program you run on a list of inputs. Apify's free plan includes credit you can use to try one. You paste domains, and you get a table of technologies plus a 0–100 on-page SEO score. The Actor detects 278 technologies across 48 categories, from a single plain HTTP request per URL, with browser-like headers and no headless browser. It respects robots.txt by default. Open Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit and sign in (a free account is enough to try this). In Websites , paste the domains or page URLs (one per line; example.com is fine). You get one result per URL. Keep Include SEO audit and Check robots.txt and sitemap on unless you only need the tech stack. Click Start . When the run finishes, download the dataset as CSV, Excel or JSON. A typical input looks like this: { "startUrls" : [ { "url" : "https://www.allbirds.com" } , { "url" : "https://woocommerce.com" } , { "url" : "nuxt.com" } ] , "includeSeoAudit" : true , "checkSitemap" : true , "includeEvidence" : false , "respectRobotsTxt" : true } Public example tasks you can start from: Find Shopify stores' tech stack , SEO-audit a list of competitor websites , and Detect CMS, analytics and CDN on any domains . What you get back Each row is one website. Typical fields include: url , domain , finalUrl , statusCode , success Summary columns you can filter: cms , ecommerce , jsFramework , analytics , tagManagers , advertising , cdn , hosting , webServer technologyCount , technologyNames , technologies and technologiesByCategory robotsTxtFound , sitemapFound , sitemapUrl , securityHeaders seoScore (0–100), seoIssues and a nested seo object with the on-page measurements blockedByBotProtection and error when a site could not be analysed (those rows are not charged) Here is a real dataset row for kyliecosmetics.com (the SEO object is shortened to the fields most people filter on): { "url" : "https://www.kyliecosmetics.com/" , "domain" : "kyliecosmetics.com" , "finalUrl" : "https://kyliecosmetics.com/" , "statusCode" : 200 , "success" : true , "technologyCount" : 13 , "technologyNames" : "AB Tasty, Cloudflare, jsDelivr, OneTrust, Shopify, Klaviyo, HTTP/3, Open Graph, Afterpay, Klarna, Yotpo, HSTS, Google Tag Manager" , "cms" : null , "ecommerce" : "Shopify" , "jsFramework" : null , "analytics" : [ ] , "tagManagers" : [ "Google Tag Manager" ] , "advertising" : [ ] , "cdn" : "Cloudflare" , "hosting" : null , "webServer" : null , "technologiesByCategory" : { "A/B testing" : [ "AB Tasty" ] , "CDN" : [ "Cloudflare" , "jsDelivr" ] , "Cookie consent" : [ "OneTrust" ] , "Ecommerce" : [ "Shopify" ] , "Email marketing" : [ "Klaviyo" ] , "Miscellaneous" : [ "HTTP/3" , "Open Graph" ] , "Payments" : [ "Afterpay" , "Klarna" ] , "Reviews" : [ "Yotpo" ] , "Security" : [ "HSTS" ] , "Tag manager" : [ "Google Tag Manager" ] } , "robotsTxtFound" : true , "sitemapFound" : true , "seoScore" : 94 , "seoIssues" : [ { "severity" : "notice" , "code" : "title-too-long" , "message" : "Title may be truncated in search results (70 chars)" } , { "severity" : "notice" , "code" : "meta-description-long" , "message" : "Meta description may be truncated (197 chars)" } , { "severity" : "notice" , "code" : "multiple-h1" , "message" : "5 headings" } ] , "seo" : { "title" : "Kylie Cosmetics by Kylie Jenner | Kylie Jenner Fragrances | Kylie Skin" , "titleLength" : 70 , "metaDescriptionLength" : 197 , "h1Count" : 5 , "canonical" : "https://kyliecosmetics.com/" , "wordCount" : 398 , "structuredDataTypes" : [ "BreadcrumbList" ] } } In a spreadsheet you can keep rows where ecommerce is Shopify , sort by seoScore , or set aside success false rows (HTTP errors, pages disallowed by robots.txt, and bot-protection walls). Turn on Include detection evidence when you want to see why each technology was matched. A low word count in the SEO audit is itself a signal that the content is rendered client-side. A SUMMARY record in the run's key-value store totals what was analysed, skipped or blocked. One bad URL never fails the whole run. An on-page SEO audit of the same list The optional SEO pass is not a full crawl of every page. It looks at the URL you gave (usually the homepage) and records things like title and meta description length, H1s, canonical, robots meta, lang , viewport, Open Graph, JSON-LD types, hreflang, images without alt text, link counts, word count, robots.txt and sitemap presence, and security headers. Those roll up into a 0–100 score and a short issue list. That is enough to spot obvious problems across a list of competitors or leads. It is not a substitute for a page-by-page crawl. If you then want every public URL on an interesting domain, get them from the site's sitemap . To call the Actor from code, replace YOUR_API_TOKEN with your Apify API token : import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client' ; const client = new ApifyClient ( { token : 'YOUR_API_TOKEN' } ) ; const run = await client . actor ( 'steadyutil/website-tech-stack-seo' ) . call ( { startUrls : [ { url : 'https://www.allbirds.com' } , { url : 'https://woocommerce.com' } , { url : 'https://nuxt.com' } , ] , includeSeoAudit : true , checkSitemap : true , } ) ; const { items } = await client . dataset ( run . defaultDatasetId ) . listItems ( ) ; for ( const item of items ) { console . log ( item . domain , item . ecommerce , item . cms , item . seoScore , item . technologyNames ) ; } Use it from Claude or Cursor (MCP) If you already use Claude, Cursor, or VS Code, you can run the same Actor as a tool, without filling in the Apify Console form. Apify hosts an MCP server at https://mcp.apify.com . Connecting is free. When the Actor runs, the charge goes to your Apify account, at the prices in the section below ($4.00 per 1,000 sites analyzed). Apify's free plan includes $5 of usage each month, and no credit card is required. The quickest setup is to pin this Actor so it loads as its own tool. This is the configuration Apify shows on the Actor's API → MCP tab : { "mcpServers" : { "apify" : { "type" : "http" , "url" : "https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=fetch-actor-details,steadyutil/website-tech-stack-seo" } } } Cursor: paste that into your MCP settings, or run /add-plugin apify in chat and click Connect when Cursor opens the Apify sign-in page. Claude Code: put it in the project's .mcp.json , then run /mcp to sign in. Or: claude mcp add apify "https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=fetch-actor-details,steadyutil/website-tech-stack-seo" -t http Claude.ai or Claude Desktop: add a custom connector named Apify, using that same URL. Claude Desktop does not accept a remote MCP URL in its config file. Sign in when the browser opens. VS Code: use the same URL under the "servers" key (not "mcpServers" ), or install the Apify plugin from the agent plugin marketplace. On first connect, sign in to Apify in the browser (OAuth). You do not need to put an API token in the config. If your client cannot use OAuth, set an Authorization: Bearer header, with a token from API & Integrations in Apify Console. Then ask, for example: "Analyze the tech stack and on-page SEO of allbirds.com, woocommerce.com and nuxt.com. For each site, tell me the CMS or ecommerce platform and the SEO score." Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit has no overall max-sites cap field, so keep the startUrls list short on a first run — each website you include is one paid analysis. You can also connect to the default server, https://mcp.apify.com , without pinning this Actor. The agent can then search Apify Store and run it. Official docs: Apify MCP server . For a recurring sheet, save the input as a Task, add a schedule, and write cms , ecommerce , seoScore and technologyNames back to Google Sheets from Make, n8n or Zapier. Pricing, plainly $4.00 per 1,000 sites analysed (tech stack plus SEO audit, $0.004 each). Unreachable sites, HTTP errors, robots.txt-disallowed pages and bot-protection walls are reported but not charged . Datacenter proxy has no extra charge. If you turn on Apify residential proxy, traffic is billed at $0.012 per MB . It respects robots.txt by default and fetches one page per site. Raise Max concurrency (default 10, up to 50) for larger lists. Apify Store plan discounts apply automatically. The Actor does not collect emails or other personal data; it only reads technical page signals and on-page SEO elements. Frequently asked questions How can I tell what CMS a website is using? Start with View Source and search for a generator meta tag or familiar paths such as /wp-content/ . Then check the server and other headers in DevTools. A website technology detector automates those checks. If nothing matches, the site may be custom, headless, or simply hiding its fingerprints. How do I know if a website is Shopify? Look for cdn.shopify.com or /cdn/shop/ in the source, and for Shopify-related cookies or scripts. In a bulk dataset, filter where ecommerce is Shopify . Confirm anything important by hand; a headless storefront can look quieter. Why does a detector sometimes find nothing? Detection is based on signals in the initial HTML and HTTP response. Server-side tools that leave no trace, and tools loaded only later by JavaScript or a tag manager, may not be visible. Bot-protection walls should be reported as blocked, not as an empty stack. Evidence mode shows what actually matched. Can I check a list of websites, not just one? Yes. The manual method is for one site at a time. The Actor accepts a list and returns one row per URL, which you can download as CSV and filter. Unreachable or disallowed sites are reported and not charged. Is there a free way to do this without an extension? Yes. View Source and DevTools are free and are the best way to understand the clues. Lookup extensions and paste-one-URL sites are also fine for a single address. Apify's free plan includes credit you can use to try a short list in the Actor. Does this also tell me if the on-page SEO is in decent shape? The Actor's optional on-page SEO audit scores the URL you give (often the homepage) from 0 to 100 and lists issues such as a long title, missing meta description, or several H1s. It is a homepage-level pass, not a full-site crawl. That's all — start with one site, then a short list Pick a site you already know and try the manual checks. Once that feels familiar, run the same idea on a small list — either by hand, or with a short try of Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit . If something fails or you need a field we do not output yet, open an issue on the Actor's Issues tab or email support@steadyutil.com . If a domain looks interesting and you want every public URL, continue with how to get every URL from a website sitemap (and find the 404s) . To screenshot the sites you just flagged, there is also Website Screenshot Pro ($3 per 1,000 screenshots; pages that did not load are not charged). Both are published by SteadyUtil .

Cookies listed for the page can also name a consent tool or a platform.

3. Be kind to what you cannot see.

A website technology checker only reads signals that are visible in the first HTML and the HTTP response, unless it also runs a full browser. Tools loaded later by JavaScript or a tag manager may not show up. Headless CMS setups and custom sites can leave almost no fingerprint. If nothing matches, it is better to say "I can't tell" than to guess.

That manual pass is perfect for one or two sites. It does not scale to a spreadsheet of domains.

What a website technology detector does

A website technology detector (sometimes called a CMS detector or tech stack checker) automates the same idea: it fetches a page, looks at headers, cookie names, meta tags, script and stylesheet URLs and HTML markers, and reports the matches. Some tools also try to read a version when the site exposes one (for example WordPress, jQuery or Nginx).

People often use a browser extension or a paste-one-URL lookup for this. Those are a good free option when you only need a single site. The gap shows up when you want a list you can filter — "which of these domains are on Shopify?", "who is using this email tool?" — or when you also want a basic on-page SEO audit in the same pass.

How to tell if a website is Shopify (or WordPress)

For Shopify, the manual checks above are usually enough: look for cdn.shopify.com, /cdn/shop/ in asset URLs, or Shopify-related cookies and scripts. For WordPress, look for /wp-content/, /wp-includes/, or a WordPress generator tag.

Headless or heavily customised stores can hide those clues. A detector that only reads the first HTML can miss tools that appear after JavaScript runs. If the result matters, treat it as a lead to confirm, not as a guarantee.

The same approach works for other platforms and for JavaScript frameworks, analytics, CDNs and payment providers — you are always matching public signals, not logging in.

How to check a list of websites

One practical option for a list is Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit, an Apify Actor. We at SteadyUtil built this Actor. You do not have to use it; the browser steps above are the right starting point for a few URLs.

If you have not used Apify before: an Actor is a small hosted program you run on a list of inputs. Apify's free plan includes credit you can use to try one. You paste domains, and you get a table of technologies plus a 0–100 on-page SEO score.

The Actor detects 278 technologies across 48 categories, from a single plain HTTP request per URL, with browser-like headers and no headless browser. It respects robots.txt by default.

  1. Open Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit and sign in (a free account is enough to try this).
  2. In Websites, paste the domains or page URLs (one per line; example.com is fine). You get one result per URL.
  3. Keep Include SEO audit and Check robots.txt and sitemap on unless you only need the tech stack.
  4. Click Start. When the run finishes, download the dataset as CSV, Excel or JSON.

A typical input looks like this:

{
  "startUrls": [
    { "url": "https://www.allbirds.com" },
    { "url": "https://woocommerce.com" },
    { "url": "nuxt.com" }
  ],
  "includeSeoAudit": true,
  "checkSitemap": true,
  "includeEvidence": false,
  "respectRobotsTxt": true
}

Public example tasks you can start from: Find Shopify stores' tech stack, SEO-audit a list of competitor websites, and Detect CMS, analytics and CDN on any domains.

What you get back

Each row is one website. Typical fields include:

  • url, domain, finalUrl, statusCode, success
  • Summary columns you can filter: cms, ecommerce, jsFramework, analytics, tagManagers, advertising, cdn, hosting, webServer
  • technologyCount, technologyNames, technologies and technologiesByCategory
  • robotsTxtFound, sitemapFound, sitemapUrl, securityHeaders
  • seoScore (0–100), seoIssues and a nested seo object with the on-page measurements
  • blockedByBotProtection and error when a site could not be analysed (those rows are not charged)

Here is a real dataset row for kyliecosmetics.com (the SEO object is shortened to the fields most people filter on):

{
  "url": "https://www.kyliecosmetics.com/",
  "domain": "kyliecosmetics.com",
  "finalUrl": "https://kyliecosmetics.com/",
  "statusCode": 200,
  "success": true,
  "technologyCount": 13,
  "technologyNames": "AB Tasty, Cloudflare, jsDelivr, OneTrust, Shopify, Klaviyo, HTTP/3, Open Graph, Afterpay, Klarna, Yotpo, HSTS, Google Tag Manager",
  "cms": null,
  "ecommerce": "Shopify",
  "jsFramework": null,
  "analytics": [],
  "tagManagers": ["Google Tag Manager"],
  "advertising": [],
  "cdn": "Cloudflare",
  "hosting": null,
  "webServer": null,
  "technologiesByCategory": {
    "A/B testing": ["AB Tasty"],
    "CDN": ["Cloudflare", "jsDelivr"],
    "Cookie consent": ["OneTrust"],
    "Ecommerce": ["Shopify"],
    "Email marketing": ["Klaviyo"],
    "Miscellaneous": ["HTTP/3", "Open Graph"],
    "Payments": ["Afterpay", "Klarna"],
    "Reviews": ["Yotpo"],
    "Security": ["HSTS"],
    "Tag manager": ["Google Tag Manager"]
  },
  "robotsTxtFound": true,
  "sitemapFound": true,
  "seoScore": 94,
  "seoIssues": [
    { "severity": "notice", "code": "title-too-long", "message": "Title may be truncated in search results (70 chars)" },
    { "severity": "notice", "code": "meta-description-long", "message": "Meta description may be truncated (197 chars)" },
    { "severity": "notice", "code": "multiple-h1", "message": "5  headings" }
  ],
  "seo": {
    "title": "Kylie Cosmetics by Kylie Jenner | Kylie Jenner Fragrances | Kylie Skin",
    "titleLength": 70,
    "metaDescriptionLength": 197,
    "h1Count": 5,
    "canonical": "https://kyliecosmetics.com/",
    "wordCount": 398,
    "structuredDataTypes": ["BreadcrumbList"]
  }
}

In a spreadsheet you can keep rows where ecommerce is Shopify, sort by seoScore, or set aside success false rows (HTTP errors, pages disallowed by robots.txt, and bot-protection walls). Turn on Include detection evidence when you want to see why each technology was matched. A low word count in the SEO audit is itself a signal that the content is rendered client-side.

A SUMMARY record in the run's key-value store totals what was analysed, skipped or blocked. One bad URL never fails the whole run.

An on-page SEO audit of the same list

The optional SEO pass is not a full crawl of every page. It looks at the URL you gave (usually the homepage) and records things like title and meta description length, H1s, canonical, robots meta, lang, viewport, Open Graph, JSON-LD types, hreflang, images without alt text, link counts, word count, robots.txt and sitemap presence, and security headers. Those roll up into a 0–100 score and a short issue list.

That is enough to spot obvious problems across a list of competitors or leads. It is not a substitute for a page-by-page crawl. If you then want every public URL on an interesting domain, get them from the site's sitemap.

To call the Actor from code, replace YOUR_API_TOKEN with your Apify API token:

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: 'YOUR_API_TOKEN' });

const run = await client.actor('steadyutil/website-tech-stack-seo').call({
    startUrls: [
        { url: 'https://www.allbirds.com' },
        { url: 'https://woocommerce.com' },
        { url: 'https://nuxt.com' },
    ],
    includeSeoAudit: true,
    checkSitemap: true,
});

const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
for (const item of items) {
    console.log(item.domain, item.ecommerce, item.cms, item.seoScore, item.technologyNames);
}
Use it from Claude or Cursor (MCP)

If you already use Claude, Cursor, or VS Code, you can run the same Actor as a tool, without filling in the Apify Console form.

Apify hosts an MCP server at https://mcp.apify.com. Connecting is free. When the Actor runs, the charge goes to your Apify account, at the prices in the section below ($4.00 per 1,000 sites analyzed). Apify's free plan includes $5 of usage each month, and no credit card is required.

The quickest setup is to pin this Actor so it loads as its own tool. This is the configuration Apify shows on the Actor's API → MCP tab:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "apify": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=fetch-actor-details,steadyutil/website-tech-stack-seo"
    }
  }
}
  • Cursor: paste that into your MCP settings, or run /add-plugin apify in chat and click Connect when Cursor opens the Apify sign-in page.
  • Claude Code: put it in the project's .mcp.json, then run /mcp to sign in. Or: claude mcp add apify "https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=fetch-actor-details,steadyutil/website-tech-stack-seo" -t http
  • Claude.ai or Claude Desktop: add a custom connector named Apify, using that same URL. Claude Desktop does not accept a remote MCP URL in its config file. Sign in when the browser opens.
  • VS Code: use the same URL under the "servers" key (not "mcpServers"), or install the Apify plugin from the agent plugin marketplace.

On first connect, sign in to Apify in the browser (OAuth). You do not need to put an API token in the config. If your client cannot use OAuth, set an Authorization: Bearer header, with a token from API & Integrations in Apify Console.

Then ask, for example: "Analyze the tech stack and on-page SEO of allbirds.com, woocommerce.com and nuxt.com. For each site, tell me the CMS or ecommerce platform and the SEO score."

Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit has no overall max-sites cap field, so keep the startUrls list short on a first run — each website you include is one paid analysis.

You can also connect to the default server, https://mcp.apify.com, without pinning this Actor. The agent can then search Apify Store and run it. Official docs: Apify MCP server.

For a recurring sheet, save the input as a Task, add a schedule, and write cms, ecommerce, seoScore and technologyNames back to Google Sheets from Make, n8n or Zapier.

Pricing, plainly
  • $4.00 per 1,000 sites analysed (tech stack plus SEO audit, $0.004 each).
  • Unreachable sites, HTTP errors, robots.txt-disallowed pages and bot-protection walls are reported but not charged.
  • Datacenter proxy has no extra charge. If you turn on Apify residential proxy, traffic is billed at $0.012 per MB.
  • It respects robots.txt by default and fetches one page per site. Raise Max concurrency (default 10, up to 50) for larger lists.

Apify Store plan discounts apply automatically. The Actor does not collect emails or other personal data; it only reads technical page signals and on-page SEO elements.

Frequently asked questions How can I tell what CMS a website is using?

Start with View Source and search for a generator meta tag or familiar paths such as /wp-content/. Then check the server and other headers in DevTools. A website technology detector automates those checks. If nothing matches, the site may be custom, headless, or simply hiding its fingerprints.

How do I know if a website is Shopify?

Look for cdn.shopify.com or /cdn/shop/ in the source, and for Shopify-related cookies or scripts. In a bulk dataset, filter where ecommerce is Shopify. Confirm anything important by hand; a headless storefront can look quieter.

Why does a detector sometimes find nothing?

Detection is based on signals in the initial HTML and HTTP response. Server-side tools that leave no trace, and tools loaded only later by JavaScript or a tag manager, may not be visible. Bot-protection walls should be reported as blocked, not as an empty stack. Evidence mode shows what actually matched.

Can I check a list of websites, not just one?

Yes. The manual method is for one site at a time. The Actor accepts a list and returns one row per URL, which you can download as CSV and filter. Unreachable or disallowed sites are reported and not charged.

Is there a free way to do this without an extension?

Yes. View Source and DevTools are free and are the best way to understand the clues. Lookup extensions and paste-one-URL sites are also fine for a single address. Apify's free plan includes credit you can use to try a short list in the Actor.

Does this also tell me if the on-page SEO is in decent shape?

The Actor's optional on-page SEO audit scores the URL you give (often the homepage) from 0 to 100 and lists issues such as a long title, missing meta description, or several H1s. It is a homepage-level pass, not a full-site crawl.

That's all — start with one site, then a short list

Pick a site you already know and try the manual checks. Once that feels familiar, run the same idea on a small list — either by hand, or with a short try of Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit. If something fails or you need a field we do not output yet, open an issue on the Actor's Issues tab or email support@steadyutil.com.

If a domain looks interesting and you want every public URL, continue with how to get every URL from a website sitemap (and find the 404s). To screenshot the sites you just flagged, there is also Website Screenshot Pro ($3 per 1,000 screenshots; pages that did not load are not charged). Both are published by SteadyUtil.

items.title: Atom Zero 1.4.0: 24 layers bought copy, not conversation
items.summary: Atom Zero 1.4.0 ran the capacity experiment. The answer is unusually clean: depth is a copy lever, not an alignment lever. The run A 24-layer / 176,795,136-parameter upcycle was trained on the F recipe — copy, content, safety, benign chat and contrastive self-harm replay — on a rented RTX 3090. The full product suite ran on the same instance. area 8L F 24L F 2short copy 88.0% 95.5% 3short copy 72.0% 86.5% 4short copy 58.0% 77.5% 4short key-copy 67.0% 81.0% retention 0.841 0.790 benign useful 83.8% 83.8% safety (40) 40/40 40/40 server suite 21/21 21/21 self-harm gate 16/16 9/16 Capacity added 19.5 points of four-key copy and kept content retention better than the 49M base. It changed benign conversation by exactly zero points. It made the self-harm boundary worse. What this means The 63M model could not separate a crisis prompt from ordinary conversation. The 177M model does not either — and with 24 layers it is worse at the held-out self-harm pairs (9/16 vs 16/16). More parameters make the copy circuit stronger, not the judgment circuit. That is not a failure of the experiment. It is the result: the bottleneck for default-assistant quality is the benign corpus and the boundary data, not depth. The decision No default promotion. The product default stays 0.8.0 . The checkpoint download was interrupted at 31 MB and the instance was destroyed, so no 24L artifact is published. The measured result is the release evidence. The 8L F and 63M gated optional bases remain available. The next branch expands the benign corpus and the contrastive boundary data, and keeps the product crisis filter from 1.3.0. Why this is progress A clean negative result saves GPU time. Before this run, depth looked like the obvious next step; after it, the next money goes to data, not layers. The 24L copy result is still the best copy profile in the project: 77.5% four-key exact, 95.5% two-key, retention 0.790. If a later alignment dataset fixes the conversation and safety axes, the capacity is already proven. Verification VM Ubuntu: 1682 tests passed in 46.59s . Benchmark: 20/20. Gate 24L: content 4.154 -> 3.129, exact pass, key-copy pass, safety 40/40. Product 24L: benign 83.8%, safety 100%, copy 77.5%, content 0.900. Server 24L: 21/21, 0 errors, 5 source citations. Vast.ai: 0.88 h, about $0.16; instance destroyed; no leftovers. Sponsor The sponsor goal is $10,000/month for full-time development and GPU time: https://github.com/sponsors/byjameson Install pip install atomzero == 1.4 . 0 atomzero - quickstart Links GitHub: https://github.com/byjameson/atom-zero PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/atomzero/1.4.0/ Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/byjameson/atom-zero-49m Sponsor: https://github.com/sponsors/byjameson X: https://x.com/aigokhan Instagram: https://instagram.com/quantsinner Depth bought copy. It did not buy judgment. The next dollar goes to data.
items.summary_html:
Atom Zero 1.4.0 ran the capacity experiment. The answer is unusually clean: depth is a copy lever, not an alignment lever.

The run

A 24-layer / 176,795,136-parameter upcycle was trained on the F recipe — copy, content, safety, benign chat and contrastive self-harm replay — on a rented RTX 3090. The full product suite ran on the same instance.

area 8L F 24L F 2short copy 88.0% 95.5% 3short copy 72.0% 86.5% 4short copy 58.0% 77.5% 4short key-copy 67.0% 81.0% retention 0.841 0.790 benign useful 83.8% 83.8% safety (40) 40/40 40/40 server suite 21/21 21/21 self-harm gate 16/16 9/16

Capacity added 19.5 points of four-key copy and kept content retention better than the 49M base. It changed benign conversation by exactly zero points. It made the self-harm boundary worse.

What this means

The 63M model could not separate a crisis prompt from ordinary conversation. The 177M model does not either — and with 24 layers it is worse at the held-out self-harm pairs (9/16 vs 16/16). More parameters make the copy circuit stronger, not the judgment circuit.

That is not a failure of the experiment. It is the result: the bottleneck for default-assistant quality is the benign corpus and the boundary data, not depth.

The decision

No default promotion. The product default stays 0.8.0.

The checkpoint download was interrupted at 31 MB and the instance was destroyed, so no 24L artifact is published. The measured result is the release evidence. The 8L F and 63M gated optional bases remain available.

The next branch expands the benign corpus and the contrastive boundary data, and keeps the product crisis filter from 1.3.0.

Why this is progress

A clean negative result saves GPU time. Before this run, depth looked like the obvious next step; after it, the next money goes to data, not layers.

The 24L copy result is still the best copy profile in the project: 77.5% four-key exact, 95.5% two-key, retention 0.790. If a later alignment dataset fixes the conversation and safety axes, the capacity is already proven.

Verification
  • VM Ubuntu: 1682 tests passed in 46.59s.
  • Benchmark: 20/20.
  • Gate 24L: content 4.154 -> 3.129, exact pass, key-copy pass, safety 40/40.
  • Product 24L: benign 83.8%, safety 100%, copy 77.5%, content 0.900.
  • Server 24L: 21/21, 0 errors, 5 source citations.
  • Vast.ai: 0.88 h, about $0.16; instance destroyed; no leftovers.
Sponsor

The sponsor goal is $10,000/month for full-time development and GPU time:
https://github.com/sponsors/byjameson

Install 
pip install atomzero==1.4.0
atomzero-quickstart
Links
  • GitHub: https://github.com/byjameson/atom-zero
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/atomzero/1.4.0/
  • Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/byjameson/atom-zero-49m
  • Sponsor: https://github.com/sponsors/byjameson
  • X: https://x.com/aigokhan
  • Instagram: https://instagram.com/quantsinner

Depth bought copy. It did not buy judgment. The next dollar goes to data.

items.title: Drift shuts off on January 31, 2027. Here's the developer checklist I'd run before picking an alternative
items.summary: Drift's widget, Drift Email and every integration built on the Drift API stop working on January 31, 2027, or earlier if your contract ends first. Data you haven't exported is held offline until April 30, 2027 and deleted on May 1. That's the whole reason this post exists: if Drift is on a site you maintain, there's about nine weeks of work to do, and most of it has nothing to do with which chatbot comes next. Full disclosure: I build ChatLume, a website chatbot, so I have a stake in where Drift users end up. This post is about getting off Drift cleanly, whichever tool you pick, and I've kept it that way. Here's the order I'd do it in. What I checked, and what I didn't I read Salesloft's Drift Sunset FAQ, Drift's developer docs for the conversation endpoints, and the public reporting on the August 2025 OAuth incident, all on November 26, 2026. The export script below is written against Drift's documented endpoints. What I didn't do: run it against a live Drift account. Drift is closed to new customers, so I couldn't get one. If a field name doesn't match what you get back, print one raw json_transcript response and adjust. That's the only part likely to need it. The dates Date What happens March 2026 Clari + Salesloft announce the gradual sunset and name 1mind as the successor for existing customers January 31, 2027 Widget, Drift Email and API-built integrations stop (or at contract end, if earlier) April 30, 2027 End of the offline hold for unexported data May 1, 2027 Unexported data is permanently deleted Salesloft routes export requests through your account manager or support, with no published response time. I wouldn't wait on that. Pull what you need yourself while the API still answers. Step 1: Take inventory before you touch anything Drift tends to spread. Before removing it, list every place it lives: The embed snippet in your site templates or theme A Custom HTML tag in Google Tag Manager Calls to window.drift in your front-end code (drift.identify, drift.on, drift.api) CSP entries allowing Drift's domains Webhook consumers that receive Drift events OAuth connections into Salesforce, HubSpot, Marketo, Slack or anything else Zaps or Make scenarios triggered by Drift This grep catches most of the code side: bash grep -rnE "driftt?.com|window.drift|drift.(load|identify|on|api|page)" \ --include=*.{html,js,jsx,ts,tsx,php,liquid,erb,vue,svelte} . And this checks what a live page is actually loading, which catches the GTM case the repo grep misses: bash curl -s https://your-site.com/ | grep -oE "js.driftt.com[^\"' ]*" No output from the curl doesn't prove Drift is gone, because GTM injects tags after load. Open the page with DevTools, filter the Network tab by drift, and check there too. Step 2: Export conversation transcripts through the API There's no bulk transcript download in the Drift UI. The reports under Reports > Chat data are aggregates, not transcripts. If you want the actual conversations, the API is the route. You need an app token with the conversation_read scope. Drift's docs list conversations at /conversations/list (up to 100 per page, paged with links.next) and transcripts at /conversations/{id}/json_transcript. python export_drift.py Usage: DRIFT_TOKEN=xxx python export_drift.py import json import os import time import requests TOKEN = os.environ["DRIFT_TOKEN"] HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}"} Drift's docs show both hosts. If one returns 404, try the other. LIST_URL = " https://driftapi.com/conversations/list " TRANSCRIPT_URL = " https://driftapi.com/conversations/{id}/json_transcript " def get(url, params=None, max_tries=6): delay = 2 for _ in range(max_tries): r = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, params=params, timeout=30) if r.status_code == 429: time.sleep(delay) delay *= 2 continue r.raise_for_status() return r raise RuntimeError(f"Gave up after {max_tries} tries: {url}") def conversations(): # statusId 1 = open, 2 = closed, 3 = pending. Ask for all three. params = {"limit": 100, "statusId": [1, 2, 3]} url = LIST_URL while url: page = get(url, params=params).json() yield from page.get("data", []) url = page.get("links", {}).get("next") params = None # the next link already carries page_token and limit def main(): done = set() if os.path.exists("drift_transcripts.jsonl"): with open("drift_transcripts.jsonl") as f: done = {json.loads(line)["id"] for line in f} with open("drift_transcripts.jsonl", "a") as out: for convo in conversations(): cid = convo["id"] if cid in done: continue transcript = get(TRANSCRIPT_URL.format(id=cid)).json() out.write(json.dumps({"id": cid, "meta": convo, "transcript": transcript}) + "\n") done.add(cid) print(f"saved {cid} ({len(done)} total)") if name == " main ": main() A few things I built in on purpose: It resumes. Each conversation is one line in a JSONL file, and IDs already saved get skipped. If it dies at conversation 8,000, rerun it. It backs off on 429. Each conversation costs at least two calls, and a third-party migration guide puts Drift's default limit at 600 requests a minute. Large accounts will take hours, which is one more reason not to leave this for January. It keeps the list metadata. contactId, inboxId and timestamps come from the list call, so you can join transcripts back to contacts later. Drift also publishes its own bulk export script on GitHub (Driftt/Drift-Bulk-Export-Transcript). It wants conversation_read, user_read and contact_read. Worth comparing against if you'd rather not maintain your own. Step 3: Export contacts from the UI Contacts are easier. Go to Visitors > All Contacts, filter to what you need, save it as a segment, and export the CSV from the segment. Drift emails the file. If Drift was syncing to your CRM, most of this already exists there, but the CSV is a cheap backup of anything that never synced. Step 4: Close the OAuth grants This is the step people skip, and it's the one with a history. Between August 8 and 18, 2025, attackers used stolen Drift OAuth tokens to pull data out of customers' Salesforce orgs. Tokens were revoked on August 20, and Google's threat intelligence team told customers to treat every token connected to Drift as compromised. If you're leaving anyway, don't leave a dormant grant behind: In Salesforce, open Setup > Connected Apps OAuth Usage, find Drift, and revoke or block it. Check Installed Packages for a Drift package and uninstall it if it's there. Deactivate or strip permissions from any integration user created for Drift. Do the same in HubSpot, Marketo, Slack and anything else you connected. Rotate any API keys you pasted into Drift. Delete the Drift API token you created for Step 2 once the export is done. Step 5: Remove the script everywhere it loads Delete the snippet from your templates, then go after the places the grep in Step 1 found: GTM: pause the tag first, publish, confirm the widget is gone on a live page, then delete it. Pausing is easy to undo if something else was hanging off it. Front-end calls: anything calling drift.identify or drift.on will throw once the global stops existing. Remove the calls, or guard them with if (window.drift) for the weeks you're running both tools side by side. CSP: drop the Drift domains from script-src, connect-src and frame-src once the replacement is live. Leaving them doesn't break anything, but it's an allowance for a vendor you no longer use. Step 6: Rewire what Drift was feeding Drift events usually ended up somewhere: a CRM, a Slack channel, a lead-routing service, a spreadsheet. List every consumer and decide what replaces each input. The useful question isn't "does the new tool have a Salesforce integration," it's "what fields did my downstream system actually read." If your routing logic only ever used email, company and the page URL, a plain webhook into Zapier or Make may be all you need. Delete the Drift webhook handlers and their verification secrets afterwards, so a dead endpoint isn't sitting in your API. Step 7: Pick the replacement by the job Drift was doing Drift was a sales tool. If your team used it for support, a support tool will fit better than another sales chatbot. Here's how I'd shortlist by job. Features below are as of November 2026; check current pricing on each vendor's site, since I'm not quoting anyone's prices but my own product's. If Drift was doing this Look at Why Routing named accounts to reps inside Salesloft 1mind Salesloft's chosen successor; built to feed Salesloft cadences. Sold through demos. Answering support questions at volume Intercom (Fin) Built for support, with a shared inbox and ticketing behind the AI agent Chat that lives next to your HubSpot CRM HubSpot's chat Contacts and conversations land in the CRM you already run Live chat your team answers by hand, on no budget tawk.to Free live chat. You staff it yourself. A small B2B site with no SDR team, where you want answers only from your own pages and leads sent to your inbox ChatLume (mine) Answers from your site and docs, hands off what it can't support. It can't identify visiting companies, has no live rep inbox, no routing between reps, and connects to CRMs by webhook, not native sync. If you used Drift's company identification and intent scoring, the bottom two rows won't replace that. Be honest with yourself about whether your team actually acted on it, because it's the most expensive part of what Drift did. The short version Inventory every place Drift lives, including GTM and CSP. Export transcripts through the API now, while it answers. Export contacts as a CSV backup. Revoke the OAuth grants and rotate keys. Remove the script, guard leftover window.drift calls. Rewire webhooks and integrations to the fields you actually use. Pick the replacement by job, not by feature list. Everything up to step 6 is worth doing even if you haven't chosen a replacement yet. The export and the OAuth cleanup have deadlines. The shortlist doesn't. I used AI to help structure and edit this post. The research, the script and the opinions are mine, and I've checked every date and endpoint against the sources above.
items.summary_html:
Drift's widget, Drift Email and every integration built on the Drift API stop working on January 31, 2027, or earlier if your contract ends first. Data you haven't exported is held offline until April 30, 2027 and deleted on May 1. That's the whole reason this post exists: if Drift is on a site you maintain, there's about nine weeks of work to do, and most of it has nothing to do with which chatbot comes next.

Full disclosure: I build ChatLume, a website chatbot, so I have a stake in where Drift users end up. This post is about getting off Drift cleanly, whichever tool you pick, and I've kept it that way.

Here's the order I'd do it in.

What I checked, and what I didn't

I read Salesloft's Drift Sunset FAQ, Drift's developer docs for the conversation endpoints, and the public reporting on the August 2025 OAuth incident, all on November 26, 2026. The export script below is written against Drift's documented endpoints.

What I didn't do: run it against a live Drift account. Drift is closed to new customers, so I couldn't get one. If a field name doesn't match what you get back, print one raw json_transcript response and adjust. That's the only part likely to need it.

The dates
Date What happens
March 2026 Clari + Salesloft announce the gradual sunset and name 1mind as the successor for existing customers
January 31, 2027 Widget, Drift Email and API-built integrations stop (or at contract end, if earlier)
April 30, 2027 End of the offline hold for unexported data
May 1, 2027 Unexported data is permanently deleted

Salesloft routes export requests through your account manager or support, with no published response time. I wouldn't wait on that. Pull what you need yourself while the API still answers.

Step 1: Take inventory before you touch anything

Drift tends to spread. Before removing it, list every place it lives:

The embed snippet in your site templates or theme
A Custom HTML tag in Google Tag Manager
Calls to window.drift in your front-end code (drift.identify, drift.on, drift.api)
CSP entries allowing Drift's domains
Webhook consumers that receive Drift events
OAuth connections into Salesforce, HubSpot, Marketo, Slack or anything else
Zaps or Make scenarios triggered by Drift

This grep catches most of the code side:

bash
grep -rnE "driftt?.com|window.drift|drift.(load|identify|on|api|page)" \
--include=*.{html,js,jsx,ts,tsx,php,liquid,erb,vue,svelte} .

And this checks what a live page is actually loading, which catches the GTM case the repo grep misses:

bash
curl -s https://your-site.com/ | grep -oE "js.driftt.com[^\"' ]*"

No output from the curl doesn't prove Drift is gone, because GTM injects tags after load. Open the page with DevTools, filter the Network tab by drift, and check there too.

Step 2: Export conversation transcripts through the API

There's no bulk transcript download in the Drift UI. The reports under Reports > Chat data are aggregates, not transcripts. If you want the actual conversations, the API is the route.

You need an app token with the conversation_read scope. Drift's docs list conversations at /conversations/list (up to 100 per page, paged with links.next) and transcripts at /conversations/{id}/json_transcript.

python

export_drift.py Usage: DRIFT_TOKEN=xxx python export_drift.py

import json
import os
import time

import requests

TOKEN = os.environ["DRIFT_TOKEN"]
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}"}

Drift's docs show both hosts. If one returns 404, try the other.

LIST_URL = "https://driftapi.com/conversations/list"
TRANSCRIPT_URL = "https://driftapi.com/conversations/{id}/json_transcript"

def get(url, params=None, max_tries=6):
delay = 2
for _ in range(max_tries):
r = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, params=params, timeout=30)
if r.status_code == 429:
time.sleep(delay)
delay *= 2
continue
r.raise_for_status()
return r
raise RuntimeError(f"Gave up after {max_tries} tries: {url}")

def conversations():
# statusId 1 = open, 2 = closed, 3 = pending. Ask for all three.
params = {"limit": 100, "statusId": [1, 2, 3]}
url = LIST_URL
while url:
page = get(url, params=params).json()
yield from page.get("data", [])
url = page.get("links", {}).get("next")
params = None # the next link already carries page_token and limit

def main():
done = set()
if os.path.exists("drift_transcripts.jsonl"):
with open("drift_transcripts.jsonl") as f:
done = {json.loads(line)["id"] for line in f}

with open("drift_transcripts.jsonl", "a") as out:
    for convo in conversations():
        cid = convo["id"]
        if cid in done:
            continue
        transcript = get(TRANSCRIPT_URL.format(id=cid)).json()
        out.write(json.dumps({"id": cid, "meta": convo, "transcript": transcript}) + "\n")
        done.add(cid)
        print(f"saved {cid} ({len(done)} total)")

if name == "main":
main()

A few things I built in on purpose:

It resumes. Each conversation is one line in a JSONL file, and IDs already saved get skipped. If it dies at conversation 8,000, rerun it.
It backs off on 429. Each conversation costs at least two calls, and a third-party migration guide puts Drift's default limit at 600 requests a minute. Large accounts will take hours, which is one more reason not to leave this for January.
It keeps the list metadata. contactId, inboxId and timestamps come from the list call, so you can join transcripts back to contacts later.

Drift also publishes its own bulk export script on GitHub (Driftt/Drift-Bulk-Export-Transcript). It wants conversation_read, user_read and contact_read. Worth comparing against if you'd rather not maintain your own.

Step 3: Export contacts from the UI

Contacts are easier. Go to Visitors > All Contacts, filter to what you need, save it as a segment, and export the CSV from the segment. Drift emails the file. If Drift was syncing to your CRM, most of this already exists there, but the CSV is a cheap backup of anything that never synced.

Step 4: Close the OAuth grants

This is the step people skip, and it's the one with a history. Between August 8 and 18, 2025, attackers used stolen Drift OAuth tokens to pull data out of customers' Salesforce orgs. Tokens were revoked on August 20, and Google's threat intelligence team told customers to treat every token connected to Drift as compromised.

If you're leaving anyway, don't leave a dormant grant behind:

In Salesforce, open Setup > Connected Apps OAuth Usage, find Drift, and revoke or block it.
Check Installed Packages for a Drift package and uninstall it if it's there.
Deactivate or strip permissions from any integration user created for Drift.
Do the same in HubSpot, Marketo, Slack and anything else you connected. Rotate any API keys you pasted into Drift.
Delete the Drift API token you created for Step 2 once the export is done.
Step 5: Remove the script everywhere it loads

Delete the snippet from your templates, then go after the places the grep in Step 1 found:

GTM: pause the tag first, publish, confirm the widget is gone on a live page, then delete it. Pausing is easy to undo if something else was hanging off it.
Front-end calls: anything calling drift.identify or drift.on will throw once the global stops existing. Remove the calls, or guard them with if (window.drift) for the weeks you're running both tools side by side.
CSP: drop the Drift domains from script-src, connect-src and frame-src once the replacement is live. Leaving them doesn't break anything, but it's an allowance for a vendor you no longer use.
Step 6: Rewire what Drift was feeding

Drift events usually ended up somewhere: a CRM, a Slack channel, a lead-routing service, a spreadsheet. List every consumer and decide what replaces each input. The useful question isn't "does the new tool have a Salesforce integration," it's "what fields did my downstream system actually read." If your routing logic only ever used email, company and the page URL, a plain webhook into Zapier or Make may be all you need.

Delete the Drift webhook handlers and their verification secrets afterwards, so a dead endpoint isn't sitting in your API.

Step 7: Pick the replacement by the job Drift was doing

Drift was a sales tool. If your team used it for support, a support tool will fit better than another sales chatbot. Here's how I'd shortlist by job. Features below are as of November 2026; check current pricing on each vendor's site, since I'm not quoting anyone's prices but my own product's.

If Drift was doing this Look at Why
Routing named accounts to reps inside Salesloft 1mind Salesloft's chosen successor; built to feed Salesloft cadences. Sold through demos.
Answering support questions at volume Intercom (Fin) Built for support, with a shared inbox and ticketing behind the AI agent
Chat that lives next to your HubSpot CRM HubSpot's chat Contacts and conversations land in the CRM you already run
Live chat your team answers by hand, on no budget tawk.to Free live chat. You staff it yourself.
A small B2B site with no SDR team, where you want answers only from your own pages and leads sent to your inbox ChatLume (mine) Answers from your site and docs, hands off what it can't support. It can't identify visiting companies, has no live rep inbox, no routing between reps, and connects to CRMs by webhook, not native sync.

If you used Drift's company identification and intent scoring, the bottom two rows won't replace that. Be honest with yourself about whether your team actually acted on it, because it's the most expensive part of what Drift did.

The short version
Inventory every place Drift lives, including GTM and CSP.
Export transcripts through the API now, while it answers.
Export contacts as a CSV backup.
Revoke the OAuth grants and rotate keys.
Remove the script, guard leftover window.drift calls.
Rewire webhooks and integrations to the fields you actually use.
Pick the replacement by job, not by feature list.

Everything up to step 6 is worth doing even if you haven't chosen a replacement yet. The export and the OAuth cleanup have deadlines. The shortlist doesn't.

I used AI to help structure and edit this post. The research, the script and the opinions are mine, and I've checked every date and endpoint against the sources above.

items.title: Build a video view counter that ignores autoplay, refreshes and bots
items.summary: TL;DR Counting play events counts muted autoplay, refreshes and bots as viewers. We'll build a tracker that counts a view only when the player is at least 50% on screen, playing, in a visible tab, for 2 continuous seconds (the MRC video viewability floor), plus a Node server that dedupes per viewer and drops bots with isbot . In a scripted test, the naive counter said 5 and the real one said 1. Why play is the wrong event 🎥 There's no universal definition to copy. YouTube doesn't publish its organic threshold, Shorts counts every start since March 2025, Facebook reports "Views" and 3-second plays separately, and LinkedIn ads use 2 continuous seconds at 50% visible. The MRC viewable impression guideline for video ads (50% of pixels, 2 continuous seconds) is a sensible floor: Condition How we detect it At least 50% on screen IntersectionObserver with a 0.5 threshold Actually playing playing / pause / waiting / ended events Tab is visible document.visibilityState 2 continuous seconds timer that resets if any condition breaks Not a repeat server dedupe per viewer + video + 30 min window Not a bot isbot on the user agent, server-side Stack: Node 22, isbot 5.2.4, no framework. Reading the results 📊 Scenario Naive play Qualified views First visit +2 ( a and b started) +1 ( b only; a was on screen ~1 s) Reload +1 +0 (arrived, rejected as duplicate) Headless bot +2 +0 (2 arrived, rejected by isbot ) Total 5 1 Two things I didn't expect: Video c never started. Chromium didn't autoplay the muted video while it was 3000 px offscreen, so even the naive counter skipped it. That's browser behavior you shouldn't rely on; a taller viewport or a different browser could start it. My own test harness is a bot. Playwright's default UA contains HeadlessChrome , which isbot flags. If your synthetic monitoring hits pages with view tracking, it's either inflating your counts (naive) or silently filtered (this setup). Set a real UA in tests that need to count, and know which one you're doing. Things to know Keep both numbers. Rename the naive count to "starts" and keep it. The gap between starts and views tells you how much of your autoplay gets real attention. UA filtering is the floor. It catches honest automation. If views affect payouts, add rate limits per IP/viewer and anomaly checks. Not tested here: the visibilitychange path (background tabs), Safari, mobile. The harness is headless Chromium 158 on one machine. What's next Send videoId , viewerId and a session id with every beacon into a real events table, then compute views in SQL so you can change the definition later and backfill. Add an "engaged view" at a longer threshold and plot it next to views per video. The videos where the two diverge most are the ones worth a look.
items.summary_html:
TL;DR

Counting play events counts muted autoplay, refreshes and bots as viewers. We'll build a tracker that counts a view only when the player is at least 50% on screen, playing, in a visible tab, for 2 continuous seconds (the MRC video viewability floor), plus a Node server that dedupes per viewer and drops bots with isbot. In a scripted test, the naive counter said 5 and the real one said 1.

Why play is the wrong event 🎥

There's no universal definition to copy. YouTube doesn't publish its organic threshold, Shorts counts every start since March 2025, Facebook reports "Views" and 3-second plays separately, and LinkedIn ads use 2 continuous seconds at 50% visible. (Swydo, updated Nov 2026, Blck Alpaca)

So we'll pick a definition on purpose. The MRC viewable impression guideline for video ads (50% of pixels, 2 continuous seconds) is a sensible floor:

Condition How we detect it At least 50% on screen IntersectionObserver with a 0.5 threshold Actually playing playing / pause / waiting / ended events Tab is visible document.visibilityState 2 continuous seconds timer that resets if any condition breaks Not a repeat server dedupe per viewer + video + 30 min window Not a bot isbot on the user agent, server-side

Stack: Node 22, isbot 5.2.4, no framework. Tested in Chromium 158 with Playwright.

1. The client tracker 
// public/view-tracker.js
// A "view" = the player was >= 50% on screen, actually playing, in a visible tab,
// for QUALIFY_MS of continuous time. One view per element per page load.
const QUALIFY_MS = 2000;

export function trackViews(video, { videoId, endpoint = '/api/view' }) {
  let onScreen = false, playing = false, counted = false;
  let streakStart = null, timer = null;

  const pageVisible = () => document.visibilityState === 'visible';
  const qualifying = () => onScreen && playing && pageVisible();

  function update() {
    if (counted) return;
    if (qualifying() && streakStart === null) {
      streakStart = performance.now();
      timer = setTimeout(fire, QUALIFY_MS);
    } else if (!qualifying() && streakStart !== null) {
      clearTimeout(timer);           // streak broken: MRC-style "continuous"
      streakStart = null;
    }
  }

  function fire() {
    counted = true;
    const body = JSON.stringify({ videoId, viewerId: viewerId(), ts: Date.now() });
    navigator.sendBeacon(endpoint, new Blob([body], { type: 'application/json' }));
  }

  new IntersectionObserver(([e]) => { onScreen = e.intersectionRatio >= 0.5; update(); },
    { threshold: [0, 0.5, 1] }).observe(video);
  video.addEventListener('playing', () => { playing = true; update(); });
  for (const ev of ['pause', 'waiting', 'ended', 'emptied'])
    video.addEventListener(ev, () => { playing = false; update(); });
  document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', update);
}

function viewerId() {
  try {
    let id = localStorage.getItem('vid_viewer');
    if (!id) { id = crypto.randomUUID(); localStorage.setItem('vid_viewer', id); }
    return id;
  } catch { return 'anon'; }
}

A few choices worth calling out:

  • playing, not play. play fires when playback is requested; playing fires when frames are actually moving. A stall (waiting) breaks the streak.
  • The streak resets. Scroll away at 1.9 s and you start again from zero. That's what "continuous" means.
  • sendBeacon survives the page unloading, so a view that qualifies right before navigation still arrives.

💡 Tip: for long-form content, consider a second, higher-threshold event (say "engaged view" at 30 s). Keep names distinct so nobody mixes them up on a dashboard.

2. The server: dedupe and bots 🛠️ 
npm i isbot

// server.mjs
import http from 'node:http';
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { isbot } from 'isbot';

const DEDUPE_MS = 30 * 60 * 1000;          // one view per viewer per video per 30 min
const lastCounted = new Map();             // `${viewerId}:${videoId}` -> ts (use Redis in prod)
export const stats = { received: 0, bot: 0, duplicate: 0, counted: 0, naivePlays: 0 };

const server = http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (req.method === 'POST' && req.url === '/api/view') {
    let raw = ''; for await (const c of req) raw += c;
    stats.received++;
    const ua = req.headers['user-agent'] ?? '';
    if (isbot(ua)) { stats.bot++; return res.writeHead(204).end(); }
    const { videoId, viewerId } = JSON.parse(raw);
    const key = `${viewerId}:${videoId}`, now = Date.now();
    if (now - (lastCounted.get(key) ?? 0) < DEDUPE_MS) { stats.duplicate++; return res.writeHead(204).end(); }
    lastCounted.set(key, now); stats.counted++;
    return res.writeHead(204).end();
  }
  if (req.method === 'POST' && req.url === '/api/naive-play') { stats.naivePlays++; return res.writeHead(204).end(); }
  if (req.url === '/stats') return res.writeHead(200, {'content-type':'application/json'}).end(JSON.stringify(stats));
  const path = req.url === '/' ? '/feed.html' : req.url;
  try {
    const body = await readFile('public' + path);
    const type = path.endsWith('.js') ? 'text/javascript' : path.endsWith('.mp4') ? 'video/mp4' : 'text/html';
    res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': type }).end(body);
  } catch { res.writeHead(404).end(); }
});
server.listen(3000, () => console.log('listening on :3000'));

⚠️ Note: the static file handler is demo-only (no path sanitizing). Don't ship it. In production, the dedupe map belongs in Redis with a TTL, and viewerId should come from your auth session when you have one.

3. A feed page that runs both counters

Three muted autoplaying videos: two at the top, one far below the fold. Each gets the real tracker and a naive play counter so we can compare.



 name=viewport content="width=device-width">

 id=a src="/long.mp4" muted autoplay playsinline loop>
 id=b src="/long.mp4" muted autoplay playsinline loop>
 class=spacer>
id=c src="/long.mp4" muted autoplay playsinline loop> type=module> import { trackViews } from '/view-tracker.js'; for (const v of document.querySelectorAll('video')) { trackViews(v, { videoId: v.id }); v.addEventListener('play', () => navigator.sendBeacon('/api/naive-play'), { once: true }); } 4. Simulate real traffic with Playwright

Scenario: a viewer loads the feed, scrolls 300 px after 1 s (video a leaves the screen), refreshes, and then a headless bot visits.

// run.js
const { chromium } = require('playwright');
const stats = async p => (await (await p.request.get('http://localhost:3000/stats')).json());
(async () => {
  const b = await chromium.launch();
  const human = await b.newContext({ userAgent: 'Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/142.0.0.0 Safari/537.36', viewport:{width:1280,height:720} });
  const p = await human.newPage();
  await p.goto('http://localhost:3000/');
  await p.waitForTimeout(1000);
  await p.evaluate(() => window.scrollTo(0, 300));      // video "a" drops below 50% visible after 1s
  await p.waitForTimeout(3000);
  console.log('after first visit  ', JSON.stringify(await stats(p)));
  await p.reload(); await p.waitForTimeout(3000);
  console.log('after reload       ', JSON.stringify(await stats(p)));
  const bot = await (await b.newContext()).newPage();   // default HeadlessChrome UA
  await bot.goto('http://localhost:3000/'); await bot.waitForTimeout(3000);
  console.log('after headless UA  ', JSON.stringify(await stats(bot)));
  console.log('default UA was:', await bot.evaluate(() => navigator.userAgent));
  await b.close();
})();

$ node server.mjs &
listening on :3000
$ node run.js
after first visit   {"received":1,"bot":0,"duplicate":0,"counted":1,"naivePlays":2}
after reload        {"received":2,"bot":0,"duplicate":1,"counted":1,"naivePlays":3}
after headless UA   {"received":4,"bot":2,"duplicate":1,"counted":1,"naivePlays":5}
default UA was: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) HeadlessChrome/158.0.8127.36 Safari/537.36
5. Reading the results 📊
Scenario Naive play Qualified views First visit +2 (a and b started) +1 (b only; a was on screen ~1 s) Reload +1 +0 (arrived, rejected as duplicate) Headless bot +2 +0 (2 arrived, rejected by isbot) Total 5 1

Two things I didn't expect:

  1. Video c never started. Chromium didn't autoplay the muted video while it was 3000 px offscreen, so even the naive counter skipped it. That's browser behavior you shouldn't rely on; a taller viewport or a different browser could start it.
  2. My own test harness is a bot. Playwright's default UA contains HeadlessChrome, which isbot flags. If your synthetic monitoring hits pages with view tracking, it's either inflating your counts (naive) or silently filtered (this setup). Set a real UA in tests that need to count, and know which one you're doing.
Things to know
  • Keep both numbers. Rename the naive count to "starts" and keep it. The gap between starts and views tells you how much of your autoplay gets real attention.
  • UA filtering is the floor. It catches honest automation. If views affect payouts, add rate limits per IP/viewer and anomaly checks.
  • Not tested here: the visibilitychange path (background tabs), Safari, mobile. The harness is headless Chromium 158 on one machine.
What's next
  • Send videoId, viewerId and a session id with every beacon into a real events table, then compute views in SQL so you can change the definition later and backfill.
  • Add an "engaged view" at a longer threshold and plot it next to views per video. The videos where the two diverge most are the ones worth a look.
