items.title: My AI agents now leave a receipt: an action history for a self-hosted app store
items.summary: A few days ago someone on LinkedIn listed six questions every team should answer before building an AI agent. Number 5 was short: "Can you trace what it did?" I thought my answer was yes. It wasn't. The setup I build Agentic App Store , an open-source (MIT) app store you host yourself. You install apps with one click on your own Mac or Linux box, and AI agents can work inside those apps through one door, the AI Hub : Agents like Claude Code or Codex connect to one MCP address and see every installed app's tools. The hub's own assistant can use the same tools from a chat window. Each app marks its tools as read , write or danger . A danger call (delete shapes, replace text) stops in the hub and shows the person a card with Accept / Accept all in this chat / Reject . The prompt never decides that; the hub does. So the approval part was there. What was missing was the record. The hub kept the last 200 tool calls in memory, without the person's answer, and a restart wiped them. That's a status page, not a history. What I wanted to be able to answer For any AI action, a week later: When , and through which door (an MCP agent or the assistant chat)? For whom , which app and tool ? Exactly what the AI sent ? How it ended : done, failed, or never ran? What the person answered , if the call needed an answer? Number 4 matters more than I expected. A rejected change never reaches the app, so the app has no record of it. But "the AI tried to delete everything and I said no" is exactly what you want to find later. The design: one line per call, written where every call passes Every tool call, from every door, already goes through one function in the hub: calls.call() . That's the natural place to write the history. One JSON line per call, appended to a file in the hub's data folder: def record ( * , via , user , app , tool , kind , args , ok , error = "" , ms = 0 , approval = "" , ran = True ) : entry = { "id" : secrets . token_hex ( 6 ) , "at" : time . time ( ) , "via" : via , "user" : user , "app" : app , "tool" : tool , "kind" : kind , "args" : _args_text ( args ) , # what the AI sent, cut at 4,000 chars "ok" : ok , "ran" : ran , "error" : error [ : 500 ] , "ms" : ms , "approval" : approval , # accepted, rejected, allowed, declined, no answer... } with _lock , _file ( ) . open ( "a" , encoding = "utf-8" ) as f : f . write ( json . dumps ( entry , ensure_ascii = False ) + "\n" ) Plain JSONL on purpose: it's easy to read, easy to back up, and easy to delete. The file keeps the newest 10,000 entries and is readable only by the hub's owner. Getting the person's answer into the same line The approval happens in one module ( approvals ) and the call in another ( calls ). Both run in the same asyncio task, one tool call at a time, so a ContextVar carries the answer from one to the other without changing every function signature in between: APPROVAL : ContextVar [ str ] = ContextVar ( "ai_hub_approval" , default = "" ) # approvals.ask(), after the person clicks Accept: history . APPROVAL . set ( "accepted" ) # calls.call(), when it writes the line: approval = history . APPROVAL . get ( ) history . APPROVAL . set ( "" ) # the answer belongs to this one call only The reset is important. Without it, the next harmless read in the same chat would show up as "accepted" too. Calls that never run get their own line with ran: false : rejected changes, reads the person declined, and calls from places that have no chat to ask in (the voice companion, say). Those don't run either. The model is told to ask in the chat. The bug I found while taking screenshots I tried it live: I asked the AI to clear a demo drawing and planned to click Reject for the screenshot. I was too slow. Claude Code gave up waiting for the tool call before the hub's own 4-minute timeout, and the history showed... nothing for that call. When the client gives up, the hub's waiting coroutine gets cancelled . My code only wrote a line after a decision, and a cancellation is not a decision. So "never asked" and "asked, but nobody answered" looked the same, which is exactly the gap the history was supposed to close. The fix is small: async def _kept_answer ( tool , args , user , via , chat , post , card , waiting ) : try : return await _answer ( chat , post , card , waiting ) except asyncio . CancelledError : history . record ( . . . , ok = False , ran = False , approval = "no answer: the AI stopped waiting" ) raise Record, then re-raise: the cancellation still does what it should, and the history keeps the attempt. There's a test for it now too. What the owner sees On the hub page, the old "Recent tool calls" card became History of the AI's actions : Search across everything (an app, a tool, a person, words the AI sent, "rejected"). Click a row to see the whole entry, and delete it if you want. Delete all, after a question that says how many entries will go. Download the whole history as JSON. Times show in your browser's time zone (the containers run on UTC). Only the hub's owner can see it, because an entry holds whatever the AI sent, and that can be anyone's data. What it is, and what it isn't It is the everyday kind of audit trail: on your own server, next to your data, covering every agent that goes through the hub. It is not a validated compliance system. If you work in a regulated field, the hub's history can support your own validation, but it doesn't replace it. Try it Agentic App Store is open source (MIT): https://about.reflex-ddns.com If you run agents against real systems, I'm curious: who reviews what your agents did last week, and where do they look?
items.summary_html:
A few days ago someone on LinkedIn listed six questions every team should answer before building an AI agent. Number 5 was short: "Can you trace what it did?"

I thought my answer was yes. It wasn't.

The setup

I build Agentic App Store, an open-source (MIT) app store you host yourself. You install apps with one click on your own Mac or Linux box, and AI agents can work inside those apps through one door, the AI Hub:

  • Agents like Claude Code or Codex connect to one MCP address and see every installed app's tools.
  • The hub's own assistant can use the same tools from a chat window.
  • Each app marks its tools as read, write or danger. A danger call (delete shapes, replace text) stops in the hub and shows the person a card with Accept / Accept all in this chat / Reject. The prompt never decides that; the hub does.

So the approval part was there. What was missing was the record. The hub kept the last 200 tool calls in memory, without the person's answer, and a restart wiped them.

That's a status page, not a history.

What I wanted to be able to answer

For any AI action, a week later:

  1. When, and through which door (an MCP agent or the assistant chat)?
  2. For whom, which app and tool?
  3. Exactly what the AI sent?
  4. How it ended: done, failed, or never ran?
  5. What the person answered, if the call needed an answer?

Number 4 matters more than I expected. A rejected change never reaches the app, so the app has no record of it. But "the AI tried to delete everything and I said no" is exactly what you want to find later.

The design: one line per call, written where every call passes

Every tool call, from every door, already goes through one function in the hub: calls.call(). That's the natural place to write the history. One JSON line per call, appended to a file in the hub's data folder:

def record(*, via, user, app, tool, kind, args, ok,
           error="", ms=0, approval="", ran=True):
    entry = {
        "id": secrets.token_hex(6),
        "at": time.time(),
        "via": via, "user": user, "app": app, "tool": tool, "kind": kind,
        "args": _args_text(args),      # what the AI sent, cut at 4,000 chars
        "ok": ok, "ran": ran, "error": error[:500], "ms": ms,
        "approval": approval,          # accepted, rejected, allowed, declined, no answer...
    }
    with _lock, _file().open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(entry, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")

Plain JSONL on purpose: it's easy to read, easy to back up, and easy to delete. The file keeps the newest 10,000 entries and is readable only by the hub's owner.

Getting the person's answer into the same line

The approval happens in one module (approvals) and the call in another (calls). Both run in the same asyncio task, one tool call at a time, so a ContextVar carries the answer from one to the other without changing every function signature in between:

APPROVAL: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("ai_hub_approval", default="")

# approvals.ask(), after the person clicks Accept:
history.APPROVAL.set("accepted")

# calls.call(), when it writes the line:
approval = history.APPROVAL.get()
history.APPROVAL.set("")   # the answer belongs to this one call only

The reset is important. Without it, the next harmless read in the same chat would show up as "accepted" too.

Calls that never run get their own line with ran: false: rejected changes, reads the person declined, and calls from places that have no chat to ask in (the voice companion, say). Those don't run either. The model is told to ask in the chat.

The bug I found while taking screenshots

I tried it live: I asked the AI to clear a demo drawing and planned to click Reject for the screenshot. I was too slow. Claude Code gave up waiting for the tool call before the hub's own 4-minute timeout, and the history showed... nothing for that call.

When the client gives up, the hub's waiting coroutine gets cancelled. My code only wrote a line after a decision, and a cancellation is not a decision. So "never asked" and "asked, but nobody answered" looked the same, which is exactly the gap the history was supposed to close.

The fix is small:

async def _kept_answer(tool, args, user, via, chat, post, card, waiting):
    try:
        return await _answer(chat, post, card, waiting)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        history.record(..., ok=False, ran=False,
                       approval="no answer: the AI stopped waiting")
        raise

Record, then re-raise: the cancellation still does what it should, and the history keeps the attempt. There's a test for it now too.

What the owner sees

On the hub page, the old "Recent tool calls" card became History of the AI's actions:

  • Search across everything (an app, a tool, a person, words the AI sent, "rejected").
  • Click a row to see the whole entry, and delete it if you want.
  • Delete all, after a question that says how many entries will go.
  • Download the whole history as JSON.
  • Times show in your browser's time zone (the containers run on UTC).

Only the hub's owner can see it, because an entry holds whatever the AI sent, and that can be anyone's data.

What it is, and what it isn't

It is the everyday kind of audit trail: on your own server, next to your data, covering every agent that goes through the hub.

It is not a validated compliance system. If you work in a regulated field, the hub's history can support your own validation, but it doesn't replace it.

Try it

Agentic App Store is open source (MIT): https://about.reflex-ddns.com

If you run agents against real systems, I'm curious: who reviews what your agents did last week, and where do they look?

items.title: BharatGen Launches Patram 1.5, a 7B Vision-Language Model for Document Processing
items.summary: BharatGen has launched Patram 1.5, a seven-billion-parameter vision-language model (VLM) built to read and process scanned, handwritten, stamped and multilingual documents. The model is available as open weights on Hugging Face and can also be accessed through the BharatGen Playground. Unlike conventional optical character recognition (OCR) systems, which convert documents into text before passing the output to a large language model (LLM), Patram 1.5 processes documents as images. This lets it interpret elements such as tables, signatures, stamps, photographs, charts, and handwritten notes alongside the text. The model targets organisations in banking, insurance, healthcare, and government, where document processing often involves poor-quality scans, handwritten entries, and documents in multiple languages. Patram 1.5 also introduces what BharatGen calls OCR 3.0. Instead of extracting all the text from a document, users can specify the information they need in natural language and receive the output in a format compatible with their systems, including JSON, HTML and Markdown. For instance, a bank processing account statements can ask the model to extract only customer IDs and branch details, with the output returned in a predefined JSON structure. Another feature is the model's ability to identify information it cannot read. If a field is blank or a figure is illegible, Patram 1.5 is trained to flag the issue rather than generate an answer. Where it can make a reasonable estimate, it provides the answer with a warning for human verification. It can also seek clarification when a document contains multiple possible answers to a question. This is particularly relevant for financial services and healthcare, where incorrect information extracted from documents can affect decisions. BharatGen evaluated Patram 1.5 across 49 tests, comprising 34 public benchmarks and 15 tests from its own PatramBench dataset. The evaluation included 20 other vision-language models, ranging up to 763 billion parameters, and seven specialist OCR systems. PatramBench contains 11,828 test items drawn from 8,773 pages of Indian documents. BharatGen said it would release the benchmark on Hugging Face in the coming days. The company has also made Patram 1.5 available through its BharatGen Playground, where users can upload documents and images, ask questions and extract information using natural language. The Playground includes ready-to-use solutions for parsing, extraction, classification, document splitting and section identification. Digitisation, translation and editing capabilities are expected to be added soon. These solutions can be combined into workflows for tasks such as sorting and cross-checking KYC documents. Speaking on the launch, Rishi Bal, CEO of BharatGen, said, “A model alone can only take you so far. The BharatGen Playground gives the world a full stack for document intelligence, with models, solutions and workflows working together.” Prof Ravi Kiran Sarvadevabhatla, consortium member at BharatGen and professor at IIIT Hyderabad, said, “With Patram 1.5 and BharatGen Playground, we chart a new capability frontier for sovereign vision models and document understanding workflows.” With seven billion parameters, Patram 1.5 can be deployed on an organisation's own infrastructure, allowing banks, hospitals and government departments to process sensitive documents without sending them to external systems. The model supports English and English mixed with Indian languages, has a context window of up to 32,000 tokens and can process multiple images in a single request. Patram 1.5 is the latest release in BharatGen's Patram model family, which began with Patram 1 in June last year.

items.title: India Wants Its Own Jet Engines, Green Aero is Taking a Shot
items.summary: India has been building aircraft, launching rockets and manufacturing drones . But when it comes to jet engines, the country still has a significant gap to close. Developing an engine is not simply another engineering challenge. It requires expertise in metallurgy, precision manufacturing, thermodynamics and materials science, alongside years of testing. Only a handful of countries have mastered the technology at scale. For India, dependence on imported propulsion systems remains a strategic vulnerability, particularly as its defence requirements evolve. Modern warfare is creating demand for autonomous aircraft that can fly faster, operate in contested environments and work alongside crewed fighter jets. These systems need more than an airframe. They require engines, avionics and flight-control systems designed to work together. This is the gap Bengaluru-based Green Aero wants to address. Founded in November 2023 by aerospace engineer Prithwish Kundu, the startup is developing jet engines, avionics and airframes under one roof. It is starting with smaller engines and working towards high-speed autonomous aircraft. The company has raised $14 million in a Series A round led by Crane Venture Partners. The round also includes 3one4 Capital, Antler Elevate and existing investors pi Ventures, Antler India and Rebalance. Kundu describes this to AIM as the largest venture capital round in India’s private jet engine and Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) sector. The company plans to use the capital to expand its testing infrastructure, hire engineers and accelerate product development. Over the next 12 to 18 months, it will focus on larger-thrust engines and flight qualification for its transonic and supersonic drone platforms. The funding comes as India increases investment in domestic defence production. The Ministry of Defence said production reached ₹1.78 lakh crore in 2025–26. Private companies accounted for 24% of output. The government has also opened 25% of its defence R&D budget to industry, startups and academia. For Green Aero, the opportunity lies in a difficult part of aerospace manufacturing. “India does not have a private ecosystem that develops jet engines or aero engines,” Kundu says in the interview. He calls this “the Achilles heel of India’s defence ecosystem”. Building an Integrated Aerospace Stack Kundu’s interest in propulsion began long before he founded Green Aero. An aerospace engineer who studied at IIT Delhi , he went on to complete a PhD in aerospace engineering at North Carolina State University. He later worked as a research scientist at Argonne National Laboratory in the US, leading projects across aerospace and energy. His work also included hypersonics projects with NASA Langley and a brief stint with the US Army on jet engines and gas turbines. After returning to India, he spent about two years at electric vehicle maker Euler Motors as VP of Battery and Thermal Systems. However, he wanted to work on propulsion systems in India. He eventually moved from the research environment into the startup ecosystem. “I felt it was too slow,” Kundu says, explaining why he chose to leave academia and work in the startup sector. One of the gaps he identifies is the absence of a substantial private ecosystem developing jet engines in India. These engines are used beyond conventional aircraft, including military drones , cruise missiles and other defence applications. Green Aero’s approach is to develop three components together: propulsion systems, avionics and airframes. The company believes this vertical integration will allow it to co-optimise the systems rather than depend on separate suppliers. It says it has completed more than 100 hot-fire tests in the sub-kN engine category. Hot-fire tests evaluate an engine under operating conditions, but they are not the same as flight trials or formal qualification. The company has also developed an aero-engine core called The Blue Dragon. It claims this is the first such core developed from scratch in India and says it has demonstrated airblast atomisers for sub-kN engines. Green Aero describes the latter as a global first. Its smaller engines are intended for military applications, where comparable products are often imported from Europe. Kundu says the company’s engines are more efficient and optimised for air launches and cold-weather operations. They can rotate at 50,000 to 1,00,000 revolutions per minute. The startup has already begun generating revenue from small-engine sales. It has received interest from domestic and international buyers, although it has not disclosed customer names or contract values. Kundu reveals the company had received orders from the US and Europe that it was considering. “The entire manufacturing happens in India,” Kundu says, adding that the company is without imported or white-labelled critical engine components. It works with manufacturers across the country and sources superalloys from Indian suppliers and non-Chinese sources overseas. He adds that some components require machining accuracies of up to five microns. By comparison, the thickness of a strand of human hair is roughly 100 microns. Building this supply chain has required investment in manufacturing processes , quality control and alternative sources for critical materials. The company now operates an 87,000 sq ft R&D, assembly and testing facility at Bengaluru’s KIADB Aerospace Park. It says the facility brings engine and CCA research, assembly, quality control and testing together. Its team has grown to 50 members, including engineers and military veterans. The company also cites an established partnership with L&T, support from Boeing’s BUILD programme and SIDBI’s Green-Tech Accelerator. It has not detailed the scope of these associations in the announcement. The Bigger Bet on Autonomous Aircraft While small engines provide an early commercial opportunity, Green Aero sees CCAs as its larger opportunity. These aircraft are designed to operate independently or alongside crewed fighter jets. They could undertake surveillance, strike and other missions , particularly in environments where sending a pilot would carry significant risks. Kundu believes drone warfare is moving towards jet-powered platforms that can exceed 600 kmph. items.summary_html:
India has been building aircraft, launching rockets and manufacturing drones. But when it comes to jet engines, the country still has a significant gap to close. Developing an engine is not simply another engineering challenge. It requires expertise in metallurgy, precision manufacturing, thermodynamics and materials science, alongside years of testing. 

Only a handful of countries have mastered the technology at scale. For India, dependence on imported propulsion systems remains a strategic vulnerability, particularly as its defence requirements evolve.

Modern warfare is creating demand for autonomous aircraft that can fly faster, operate in contested environments and work alongside crewed fighter jets. These systems need more than an airframe. They require engines, avionics and flight-control systems designed to work together.

This is the gap Bengaluru-based Green Aero wants to address. Founded in November 2023 by aerospace engineer Prithwish Kundu, the startup is developing jet engines, avionics and airframes under one roof. It is starting with smaller engines and working towards high-speed autonomous aircraft.

The company has raised $14 million in a Series A round led by Crane Venture Partners. The round also includes 3one4 Capital, Antler Elevate and existing investors pi Ventures, Antler India and Rebalance. Kundu describes this to AIM as the largest venture capital round in India’s private jet engine and Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) sector.

The company plans to use the capital to expand its testing infrastructure, hire engineers and accelerate product development. Over the next 12 to 18 months, it will focus on larger-thrust engines and flight qualification for its transonic and supersonic drone platforms.

The funding comes as India increases investment in domestic defence production. The Ministry of Defence said production reached ₹1.78 lakh crore in 2025–26. Private companies accounted for 24% of output. The government has also opened 25% of its defence R&D budget to industry, startups and academia.

For Green Aero, the opportunity lies in a difficult part of aerospace manufacturing. “India does not have a private ecosystem that develops jet engines or aero engines,” Kundu says in the interview. He calls this “the Achilles heel of India’s defence ecosystem”.

Building an Integrated Aerospace Stack

Kundu’s interest in propulsion began long before he founded Green Aero. An aerospace engineer who studied at IIT Delhi, he went on to complete a PhD in aerospace engineering at North Carolina State University. He later worked as a research scientist at Argonne National Laboratory in the US, leading projects across aerospace and energy.

His work also included hypersonics projects with NASA Langley and a brief stint with the US Army on jet engines and gas turbines. After returning to India, he spent about two years at electric vehicle maker Euler Motors as VP of Battery and Thermal Systems.

However, he wanted to work on propulsion systems in India. He eventually moved from the research environment into the startup ecosystem.

“I felt it was too slow,” Kundu says, explaining why he chose to leave academia and work in the startup sector.

One of the gaps he identifies is the absence of a substantial private ecosystem developing jet engines in India. These engines are used beyond conventional aircraft, including military drones, cruise missiles and other defence applications.

Green Aero’s approach is to develop three components together: propulsion systems, avionics and airframes. The company believes this vertical integration will allow it to co-optimise the systems rather than depend on separate suppliers.

It says it has completed more than 100 hot-fire tests in the sub-kN engine category. Hot-fire tests evaluate an engine under operating conditions, but they are not the same as flight trials or formal qualification.

The company has also developed an aero-engine core called The Blue Dragon. It claims this is the first such core developed from scratch in India and says it has demonstrated airblast atomisers for sub-kN engines. Green Aero describes the latter as a global first.

Its smaller engines are intended for military applications, where comparable products are often imported from Europe. Kundu says the company’s engines are more efficient and optimised for air launches and cold-weather operations. They can rotate at 50,000 to 1,00,000 revolutions per minute.

The startup has already begun generating revenue from small-engine sales. It has received interest from domestic and international buyers, although it has not disclosed customer names or contract values. Kundu reveals the company had received orders from the US and Europe that it was considering.

“The entire manufacturing happens in India,” Kundu says, adding that the company is without imported or white-labelled critical engine components. It works with manufacturers across the country and sources superalloys from Indian suppliers and non-Chinese sources overseas.

He adds that some components require machining accuracies of up to five microns. By comparison, the thickness of a strand of human hair is roughly 100 microns. Building this supply chain has required investment in manufacturing processes, quality control and alternative sources for critical materials.

The company now operates an 87,000 sq ft R&D, assembly and testing facility at Bengaluru’s KIADB Aerospace Park. It says the facility brings engine and CCA research, assembly, quality control and testing together. Its team has grown to 50 members, including engineers and military veterans.

The company also cites an established partnership with L&T, support from Boeing’s BUILD programme and SIDBI’s Green-Tech Accelerator. It has not detailed the scope of these associations in the announcement.

The Bigger Bet on Autonomous Aircraft

While small engines provide an early commercial opportunity, Green Aero sees CCAs as its larger opportunity. These aircraft are designed to operate independently or alongside crewed fighter jets. items.title: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
items.summary: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025 . It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics. Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO . In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck. sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy! It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync: The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most. Update : Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released. Tags: backups , sqlite

items.title: Pine Labs Adds AI Agents To Merchant App For Sales Insights, Ad Campaigns
items.summary: Bengaluru-based fintech company Pine Labs has launched two AI agents on its merchant operating app, Pine Labs One, to help small businesses analyse transaction data and manage digital advertising campaigns. The tools, Guide and Marketer Agent, are the first in a series of agents being developed under the company’s Agentic Org platform. Pine Labs said they would be rolled out to millions of merchants in India. Guide allows merchants to query business data in natural language, including store-level sales, point-of-sale transactions, settlements, refunds, payments and value-added service activations. The tool is designed to bring information spread across multiple reports and systems into a conversational interface. Marketer Agent, meanwhile, converts business objectives into advertising campaigns . It handles keyword research, including competitor keywords, creative generation, audience targeting and campaign setup. The agent will initially support campaigns on Google platforms, with Pine Labs planning to extend it to large language model-powered discovery platforms. “Small businesses don't need AI for the sake of AI. They need it to solve everyday problems and make better decisions,” Vijeth Pandit, Chief Product Officer at Pine Labs , said. Merchants will have to review and approve campaigns before advertising spend is committed. Once approved, the agent can publish campaigns directly without requiring merchants to use Google Ads. Pine Labs said it could also match ad interactions with in-store transactions using privacy-preserving techniques to measure campaign-generated revenue. Marketer Agent is built using Google’s Gemini models as part of a collaboration between Pine Labs and Google Cloud announced in September 2026. Amit Kumar, Managing Director, Google Cloud India, said the collaboration would help smaller businesses automate campaign management and run digital campaigns without needing dedicated technical expertise. Pine Labs’ Agentic Org platform includes Grantex, a permissions and governance layer that controls the data and tools agents can access and enables human oversight at critical stages. The company also plans to launch an Agent App Store, where merchants can access specialised agents for different business functions. The marketplace is scheduled to launch first in Singapore during the Singapore FinTech Festival, followed by India by December 15. Pine Labs said its roadmap also includes Market, an agent designed to manage advertising across multiple platforms.

items.title: SpaceX Gets Nod to Deploy 1 Mn AI Data Centre Satellites
items.summary: Elon Musk’s SpaceX has received approval to deploy up to 1 million solar-powered satellites for AI data centres in space SpaceX had sought permission earlier this year from the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to deploy orbital computing modules under its proposed 'Starmind' constellation. The company has now received the authorisation in light of the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing. The constellation would run AI workloads in space for use on Earth, with the company arguing that access to solar power could reduce the energy and operating costs associated with conventional data centres. However, the approval does not mean SpaceX will necessarily deploy all satellites at once. Satellite operators sometimes seek authorisation for larger constellations than they eventually build. SpaceX had previously sought approval for 42,000 satellites for its Starlink broadband network; the network currently has just over 11,000 satellites in orbit. Under the FCC authorisation, SpaceX must begin deployment by November 2033. It will have to deploy at least 100,000 satellites by November 2035 and reach 50% of the approved constellation by November 2038. SpaceX has argued that the satellites would draw on near-constant solar power and rely on passive radiative cooling, reducing the AI power workloads back on Earth. The scale of the Starmind proposal has drawn objections from competing satellite operators, including Viasat and Amazon’s Leo unit. The latter has argued that such a large deployment would take centuries and described the proposal as an ambition rather than a concrete plan. The American Astronomical Society has also opposed the move, warning that the deployment would interfere with optical astronomy. The FCC said it had also dismissed concerns about environmental impacts and optical astronomy, stating that these fell outside its regulatory authority. SpaceX’s plan also depends on reducing the cost of launching satellites at scale. The company is betting on Starship, its next-generation reusable rocket, to support the constellation's deployment. Other technology companies are also exploring space-based computing, with Google announcing Project Suncatcher as an effort to develop AI computing infrastructure in orbit. Blue Origin, founded by Jeff Bezos, has separately sought FCC approval to deploy up to 51,600 satellites under its proposed Project Sunrise constellation.

items.title: The Bundesrat corpus: A dataset of political discourse in the German Federal Council
items.summary: The Bundesrat is Germany's second legislative chamber and a constitutional veto player within its political system. The members of the Bundesrat are delegates of state governments. Tracing the political discourse in the Bundesrat is challenging as it has a limited machine-readable corpus available. To address this issue, we present a speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 Bundesrat plenary sessions from the chamber's first session on 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026. In this period, a total of 53,362 speeches by 2,473 individuals were delivered in the chamber, including written statements. Each speech includes a speech ID, the full German text, the speaker's name, the date and location of the session, the federal state that the speaker represents, the speaker's role (if applicable), the type of contribution, and the speaker's gender. The dataset provides interdisciplinary research opportunities across computational political science, legislative studies, and parliamentary discourse analysis, coupled with discourse from the Bundestag.

items.title: MGMem: An Efficient, Deterministic, and Provenance-Preserving Framework for Long-Horizon Agent Memory
items.summary: Long-horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents need persistent memory that surfaces the right past interaction at the right time across thousands of turns. Many systems index by invoking generative LLMs to rewrite history into summaries, facts, or knowledge graphs--a step that is (a) costly (thousands of generative calls per build), (b) non-deterministic (undermining reproducibility and giving inconsistent answers across runs), and (c) provenance-erasing (the reader sees synthesized text, not the original turn). We propose MGMem, a framework with no generative indexing calls that replaces this step with a deterministic discriminative-parser pipeline: recurring mentions across sessions are organized into an incidence graph, question mentions are resolved by a subject-conditioned three-stage resolver, and raw dialogue episodes are returned to the reader. On English multi-session dialogue QA, MGMem outperforms matched-protocol baselines on LoCoMo without generative indexing calls; on the full LongMemEval-S, it remains competitive overall and leads or ties on single-session types among local retrieval comparisons. Code: https://github.com/junhong-h/MGMem

items.title: Feature-Based Explainability of Transformer Scoring Models: A Fidelity-First Framework for Automated Writing Assessment
items.summary: Transformer-based automated writing scoring models can achieve strong agreement with human scores while providing limited transparency into the response characteristics associated with their predictions. This study evaluated a feature-based post-hoc explanation approach in which explanatory fidelity was established before feature importance was interpreted. English Language Arts responses from three writing prompts in Grades 6 and 8 were analyzed, with about 12,700 responses per prompt and separate DeBERTa-v3-base research models for Expression and Conventions. Each response was represented by 61 interpretable linguistic and writing-quality features. Four approaches - theory-driven composites, hierarchical feature groupings, exploratory factor analysis, and Random Forest surrogates - were compared in their ability to reproduce DeBERTa predictions. Random Forest surrogates produced the largest observed R2 values across all six prompt-by-trait conditions, with held-out R2 values from .81 to .95. SHAP analyses showed substantial overlap in high-importance features across traits, with 75% to 90% of the top 20 features shared. Trait differentiation occurred mainly through relative feature weighting: Expression showed greater importance for lexical and conceptual indicators, whereas Conventions showed greater importance for sentence-level and syntactic-control indicators. Under researcher-defined mappings, rubric correspondence was 90%-95% for Expression and 12%-18% for Conventions. These percentages are descriptive and conditional on the mappings and available linguistic features. The findings support a fidelity-first framework for examining apparent scoring priorities while distinguishing post-hoc evidence about model behavior from direct explanation of transformer internals.

Abstract: Transformer-based automated writing scoring models can achieve strong agreement with human scores while providing limited transparency into the response characteristics associated with their predictions. This study evaluated a feature-based post-hoc explanation approach in which explanatory fidelity was established before feature importance was interpreted. English Language Arts responses from three writing prompts in Grades 6 and 8 were analyzed, with about 12,700 responses per prompt and separate DeBERTa-v3-base research models for Expression and Conventions. Each response was represented by 61 interpretable linguistic and writing-quality features. Four approaches - theory-driven composites, hierarchical feature groupings, exploratory factor analysis, and Random Forest surrogates - were compared in their ability to reproduce DeBERTa predictions. Random Forest surrogates produced the largest observed R2 values across all six prompt-by-trait conditions, with held-out R2 values from .81 to .95. SHAP analyses showed substantial overlap in high-importance features across traits, with 75% to 90% of the top 20 features shared. Trait differentiation occurred mainly through relative feature weighting: Expression showed greater importance for lexical and conceptual indicators, whereas Conventions showed greater importance for sentence-level and syntactic-control indicators. Under researcher-defined mappings, rubric correspondence was 90%-95% for Expression and 12%-18% for Conventions. These percentages are descriptive and conditional on the mappings and available linguistic features. The findings support a fidelity-first framework for examining apparent scoring priorities while distinguishing post-hoc evidence about model behavior from direct explanation of transformer internals.

items.title: Psychophysics of Duration Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary: Studies of time perception in language models focus mainly on text-based settings. Yet multimodal models are increasingly used for tasks that require perceiving the passage of time, making the limits of their temporal perception important to understand. We measure the limits of duration perception from audio against a human baseline to address this gap. Drawing from psychophysics, we operationalise duration perception as a melody recognition task, testing when a melody becomes unrecognisable as it is slowed down. Of 21 tested models, most cannot recognise well-known melodies without labelled in-context examples. With in-context examples, seven recognise melodies reliably, most peaking within the median human recognition band. Generalisation is limited: (i) recognition peaks shift with in-context example speed, (ii) melody titles induce prediction bias, and (iii) providing examples with scientific pitch notation does not prevent accuracy declining at long note durations for most models. In humans, the recognition window is a property of the perceiver; in current models, it is largely a property of the prompt.

items.title: Verified experience improves materials prediction with large language models
items.summary: Materials discovery is an iterative loop: experiments and calculations verify predictions, and each outcome can inform the next. Yet most predictors are specialized single-task models fixed after training. Large language models have recently emerged as predictors across heterogeneous tasks but generally underperform specialized models, and retrieval-augmented variants discard their own outcomes. Benchmarks also score queries in isolation, leaving improvement from outcomes untested. Here we construct MatMemBench, a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after prediction and tests online adaptation, memory retention and cross-task transfer. We present MatRecall, a framework that lets large language models store verified predictions, with evidence, outcome and error, as episodes and recall them without retraining. MatRecall improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model, exceeded specialized models on 11 tasks, remained useful after feedback stopped and transferred between related tasks. Verified experience could become a reusable resource for self-improving discovery loops.

items.title: Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models
items.summary: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) shows that human problem-solving is affected by both intrinsic load, arising from task difficulty, and extraneous load, arising from how task information is presented. Large language models (LLMs) show analogous effects: presentation alone can affect model performance, but these effects have not yet been systematically isolated from task difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce CogLoadBench, a controlled benchmark that varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families. Across models, we find that higher extraneous load conditions often reduce accuracy by either adding competition or complicating the reasoning path. To support diagnosis and mitigation of load-related effects, we propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that estimates a model's extraneous load, and show that it generalizes across reasoning task types and load levels. We further show that shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average model performance without changing prompt content.

items.title: Focus On Facts: Stylistically Invariant and Factually Sensitive Text Embeddings
items.summary: Text embedding models can conflate surface-form similarity with factual identity. Given an altered near-copy with one corrupted fact and a differently worded fact-preserving rewrite, the base model prefers the altered near-copy. We test whether hard-negative contrastive supervision can reduce this surface-similarity shortcut. We construct FOF-Bench, an 83,263-triplet benchmark spanning five domains. Each anchor is paired with an LLM-generated, fact-preserving stylistic rewrite and a matched fact-altered near-copy. We fine-tune FOF-80M (Focus On Facts), an 80M-parameter embedding model, with a triplet contrastive objective that ranks the rewrite above the factual alteration. On 8,327 held-out test triplets, the base model chooses the factually altered text in 99.58% of cases (0.42% factual preference rate; mean separation -0.1650). After fine-tuning, mean positive--negative separation is +0.0329, 98.5% of individual margins move in the intended direction, and the preference rate reaches 29.37%. On DiSC, an external style-transfer corpus, mean cross-style similarity increases from 0.7905 to 0.9559. The model also penalizes omission and transfers poorly to directional tasks such as NLI and summarization. We characterize FOF-80M as a soft factual fingerprint for studying factual retention under stylistic variation, not as a general-purpose factuality metric.

items.title: FrId\'eo: French News Outlet Ideology Scoring via Multi-Source Evidence Fusion and Distancing-Aware Lexical Scoring
items.summary: Outlet ideology is a standard explanatory variable in media framing, media effects, and political communication research, but continuous, ecosystem-wide coverage lets it enter as graded exposure rather than a coarse bin. For France, existing references are either broad but non-analytic or analytic but sparse and source-specific, and none we are aware of offers ecosystem-wide coverage on a unified continuous scale. We contribute FrId\'eo: to our knowledge the first ecosystem-wide continuous ideology scores for the French press, a transparent composite score for 30 French news outlets, fusing nine independent families of evidence with empirical-Bayes-style shrinkage toward a structural prior. For the text-based family we introduce symmetric plain/qualified scoring, which separates the plain use of ideologically loaded vocabulary from its qualified (distanced) use on both sides, a distinction bag-of-words methods miss. The resulting scale runs from L'Humanit\'e on the far left to Valeurs actuelles on the far right; the far-right pole is near-indistinguishable and CNews ties Le Figaro. Because the text family reads current articles, it also captures editorial change that static sources miss, such as the Journal du Dimanche's sharp rightward shift after its 2023 ownership change. The ordering is robust to perturbation and to dropping any single family, and agrees with held-out Media Bias Fact Check labels. We release the scores, confidence intervals, and replication code.

items.title: Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models
items.summary: Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability for each option of a typed query, which routers and guardrails threshold directly. They are built on multilingual bases but ranked almost entirely in English. We evaluate 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages, comparing each language with English on parallel items. Every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much: a threshold set for 95\% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil. The size of the loss is set by the language and the base model rather than by leaderboard rank. In 81 controlled fine-tuning runs, task skill learned in English transfers to other languages and a few thousand target-language items narrow large losses, but neither more data nor full-parameter tuning closes them. Finally, the same test items are answered more accurately in all 23 benchmark--language pairs we compare when an LLM rather than a person translated them, so LLM-translated test sets understate the gap.

items.title: Who Attributes a Mind to Whom? Mutual Theory of Mind in Simulated User-Assistant Conversation
items.summary: When users assume that an AI chatbot has mental states, they are more likely to develop over-reliance, emotional dependence, and in extreme cases, psychological harm or self-harm. However, how these mind attributions arise in conversations and how human or AI factors influence this is still unknown. We study how users attribute minds using a minimal framework: a simulated user with different characteristics chats with assistants that differ in social style and memory. We also introduce a message-level measure of who attributes a mind to whom in four directions, checked with trained coders and applied by a fine-tuned encoder that reproduces an LLM judge. Our results show that, on average, nine out of thirteen characteristics raised simulated users' attribution to the assistant. We found that relational needs such as attachment anxiety raised it as theory predicts, some general personality traits raised it as well, and AI-specific characteristics the least. By contrast, the assistant's social style barely changed simulated users' mind attribution. Instead, sycophantic instructions raised the assistant's attribution to itself. Memory raised users' attribution only with some user models. The model playing the user changed overall attribution and the effects of characteristics, style, and memory. Our framework measures how persona descriptions affect mind attribution in simulation. It gives concrete hypotheses for human studies and shows the need for more consistent user simulators.

items.title: When the Knowledge Runs Out: A Part-Level Pilot Evaluation of How Language Models Handle Partially Covered Questions
items.summary: Assistants that answer from supplied reference material often receive material that covers some parts of a user's question and not others. Existing evaluations of insufficient context mostly score one answer per question, and often treat partially sufficient context as simply insufficient. We describe a small, open evaluation that scores each part of a three-part question separately, with a verdict for parts that are answered correctly from the material but carry an added unsupported claim. On 30 cases (five scenarios, six coverage patterns, five samples each) we test claude-haiku-4-5 and llama3.1:8b. Without an explicit instruction to stay within the material, both models fill most gaps from their own knowledge (unsupported-claim rates of 0.71 and 0.90). One added sentence instructing them to answer only from the material brings these rates to 0.00 and 0.06, consistent with prior work. What remains is less visible: answers that strengthen the material, for example turning "many job sites prohibit bots" into a flat "no". We also report on the judge. Three rounds of blind hand labelling show that this added-claim verdict is the hardest to apply, for the judge and the author alike; RAGAS faithfulness is unsuitable for this task because it penalises correct withholding; and a difference between the two models that is clear under one judge disappears when the judge model is replaced. The dataset, code, hand labels and per-run figures are public.

items.title: Open-Source FUTO Keyboard Layouts and Predictive Text for a Few Endangered Languages
items.summary: We present open-source FUTO Keyboard layouts and predictive text dictionaries for five endangered Uralic languages: Erzya, Moksha, Komi-Zyrian, Livonian, and Skolt Sami. Existing Divvun Android keyboard layouts are converted automatically into the YAML format used by FUTO Keyboard. For predictive text, we construct weighted AOSP dictionaries using translated Finnish lemma frequencies together with morphological frequencies extracted from small target-language corpora using finite-state transducers. This combination provides a practical way to rank inflected word forms when large monolingual corpora are unavailable. The resulting resources offer reusable mobile keyboard support for endangered Uralic languages.

items.title: AI-human hybrid conversations: Can AI Agents Improve Discourse Quality?
items.summary: Conversations are central to how people exchange information, share experiences, and develop collective understanding. Yet, across conversational settings, discussions often suffer from uneven participation, unanswered contributions, and a narrow range of perspectives. As generative AI agents increasingly participate alongside humans, hybrid human-AI conversations present a new opportunity to address these challenges. We investigate whether AI agents can serve as catalysts for human interaction, improving conversational engagement and broadening collective discourse. We develop a framework for introducing generic and persona-conditioned AI agents into evolving discussions and evaluate it through two complementary studies. First, using agent-based simulations grounded in Reddit discussions across four domains, we find that AI-generated conversations are more positive and less toxic than human conversations, but substantially less semantically diverse. Persona conditioning produces more human-like contributions and narrows this diversity gap, while increasing the representation of underrepresented personas can shift which perspectives emerge without necessarily increasing overall diversity. Second, we conduct a pre-registered experiment with 221 participants across nine discussion threads, comparing human-only conversations with those involving generic or persona-conditioned AI agents. We find that AI participation increases responsiveness, reduces unanswered contributions, and broadens the range of ideas expressed by human participants, even though the AI agents themselves do not fully reproduce human conversational diversity. These findings suggest that the value of hybrid human-AI conversations lies not simply in the content AI agents generate, but also in their potential to stimulate more responsive and diverse interactions among humans.

items.title: Learning from Recurrence: Internalizing Depth-Induced Preferences in Looped Language Models
items.summary: A looped language model repeatedly applies the same block to its hidden state before predicting each token. The number of passes is its recurrent depth. Increasing this depth gives the model more computation per token with the same parameters. Can the shared block learn from the predictions it makes at greater depth? Following prior work, we retrofit pretrained OLMo-2-1B with a shared recurrent block and continue mid-training over varying recurrent depths. In the four-pass model, additional passes mainly redistribute probability among tokens that already rank highly after one pass. We use the continuations generated at greater depth to train only the shared block through a single pass, without reference answers or correctness filtering. We call this transfer preference write-back. Write-back further improves one-pass and multi-pass accuracy on most tasks. At their target depths, the updated models outperform a non-recurrent control matched for mid-training data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a mean relative gain in accuracy of up to 46.2% across tasks. At four-pass inference, one-pass training outperforms full-depth training on the same targets in the model with input injection. This advantage disappears in the matched model without injection. On GSM8K, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the entire four-pass gain, showing that an update learned in one pass can improve later applications of the same block.

items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models on conversational African American English: Feature classification and next-turn generation
items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to misinterpret and misrepresent regional and social varieties of English other than Mainstream American English (MAE), such as African American English (AAE), yet most evaluations of these biases have relied on synthetic, stylized or decontextualized data. This paper instead evaluates LLMs on authentic, conversational AAE to more closely reflect how such models may encounter AAE when deployed as chatbots. Concretely, we perform two complementary evaluation tasks on 100 six-turn segments randomly sampled from the Corpus of Regional African American Language (CORAAL; Kendall and Farrington, 2024), comparing three closed-weight LLM configurations: Gemini 2.5 Flash with and without reasoning, and GPT-4.1 mini. The first task compares the models against gold-standard manual annotations for five AAE morphosyntactic features, while the second assesses their ability to generate contextually appropriate next turns, evaluating outputs for AAE feature frequency, diversity (Self-BLEU), and pragmatic quality. Reasoning-enabled Gemini is the strongest feature detector by a clear margin (macro F1 of 0.91), outperforming both other LLMs as well as a finetuned BERT-based baseline (Masis et al., 2022). In generation, however, all LLMs underproduce AAE relative to the human speakers and produce relatively uniform continuations, with reasoning-enabled Gemini producing the least AAE and the least diverse output. We conclude that a model's ability to detect AAE does not straightforwardly translate into its spontaneous use of AAE in generation, and argue that addressing this gap requires changes upstream, in how pretraining and alignment data represent dialectal variation.

items.title: Using AI to Simulate the Behaviour of European Populations
items.summary: Language models can stand in for survey respondents, but leading approaches build their simulated people from interviews or individual records. We show that a model can learn how European population groups respond from published statistics, without interviews and without training on individual records. We fine-tune an open-weight language model on more than 12 million published group-level answer distributions from about 40 European countries, setting it up to predict each group's departure from a reference distribution. On opinion surveys from its training families it calls the direction of group differences right 84% of the time, ahead of a demographic statistical model (77%, paired test) and level with Claude Opus 5 and 5.5, which it also ties on accuracy; the frontier models are more accurate on new questions. On 278 held-out questions, almost all from the survey families seen in training, its error is 12% lower than that statistical model. It runs on a single 32 GB GPU or a high-memory laptop, and in a test with an earlier model, an evidence gate calibrated on half of a survey's questions fell back to the reference where the model's adjustments did not help. Coupled to a transport simulation of a planned metro closure, with a conventional elasticity as the reference, it adds a testable age gradient to the response, which we freeze for later scoring.

items.title: LogToPersona: New Benchmark and Efficient Persona Prediction through Semantic Log Filtering
items.summary: Detailed knowledge of a user's persona is valuable for personalizing generative AI models and agents, yet such details are difficult to obtain and change over time. We address the task of inferring persona attributes from a single day of mobile activity logs. No suitable publicly available benchmark exists for this task, so we introduce a synthetic benchmark of 1,600 persona-log pairs. We target on-device inference so that raw logs never leave the phone, which makes memory rather than speed the limiting constraint: a day of activity yields roughly 30K tokens, whose key-value cache alone exceeds the INT4 weights of a 4B-parameter model. We therefore propose a log filtering method that retains only behaviorally distinct entries. Filtering reduces the memory footprint by up to 39% across nine models from four families and more than halves prefill time, while maintaining or improving prediction quality. For Qwen3-4B it removes 2.5GB, bringing the model from well beyond a realistic per-process budget to a manageable one. Within our benchmark, these results indicate that preserving diverse behavioral events matters more for persona prediction than retaining every semantically similar log entry.

items.title: Failure Broadens, Success Sharpens: Continual Adaptation of Tool-Use Agents Across Diverse Tasks with Dual-Polarity Memory
items.summary: Large language model agents can self-improve over time by utilizing procedural memory derived from prior task trajectories, yet the distinct utilities of memories derived from local successes and failures remain underexplored. This work studies this question in a realistic setting with heterogeneous streams of multi-domain tool-use tasks and various environment constraints common in real-world scenarios. We develop \emph{Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance} (DualPM), a simple, retrieval-free memory workflow characterized by (1) customizable reflection and procedural memory generation from both local successes and failures within each trajectory, and (2) periodic memory consolidation over long task streams under a given memory capacity, preventing memory explosion. Online prequential evaluation with fine-grained metrics reveals that failure memory more strongly broadens coverage, success memory better streamlines execution, while combining both polarities effectively integrates both benefits. Further studies demonstrate that DualPM enables cross-domain memory generalization and continual memory adaptation, while external evaluation on EvoMemBench reveals the portability and effectiveness of DualPM as a general long-term procedural memory method.

items.title: Sparse-to-Sparse Feature Learning for Cross-Layer Analysis and Steering
items.summary: Understanding how models internally represent information is a central challenge in interpretation and control. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense hidden representations into sparse features, and cross-layer methods capture structure spanning multiple layers. However, existing objectives do not explicitly train the sparse code at one layer to predict the sparse code at the next layer. We propose sparse-to-sparse feature learning (S2S), where sparse features at each intermediate layer are trained to predict those of the immediately following layer, with the final layer anchored by an output-distribution loss and optimization proceeding sequentially from output to input. Experiments across eight language models show stronger adjacent-layer correspondence than matched sparse-feature baselines. We evaluate feature-based interventions at matched output-distribution shift, separating steering-induced effects from sparse-pathway reconstruction effects. Causal ablation provides complementary evidence beyond correspondence metrics.

items.title: Verifiable but Not Predictable: What Sentence Embeddings Know About Propositional Decomposition
items.summary: Quality control for proposition decomposition by large language models (LLMs) raises two asymmetric questions. After decomposition, one can verify: given a sentence and a candidate proposition, does the proposition belong to that sentence? Before decomposition, one would like to predict: how many propositions should the sentence yield? On PropSegmEnt, a corpus of English Wikipedia sentences each segmented by three human annotators, we find that the two questions live in different representational spaces. A natural language inference (NLI) judge verifies membership with 92.8% accuracy and an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.977, and its residual errors turn out to be mostly propositions that are true in document context rather than genuine entailment mistakes. Vector geometry cannot verify: cosine similarity saturates, and a sentence embedding is not a linear combination of its propositions' embeddings. For prediction, every symbolic anchor we test, namely token count, the CPIDR idea-density counter, and a Neo-Davidsonian predicate count, reduces to a length proxy once token count is controlled. A linear ridge probe on sentence embeddings is the only predictor that keeps genuine count signal: its length-partialled correlation with human counts is 0.40-0.49 with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) excluding zero, and it orders length-matched sentence pairs correctly 67-71% of the time against a 50% chance level, statistically matching the inter-annotator agreement ceiling. This signal survives INT8 quantization without loss, INT4 at a small cost, and Matryoshka truncation to 256 dimensions, and it works as well in a 2021 encoder as in a 2025 one. Its structured weakness is a systematic under-splitting of long sentences. We distill the protocol lessons, including a retracted pilot study, into a checklist for probing length-confounded quantities.

items.title: Rethinking Knowledge Distillation for Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: Knowledge distillation has recently proven highly effective for improving autoregressive models, but its applicability to DLMs remains poorly understood. We present the first systematic study of KD for DLMs and uncover two non-intuitive failures of classical forward-KL (FKL) distillation: (i) student perplexity does not improve monotonically with more teacher-generated data, and (ii) on the same teacher-generated corpus, FKL distillation underperforms simply training the student with the original DLM denoising objective. To address them, we propose a unified, data-free distillation framework for masked DLMs. First, the framework runs an off-policy distillation phase that absorbs general knowledge from a static set of teacher-generated data. Then, the framework employs on-policy distillation which consists of three techniques: a trajectory loss along the student's own reverse process, confidence reweighting that down-weights tokens where the teacher is unsure, and a trust-region anchor that stabilizes the moving target. On MDLM, the resulting student attains a GPT-2 perplexity of $24.75$, surpassing the teacher's $27.04$; on Dream-7B distillation to a 93M student model, the framework reduces Qwen-2.5 perplexity from the FKL-distilled baseline of $25.23$ to $19.83$ while preserving performance on zero-shot general capability benchmarks.

items.title: Refusal Is Not Scored: A Coverage Limit in Content-Based Bias Evaluation
items.summary: Bias audits of conversational models often discard refusals (responses such as "I can't assist with that request") before scoring, a filtering step which is rarely examined as a measurement decision even though it determines which responses an audit is capable of evaluating. This work examines what the step removes, applying seven bias-evaluation instruments spanning both deployed paradigms, three dictionary-based and four LLM-as-judge, to two intersectional datasets of 360 generated responses each. In both datasets, the filter removed a demographically skewed subset produced entirely by one of the three responder models, which refused North Korean prompts at 2.15 times the rate of American prompts on declarative content and 1.76 times on operational content. We then remove the filter and pass every refusal to all seven instruments. Bias-Lexicon scores refusals as clean, and including them shrinks the nationality disparity it reports. HurtLex appears to register the disparity, but we trace this entirely to a single lexicon entry matching the token "can" in "I can't". The LLM judges either flag most responses or rate refusals as unbiased. For the two judges that discriminate, including refusals lowers the nationality disparity they report, and no instrument identifies the refusal disparity. The failure is therefore a coverage limit upstream of scoring rather than a calibration gap that a better lexicon or judge prompt would be expected to close, which makes the behavioral channel an instrument is sensitive to a question of construct validity rather than one of method selection.

items.title: Rethinking Sequential Locate-Then-Edit: Optimality and Stability
items.summary: The Locate-Then-Edit framework enables efficient knowledge updates in large language models without requiring full retraining. Recent research has increasingly focused on sequential editing, where knowledge arrives continuously and the model is updated incrementally. However, existing sequential methods commonly suffer from catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only a few hundred edits. In contrast, batch editing - which jointly optimizes all edits and yields the optimal solution under a specified editing objective - can support tens of thousands of edits with high edit efficacy while preserving the model's general capabilities, resulting in a substantial performance gap between the two editing paradigms. In this paper, we demonstrate that this gap can be closed via a batch-equivalent sequential editing approach. Moreover, we investigate the underlying mechanism of model degradation in existing sequential methods by analyzing the convergence behavior of weight perturbations as edits accumulate. Our analysis reveals that current methods typically exhibit linear or logarithmic growth in perturbation, whereas the proposed batch-equivalent method achieves time-invariant growth, thereby theoretically guaranteeing long-term stability and preserving the integrity of pretrained knowledge throughout massive-scale sequential editing.

items.title: Sports Agent: A Self-Evolving System for Conversational Data Analytics
items.summary: Conversational sports analytics requires accurate, evidence-based responses with low latency. Changes in query distributions, data resources, and model behavior can degrade static agent configurations, motivating controlled evolution guided by runtime evidence. We present Sports Agent, a self-evolving framework integrating an Agentic SQL Model for structured-data reasoning, a harness for planning and tool orchestration, and a unified Feedback Engine connecting online execution with offline evolution. The engine assesses responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, diagnoses failures, and generates evolution signals. Model evolution combines SQL-to-Question Scaling for coverage expansion with Graph-Guided Scaling for error-targeted synthesis. Generated questions undergo trajectory distillation and quality filtering for iterative supervised fine-tuning, followed by a separate Post-RL stage. Harness evolution translates recurrent failures into bounded prompt and skill updates, validated through independent audits, execution replay, and regression testing. Performance-tolerance checks guard against unacceptable degradation during simplification. The resulting Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-based model outperforms Qwen3.8-Max on sports question answering and analysis while achieving approximately three times the inference efficiency. Across 30 harness-evolution rounds, the aggregate performance score improves by 10.8 points. In a live sports analytics product, the evolved system improves factual correctness by 10.5 points and average response length, a proxy for answer richness, by 158.1%, while reducing average latency by 41.3% relative to the baseline.

items.title: NORMCRAFT: Cultural Norm Generation for Context-Aware Language Model Alignment
items.summary: Cultural alignment requires large language models (LLMs) to infer often-implicit social norms from a scenario and its cultural context. Existing approaches typically adapt individual models or supply external cultural knowledge, while learning norm inference independently of downstream response generation remains underexplored. We introduce NORMCRAFT, a modular framework that decouples norm inference from response generation. Through norm-centric multi-view supervision, we train an LLM as a norm generator to recover shared norms from prospective, adherence, and violation scenarios without downstream response labels. The generated norms guide a separate, frozen LLM (the responder). With Qwen3.5-4B as the responder, NORMCRAFT outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines on four of five downstream metrics. On SafeWorld, its responses reflect the reference norms more often (Coverage) and more precisely (Faithfulness), exceeding Responder SFT by 18.0 and 14.1 percentage points, respectively. Direct norm evaluation also shows higher norm quality than the base and few-shot generators. The same trained generator improves cultural alignment on SafeWorld across fourteen frozen LLMs spanning five families and 0.8B to 27B parameters, with the largest gains for the smallest models.

items.title: Tells of a Lying Machine: Analyzing LLM-Generated Strategic Dialogue in Chinese Werewolf
items.summary: Social-deduction games give models opposing objectives, but they also give roles different information and speaking obligations. We analyze 5,404 public utterances from 150 Chinese Werewolf games played by 12 models, comparing ordinary wolves with ordinary villagers so that special roles are excluded. Private knowledge and goals still differ, and no utterance is verified as true or false. After model and length adjustment, wolf utterances score higher on both certainty and uncertainty (coefficients +0.074 and +0.072). Emotional intensification has the largest rank-biserial effect (r = .145), but it depends on a single degree marker and correlates weakly with human-rated affect. Three annotators' ratings of 392 utterances show higher wolf scores on four behavioral dimensions, and five LLM judges reach 60.8%-70.2% accuracy on a shared evaluation set. In a generation probe that prompts six models with a wolf identity but a villager speaking goal under fixed public context, certainty (+0.164) and emotional intensification (+0.095) increase. These findings describe role-associated language rather than verified lying, and they argue for explicit comparison groups and lexicon sensitivity checks in game-based deception evaluation. Data and code are available at https://github.com/justinchoi929/Tells-of-a-Lying-Machine

items.title: Multimodal Safety Evaluation of Vision-Language Models in Japanese
items.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in Japanese-language settings, yet multimodal safety evaluation has been largely English-centric. We extend the Multimodal Safety Test Suite (MSTS) of R\"ottger et al. (2025) to Japanese as the 12th language, contributing 320 machine-translated and post-edited cases with reference answers plus 82 culturally localized Japanese images. We introduce an evaluation framework that (i) extends MSTS's 3-class safety grouping with a 5-point scale that also rewards useful (not just safe) responses, and (ii) separates image recognition from safety judgment to isolate recognition errors. Using this framework, we evaluate five modern Japanese VLMs (Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5, InternVL3, LLM-JP-4-VL, Qwen3-VL) against human evaluation, and find substantial variance in the safety readiness across the models. Finally, we evaluate two LLM-as-a-Judge models and find that providing a reference answer improves agreement with human safety judgments, though recall for detecting unsafe responses remains limited, underscoring the difficulty of automating multimodal safety evaluation. The dataset created for our study will be released upon publication.

items.title: Pitfalls of Dependency-Ready Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have shown strong performance on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku, Trip Planning, and Countdown. MDMs introduce a freedom in the order in which tokens may be unmasked, and to exercise this freedom for good accuracy, early decoding strategies relied on signals of confidence or the downstream impact of decoding a token. However, simple examples seem to illustrate that resolving a token's dependencies before unmasking it should be important. Therefore, we examine whether this principle, which we call dependency-ready decoding, would contribute to better accuracy, from a practical and a theoretical perspective. We examine a recent decoder that implements dependency-readiness through attention, and generally find that when it performs better than confidence-based or future utility baselines, its decoding order collapses to left-to-right decoding. For theoretical analysis, we establish a definition of dependency without resorting to attention, measured by an information-theoretic score of how much revealing a single masked token (or a set) would shift the model's prediction for another. We prove that when the margin is large relative to this score, no such revelation can change the top prediction, so in this regime Maximum-Margin decoding already commits dependency-ready tokens. items.title: Teaching a Multilingual Translation Model Regional Varieties: Castilian and Latin American Spanish, Asturian, Aragonese and Aranese with MADLAD-400-3B-MT
items.summary: Massively multilingual translation models usually have one tag per language and no control over regional varieties, and they cover a region's smaller languages poorly or not at all. We report three fine-tunes of MADLAD-400-3B-MT, each adding target tags with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), back-translation of monolingual text and replay of the base model's own translations: <2es_ES> for Spanish as written in Spain, <2es_419> for Latin American Spanish, and one model for three Romance languages of the Iberian Peninsula, Asturian (<2ast>), Aragonese (<2an>) and Aranese (<2oc_aranes>). For the Spanish varieties we annotate the 250.9M documents of MADLAD-400's Spanish split with a domain-supervised Spain vs. Latin America classifier and select variety text with a rule that admitted no Latin American document in a 340-document reference set. The Castilian model chooses Spain's everyday vocabulary in 97% of a targeted test (base model 62%) and vosotros for informal plural address in 70% (10%), while improving chrF++ on human references. A first finding is tag collapse: with a new tag initialised from <2es>, the parent tag drifts to the new variety (84-87% identical outputs). In the Iberian model, contrastive pairs and a separate learning rate for the tag embeddings keep each tag in its own language. Trained only on publicly available data, mostly the TAN-IBE Wikipedia corpora, the Iberian model matches or beats the TAN-IBE Marian systems in four of six Spanish directions on FLORES+, is 1.9 BLEU behind in Spanish->Aranese, and is second only to SalamandraTA-7B in most directions. The exception, Spanish->Aragonese, reflects a difference of written variety between Aragonese Wikipedia and the FLORES+ reference, not model quality. All three fine-tunes lose 0.6-0.7 chrF++ on average in thirteen other FLORES-200 directions. We release the models, data and variety classifier under open licences
