items.title: Where Does Free-Text 3D Grounding Fail? An Error Analysis of Report-Sentence Segmentation in Chest CT
items.summary: Free-text 3D grounding, segmenting in a CT volume the region described by one sentence of the radiology report, could link reports to images at scale, but it is unclear where current models fail. We analyse the publicly released VoxTell model on all 381 findings of the 200-scan ReXGroundingCT validation set, where it grounds 53.5% of findings. Its failures are rarely about which lesion or side is meant. No miss lies on the side opposite to the one named, and findings are almost never confused with one another. Instead, predictions are too large, land on a neighbouring lesion on the correct side, or are missing for small findings, and diffuse findings are rarely grounded. Removing location words halves performance, to the level of label-only prompting, and anatomical rules derived from the sentence never improve the full-sentence output. The same pattern holds on the hidden 300-scan test set. Further progress therefore depends on extent estimation and small-lesion sensitivity rather than on anatomical post-processing.

items.title: Embodied-VGGT: Preserving Reliable Local Geometry for Long-Sequence Reconstruction
items.summary: Long sequence reconstruction must correct accumulated drift while preserving locally consistent geometry. In robotics and autonomous driving, embodied acquisition provides recurring platform- environment geometry and repeated observations of scene structure and platform motion. We present Embodied-VGGT, which exploits these cues to establish reliable local relationships and selectively preserve them during global refinement. Memory-Augmented Grounded Chunks (MAGC) builds on Scal3R's global context memory and uses relative scale references derived from predicted ground geometry to regularize test-time memory updates, encouraging cross-chunk consistency while limiting changes to reliable local geometry. Superpoint Alignment (SA) and Cross-Loop Optimization (CL) jointly address the robust establishment and preservation of geometric relationships. SA balances ground and non-ground evidence across spatial regions to estimate inter-chunk translation. CL uses geometric and motion consistency across interleaved windows to select coherent chunk groups, each receiving a shared Sim(3) correction that preserves its internal relative transformations during global optimization. Experiments on five public driving benchmarks demonstrate consistent and substantial improvements in long sequence reconstruction. On KITTI Odometry, Embodied-VGGT achieves a mean absolute trajectory error of 7.30 m and a Chamfer distance of 2.67 m, reducing these errors by 46.8% and 23.3% compared with the state-of-the-art baseline under same evaluation protocol. To facilitate reproducibility, we released our code: https://github.com/Ang-Sheep/Embodied-VGGT.

items.title: FasterGRN: Reducing the Refinement Redundancy for Accelerating Generative Refinement Networks
items.summary: Departing from the paradigm of diffusion and autoregressive models, Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) enables high-quality image generation through iterative refinements. However, this repeated processing over the entire visual representations results in substantial computation overhead. Furthermore, the binary representations and global refinement mechanism in GRN disable the direct application of acceleration strategies developed for other generative models. To accelerate GRN model, we first observe several key properties by analyzing the entire generative process. That includes the stage characteristic, dual branch similarity and more importantly, the $\textbf{refinement redundancy}$. Motivated by the observations, we present $\textbf{FasterGRN}$, a training-free acceleration method for the Generative Refinement Network. $\textbf{FasterGRN}$ first divides the GRN into the semantic establishment stage and detail refinement stage according to its semantic establishment. For alleviating the refinement redundancy mainly resulting from the detail refinement stage, we propose Adaptive Retention Expansion ($\textbf{ARE}$) and Selective Token Freezing ($\textbf{STF}$) to shrink refinement steps and reduce token computations, respectively. In the experiments on GenEval and DPG-Bench benchmarks, our method $\textbf{FasterGRN}$ achieves a $2.03\times$ sampling speedup while largely preserving image generation performance. Our evaluation on COCO datasets additionally demonstrates that $\textbf{FasterGRN}$ even outperforms the original GRN in image fidelity.

items.title: geo-eval-harness: An Evaluation Harness for Geospatial Foundation Models
items.summary: Geospatial foundation model (GFM) research papers are plagued by inconsistent evaluation settings (e.g., different pre-processing and probes), making it difficult to separate performance from evaluation choices. We propose geo-eval-harness}, an open-source framework for controlled model comparisons. We use this harness to evaluate 100 GFMs and general vision models on 6 classification and 14 segmentation datasets, using multiple probes on frozen or low-rank-adapted encoders. We show that under controlled evaluation, general vision backbones are competitive on RGB classification and high-resolution segmentation, but GFMs shine on multispectral tasks. When we compare any two of the top-ten classification models on a single dataset, their 95% confidence intervals overlap 73% of the time. We show that bigger models are not always better: inference FLOPs correlate weakly with segmentation performance. Moreover, translating inference compute into large-area mapping workloads shows how small accuracy differences have outsized deployment cost differences: with frozen encoders on SpaceNet2, a 0.9-point mIoU difference corresponds to 5.9x the compute and days of additional projected GPU time. Our findings stress the importance of comparing models under explicit and fixed settings, and reporting uncertainty and deployment compute alongside accuracy. Our geo-eval-harness makes controlled experiments easy, fast, and fully reproducible. We release the code, configurations, and results at https://github.com/torchgeo/geo-eval-harness.

items.title: ScaleCurve: From Constant Scale to Consistent Motion for World-Space Human Mesh Recovery
items.summary: World-space human mesh recovery can lose spatial consistency even when camera-space body estimates are accurate. A single sequence-wide scale resolves global scale ambiguity but cannot correct local scale distortion along a reconstructed camera path. We present ScaleCurve, a framework that estimates time-varying metric corrections from human-ground geometry. We construct scale observations by comparing predicted foot geometry with locally fitted ground planes. Joint temporal optimization downweights inconsistent observations and couples neighboring scale estimates, allowing calibration to adapt along the camera path without freely following measurement noise. We scale camera translation increments and integrate them into a calibrated trajectory. With this camera fixed, we refine the lifted body motion using 2D image evidence and pretrained 3D dynamics, while restricting global trajectory rescaling. ScaleCurve achieves state-of-the-art performance on most evaluated metrics on both EMDB-2 and SLOPER4D. Consistent gains across three HMR backbones demonstrate its compatibility with diverse body estimates without retraining. Code will be made publicly available.

items.title: Manga Page Parser: Comprehensive Visual Parsing through Local Story Understanding
items.summary: Understanding manga requires connecting who appears and who speaks with the events, character states, and relationships that unfold across panels. We study manga visual parsing through local story understanding: analyzing each double-page spread independently to capture and organize its story information in a reusable structured representation. We propose MangaParser, an agentic reading framework that jointly performs character clustering, speaker diarization, and speaker-to-character binding within a shared multimodal conversation, without additional training or fine-tuning. The agent uses structured story memory to guide character and speaker identification, inspecting relevant image regions when uncertain and refining its predictions and story records together as evidence accumulates. Quantitative evaluations show that our parser substantially outperforms manga-specific models across multiple backbones. Parsing examples illustrate how a unified representation links the character and speaker predictions with narrative content and supporting evidence. We further test reusability through story question answering using outputs generated before the questions are provided. The results confirm output reusability, offering a foundation for manga translation, content retrieval, and question answering.

items.title: Rethinking Unsupervised Cross-Modal Homography Estimation:Spatially Aware Representations and Geometric Consistency Learning
items.summary: Unsupervised cross-modal homography estimation is challenging because appearance differences obscure shared geometric structures. Separating modality transfer from homography estimation helps reduce these differences, but accurate alignment still requires effective geometric representations and consistency constraints on the two subtasks. We propose GeoCo (Geometry-Aware and Consistency-Constrained Homography Estimation), a framework that addresses these two requirements without cross-modal transformation labels. Its homography estimator, RVHomo, adapts hierarchical features from a frozen vision foundation model (VFM) and fuses them with local CNN features to capture structural context and spatial detail. Two geometric consistency constraints encourage modality transfer to preserve geometry and homography predictions to remain consistent under synthetic geometric transformations. Through two-stage progressive distillation, we further obtain GeoCo-D, which uses the lightweight RVHomo-D estimator. An intermediate model first learns to perform cross-modal matching without modality transfer, then transfers prediction and feature knowledge to the student, eliminating online VFM extraction. Experiments on GoogleMap, OPT-SAR, FSD, and VIS-IR show that GeoCo reduces mean average corner error by 17.4-46.7% relative to the best-performing baseline on each dataset. GeoCo-D also outperforms all compared baselines while using 98.5% fewer parameters and 70.4% fewer FLOPs than the complete GeoCo teacher.

items.title: MoSk: A Unified Motion-Skeleton Foundation Model for Human Motion Understanding and Generation
items.summary: Foundation models (FMs) have advanced visual understanding and generation by providing semantically rich representations. However, this role of FMs remains underexplored in human motion. Large motion datasets offer diverse movements at scale, but often lack action labels for systematically evaluating learned representations on understanding tasks. Skeleton datasets enable such evaluation through established recognition protocols, yet are typically smaller and focus on predefined actions captured in controlled environments. To combine these strengths, we present MoSk, to the best of our knowledge, the first Motion-Skeleton foundation model to integrate motion and skeleton datasets. MoSk learns shared representations through self-supervised masked motion modeling. We incorporate joint-name embeddings to provide a common anatomical reference across various skeleton formats. A cross-attention decoder reconstructs masked motion from the encoder's features, with joint-name embeddings specifying the target joints. Experiments demonstrate strong action-recognition performance across diverse settings, including linear evaluation and fine-tuning. MoSk also substantially improves motion generation across multiple backbones through representation alignment, reducing FID on MotionMillion by up to 9.75 for unconditional generation and 3.83 for text-to-motion generation.

items.title: Incorporating the Knowledge Distillation to Improve the EfficientNet Transfer Learning Capability
items.summary: Due to the Deep Learning requirement for a large training dataset, Transfer Learning has become a central method in the field of Computer Vision, which heavily used Deep Learning. Since the adoption of transfer learning in the field, the performance of the models in computer vision is significantly upgraded. The common transfer learning practice in computer vision research is to use state-of-the-art architectures in the ImageNet dataset as the backbone network. The best performing architecture in ImageNet is currently held by EfficientNet, which is a set of architectures that were progressively grown from a baseline architecture. By observing the EfficientNet development approach, it is natural to hypothesize that the smaller EfficientNet architecture is capable to contain the knowledge of the larger architecture. This hypothesis comes from the fact that the larger EfficientNet architecture was grown from the smaller architecture. Therefore, in this study, we experimented if it is beneficial to transfer the knowledge from the larger architecture to the smaller architecture of the EfficientNet. To achieve this goal, we proposed a transfer learning method that uses Knowledge Distillation as the knowledge transfer mechanism from the larger to smaller architecture. We found that the proposed method is able to upgrade the performance of each of the EfficientNet architecture. Several smaller architectures are even able to outperform the larger architecture that was trained using the standard transfer learning method.

items.title: ContextHands: Completing Hand Motion with Learned Context and Joint-Specific Body Kinematics
items.summary: Detailed hand motion contributes to the realism and expressiveness of generated human motion. Completing these details from body motion and language requires connecting the context of an action to the articulation of the hands. We introduce ContextHands, which completes hand motion from an observed body sequence and text descriptions assigned to hands and time intervals. Our approach learns probabilistic hand features from the descriptions and body motion, using auxiliary hand prediction to connect these features to hand articulation. A body encoder preserves joint and body-part features across multiple temporal scales, allowing each hand joint to query these features for joint-specific body information. The diffusion generator combines this joint-specific body information with the learned hand context. Both encoders and the generator are trained jointly, so the final generation objective also shapes the context features. Experiments on the OakInk2 dataset show that ContextHands generates more accurate hand motion and achieves lower Fr\'echet Hand Distance than existing hand-motion and general human-motion generation methods adapted to the task. In qualitative examples of grasping and tool use, ContextHands more closely reproduces the detailed hand poses in the reference motion. We will release our code and pretrained models to support further research.

items.title: Counter-DECEIVR: Counterfactual Explanations for Deepfake Detectors using Detector-Guided Rectified Flow Inversion
items.summary: Deep-learning-generated media are increasingly passed off as real, driving an arms race between image generators and deepfake detectors. Trust in the latter is limited by their often black-box nature; and, while region-based explanations can sometimes be extracted, these become less useful as generation quality improves. Counterfactual examples, which show the minimal change that flips a detector's decision, reveal what evidence drives a verdict, helping analysts decide whether to trust it. This work introduces Counter-DECEIVR (DEtector-guided reCtifiEd flow InVeRsion for counterfactuals), a novel training-free framework that generates counterfactual examples. Counter-DECEIVR steers latents in the velocity field of a rectified flow model using gradients from off-the-shelf deepfake detectors, without training a generator or adapting the detector; unlike prior methods, it requires no per-instance or per-detector fitting and no diffusion training on the target data. items.title: Understanding Diffusion Acceleration: Methods, Trade-Offs, and Open Questions
items.summary: Diffusion and flow-based generative models support high-quality image, audio, and video synthesis. Sampling can require dozens to hundreds of denoiser evaluations, with each pass becoming more expensive as resolution, video length, or model size increases. This cost affects latency and energy use in interactive and edge applications. We examine four approaches to accelerating inference: distillation, consistency training, sampling methods, and denoiser design. We express training objectives, transition maps, and numerical updates in a common notation to compare changes to the learning target, the sampling trajectory, and the work performed within each denoiser pass. Published image and video benchmarks illustrate the quality--cost trade-offs of one- and few-step generation, the interaction between solvers and timestep schedules, the effect of feature caching, and the difference between first-frame latency and sustained streaming throughput. We close with open problems in visual-native architectures and post-compression distillation, solver-aware few-step training, and semantic trajectory alignment with factorized distribution matching.

items.title: Surf-Style: Surface-Based Scene Stylization
items.summary: Consistent and controllable 3D stylization is critical for visual computing applications such as immersive visualization, augmented and virtual reality content creation, and artistic scene rendering. While 2D image stylization has advanced significantly, extending these methods to 3D remains challenging due to the need for cross-view consistency, where stylized renderings must align across all viewpoints. Applying 2D stylization independently to each rendered view often results in inconsistencies across perspectives. Existing methods attempt to improve consistency by leveraging implicit radiance field representations, which model scene appearance as a function of spatial locations. However, these methods struggle with ambiguity in updating colors, as the indirect dependence between pixel appearance and learnable scene parameters makes it difficult to enforce consistent stylization during optimization. This work presents Surface-based Scene Stylization (Surf-Style), which reconstructs object surfaces in a 3D scene and uses these surfaces to achieve geometric consistency and localized stylization. Surf-Style defines a learnable appearance model over 3D space, which is modified to replicate the visual style of a reference image. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our method achieves superior consistency and offers greater flexibility in controllable stylization, including the ability to target specific surface regions and combine different styles.

items.title: SPARC: Geometry-Guided Attention Pruning for Long-Horizon Camera-Controlled Video Generation
items.summary: We present SPARC, a geometry-guided attention pruning framework that turns the native self-attention of pretrained video diffusion transformers into a unified mechanism for camera control and persistent scene memory. Our key insight is that attention connectivity can simultaneously serve as geometric conditioning for camera control and spatial addressing for historical memory retrieval. Motivated by the asymmetric contextual requirements of reconstructing observed content and synthesizing novel regions, SPARC restricts observed tokens to geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context, while preserving dense attention for unobserved regions. Correspondence-aware attention biasing and order-invariant historical positioning further enable stable retrieval across long temporal gaps. Without introducing additional learnable control or memory modules, SPARC achieves precise camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation while substantially reducing attention computation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of aggressive attention pruning in improving camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity, with an inference speedup of over 50x when combined with four-step distillation. Project page is available at https://zju3dv.github.io/SPARC.

items.title: When to Respond, Where to Ground: Streaming 3D Affordance Grounding
items.summary: Given a continuous RGB-D stream and a language request, streaming 3D affordance grounding requires an agent to decide when to respond and where to locate the requested functional part using only observations available so far. Existing 3D affordance grounding methods typically assume complete scene observations, while streaming vision-language models lack fine-grained 3D functional grounding. Our goal is to jointly determine response timing and functional-part localization during continuous scene observation. We propose StreamAff, an evidence-guided response strategy that makes both decisions from the grounding model's own visual evidence. The model scores the visual patches of the frames it reads: their combined support, weighed against a wait option, decides when to respond, and the highest-scoring patch selects the frame to ground in. A conditional look-back policy lets the model answer from an earlier observation at the moment of the request or wait for new evidence, and zoom-and-refine grounding segments the part named in the answer on the 3D points of the selected frame. We further introduce StreamFun3D, a benchmark derived from real-world 3D scenes that evaluates response timing and grounding across four evidence settings: Current, History, Future, and Unobserved, together with StreamIoU, a metric that credits a mask only when the response is timely and grounded in a valid source frame. We adapt offline 3D affordance grounding methods and build external-decider baselines that pair vision-language models with our mask decoder. StreamAff achieves 30.14% StreamIoU on 15-second streams, a 40.6% relative improvement over the strongest of these baselines.

items.title: Hijacking 3D Generation: Targeted Adversarial Attacks against Image-to-3D Models via Prefix Trajectory Alignment
items.summary: Online services that deploy Image-to-3D models enable users to generate high-quality 3D assets from a single image. However, the generated 3D geometry can violate content policies and cause broader security risks. To prevent such content, these services typically use policy-restricted inspectors to examine uploaded images before generation. Since the inspector examines only the visible content of the input, a visually benign image can still induce the generation of policy-restricted 3D geometry. However, turning this vulnerability into an effective attack is non-trivial in the black-box setting: global backpropagation through the long DiT generation trajectory is difficult to fit, while different image preprocessing pipelines across services can substantially reduce transferability. In this paper, we present PTA3D, a targeted adversarial attack against Image-to-3D models that addresses these challenges through Prefix Trajectory Alignment (PTA) and Preprocessing Aware Optimization (PAO). PTA progressively aligns the prefix DiT outputs of the adversarial trajectory with those of the target trajectory, where the core geometric structure is formed, allowing the final geometry to be controlled without optimizing through the complete generation trajectory. PAO exposes adversarial optimization to diverse image transformations rather than a single preprocessing pipeline, reducing sensitivity to the mismatch between surrogate and target services. We establish a prefix-to-output bound and a preprocessing-aware transfer bound to theoretically characterize the effectiveness of the two designs. Experiments on three open-source Image-to-3D models and three online services show that PTA3D achieves 41.5%-88.5% ASR on online services and 90.8%-94.6% ASR in white box settings, substantially outperforming existing attacks.

items.title: Projector Subspace Optimization for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance through instruction tuning, yet adapting them to sequential tasks requires Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT). Existing replay-free methods expand prompts or routed LoRA experts across multi-layer decoders, incurring heavy parameter and routing overhead while shifting internal feature distributions. Instead, we identify the final linear layer of the vision-language projector as a high-capacity, coordinate-stationary bridge, where sequential updates easily induce interface drift by displacing historical visual tokens. While low-rank subspace adaptation offers a compact remedy, selecting directions solely from historical statistics or task gradients sacrifices plasticity or stability, and unconstrained multi-step updates still accumulate large drift. To resolve both issues, we propose Projector Refinement through Optimized Update Directions (PROUD), a continual subspace optimization framework for the terminal projector layer. At task onset, PROUD combines retained input statistics with initial gradients to analytically extract a metric-orthonormal subspace maximizing first-order task gain under a drift budget. During training, it regularizes updates within this fixed subspace via an exact Frobenius penalty before losslessly merging them with zero inference or routing overhead. Experiments on UCIT and CoIN across MLLM backbones show that PROUD outperforms recent replay-free baselines in continual accuracy while curbing forgetting with a fraction of trainable parameters.

items.title: WorldBridge: Bridging Scattered Views for Coherent 3D World Generation
items.summary: Generating coherent and explorable 3D worlds from scattered images with little or no visual overlap is a fundamental and long-standing challenge in computer vision, which existing geometry-aware methods fail to address. Meanwhile, existing image- and video-based methods may generate unseen regions but produce inconsistent geometry across views. To bridge this gap, we present WorldBridge, a framework for coherent and controllable 3D world generation under scattered images with little or no visual overlap. WorldBridge encodes scattered references into a global scene context to guide geometry and appearance generation across views. Our temporal and spatial reference attention mechanism further enhances the fidelity of temporal references along the target trajectory and supports flexible spatial references outside it. A plug-and-play latent-reference consistency strategy improves reference fidelity through reprojection-guided test-time optimization. We also introduce the WorldBridge benchmark suite to evaluate 3D world generation from scattered, low-overlap references, which is rarely explored by current benchmarks. Both qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate that our method enables controllable and coherent 3D world generation, surpassing the existing state-of-the-art solutions. Our project page is available at https://davidyan2001.github.io/WorldBridge/.

items.title: TaCo: Rethinking Correlation for Visual Tracking on Edge Devices
items.summary: Lightweight trackers have replaced cross-correlation with attention, and on low-power edge hardware they pay for it, since memory-bound softmax, normalization and reshaping operators of attention cost far more time than their arithmetic suggests. Benchmarking efficient trackers on an edge Neural Processing Unit (NPU) and an Arm CPU under one numerically validated protocol, we find that correlation trackers are the fast ones, but they lag in accuracy unless they adopt a ViT backbone, which brings attention back. We revisit what correlation lacks. Template--search interaction serves two roles: conditioning the search features on the target and matching them against it spatially. Attention does both, whereas correlation only matches, and does so on features extracted without knowledge of the target. We present TaCo (Target-aligned Correlation), which supplies the missing conditioning without attention by letting the template enter the per-frame network only as operands computed once per video. A descriptor of the target scales and shifts the search features channel by channel inside the backbone, and kernels aligned with the target box, each with a weight predicted from the template, correlate with them in one matrix product. With the backbone fixed, our correlation remains essential while incurring negligible NPU overhead, offering a better speed-accuracy trade-off than the attention-based interactions we tested. TaCo-T achieves 62.3% LaSOT AUC at 184 FPS on the Rockchip RV1126B NPU and 96 FPS on a Raspberry Pi 5 CPU, 3.0x and 3.5x the NPU speed of HiT-Tiny and AsymTrack-T at higher accuracy. TaCo-B reaches 65.6% at 50 FPS on the NPU, more than twice the speed of HiT-Base, AsymTrack-B and LightFC-vit, again at higher accuracy. Code and models are available at https://github.com/TsingWei/TaCo-Tracker.

items.title: From Diagnosing Alignment to Joint Supervision in Multimodal Draft Training
items.summary: Multimodal drafts learn from multimodal (MM) and text-only (TXT) supervision, yet their effects on alignment and how to combine them remain unclear. We diagnose draft-target alignment through paired predictions with and without visual input, decomposing distributional error into text-conditioned and visual-response components. Drafts with similar text-conditioned alignment can still differ markedly in visual-response risk and acceptance. Controlled continuation training shows that high-risk groups outperform random and low-risk groups, and visual-response risk guides MM training more effectively than aggregate risk. Building on these diagnostics, we propose MNRS-Joint, which configures joint supervision from a given draft's component-risk distributions, using modality-specific mean risks to determine the MM:TXT mixture. Across three warm-ups, its distinct mixtures fall in high-performing regions of the ratio sweeps. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, MNRS-Joint improves mean accepted length from 3.35 to 3.53 and mean speedup from $2.04\times$ to $2.16\times$ over composition-matched random training under greedy tree decoding. The gains also hold under stochastic chain decoding.

items.title: Exploring the Design Factors of Pixel-space Diffusion
items.summary: In this paper, we introduce EiT by exploring the key design factors of pixel-space diffusion from three perspectives: model architecture, representation, and frequency domain. Inspired by Denoising Autoencoders (DAE) which perform denoising through a bottleneck, we construct a U-shaped pixel diffusion transformer that performs explicit compression along the channel dimension. In terms of representation, we find that both pixel and latent diffusion transformers exhibit a three-stage representation dynamics across layers and timesteps: denoising/local feature expansion, basis lift-up, and posterior projection. Moreover, earlier denoising and a longer basis lift-up stage are associated with better generation, which EiT naturally achieves through its channel bottleneck and increased network depth. From the frequency perspective, we establish the equivalence between pixel-space and frequency-space diffusion when keeping the network operating in pixel space. On ImageNet $256\times256$ and $512\times512$, EiT consistently outperforms JiT (Just image Transformers) in generation quality. Specifically, our EiT achieves better FID than JiT: 1.61 vs. 1.85 at $256\times256$, and 1.73 vs. 1.99 at $512\times512$. Remarkably, EiT can be seamlessly applied to video pixel diffusion by simply extending the patch size to temporal dimension and outperforms video latent diffusion in FVD evaluated on Kinetics-600 (resolution 256), under comparable total network parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/forever208/EiT

items.title: FoMNet: Adaptive Kernels Meet Contextual Matching for Cross-Modal Homography Estimation
items.summary: Cross-modal homography estimation requires reliable correspondences despite appearance differences between sensing modalities. Multi-scale refinement progressively reduces the search range, but its accuracy remains limited by the ability of matching features to distinguish nearby candidates. The vision foundation model (VFM) provides complementary representations, yet integrating these features through fixed interpolation leaves their spatial aggregation independent of image content and the correspondence objective. We propose the Foundation Model-Enhanced Matching Network (FoMNet), which combines learned spatial adaptation of VFM features with contextual correspondence estimation. Patch Feature Upsampling (PFU) progressively predicts location-specific kernels to aggregate neighboring features on upsampled grids, preparing VFM representations for fusion with CNN features at different matching scales. Contextual Correlation Refinement (CCR) then jointly processes source descriptors and local correlations with spatial context to refine candidate scores before each homography update. To reduce upsampling overhead, we develop FoMNet-D, which replaces PFU with bicubic interpolation and uses multi-scale feature-relation distillation to recover accuracy. Experiments on five cross-modal datasets show that FoMNet achieves the lowest mean average corner error (MACE) among the evaluated methods, reducing MACE by 10.6%-72.7% relative to MCNet. FoMNet-D retains competitive accuracy while reducing inference latency by 34.0% relative to FoMNet.

To reduce upsampling overhead, we develop FoMNet-D, which replaces PFU with bicubic interpolation and uses multi-scale feature-relation distillation to recover accuracy. Experiments on five cross-modal datasets show that FoMNet achieves the lowest mean average corner error (MACE) among the evaluated methods, reducing MACE by 10.6%-72.7% relative to MCNet. FoMNet-D retains competitive accuracy while reducing inference latency by 34.0% relative to FoMNet.

items.title: When Position Favors the Wrong Part: Evaluating Left-Right Discrimination in Semantic Correspondence
items.summary: Overall part-discrimination accuracy can conceal failures when image position favors the wrong bilateral part. We examine whether dense descriptors distinguish the correct part under this conflict and whether their discrimination scores help select matching coordinates. We evaluate position agreement and conflict within the same target images and annotated part pairs, using a bounding-box-side score to define the conditions. We compare the original descriptors with their even and odd components under horizontal reflection, examine feature upsampling with the backbone and adapters fixed, and test candidate-selection rules based on odd scores. On SPair-71k, odd discrimination accuracy falls from 86.66% under agreement to 19.63% under conflict for frozen DINOv2, compared with 95.27% to 86.16% for MARCO. With MARCO's input geometry fixed, odd accuracy in box-side conflict was 34.12% on the native grid and 88.84% after learned upsampling and pooling back to that grid. Odd-score rules improve on the original hard-peak matchers overall for DINOv2 and DINOv3 and on conflict queries for MARCO. With MARCO's soft decoder fixed, reranking the cosine peaks changes mean per-pair PCK by +0.47 pp. For supervised GeoAware-SC, using the odd score to select the localization window center yields only 15 net additional correct matches, with 330 corrections and 315 introduced errors. Evaluating discrimination under position conflict reveals failures hidden by aggregate accuracy. Reporting corrections and introduced errors separately also shows whether a discriminative score produces useful matching decisions.

items.title: What Makes a Gavagai? Learning Visual Concepts from One Positive and Few Negatives
items.summary: Humans can recognize novel concepts from only a few observations by identifying defining visual attributes and eliminating alternative interpretations. However, a single observation is consistent with multiple possible concepts, and accurate visual perception alone is insufficient to determine the intended interpretation. Negative evidence can reduce this ambiguity by eliminating competing hypotheses. Inspired by Quine's gavagai problem, we introduce the Gavagai Benchmark to evaluate whether vision-language models can identify the attributes defining a novel concept from positive and negative examples. The benchmark consists of synthetic images depicting novel combinations of visual attributes and real images of newly described species. Using these datasets, we examine how models use negative examples to identify novel concepts and analyze the respective roles of visual perception and reasoning. Several models struggle even when correct attributes are provided, while others show large gaps when ground-truth attributes are replaced with model predictions. These diagnostic comparisons highlight challenges in both attribute perception and inference from limited evidence.

items.title: Detectable by Design: Learning a Continuous 3D Saliency Field from 2D Detector Responses
items.summary: The 3D points kept in a map decide whether a camera can be localized against it, and this choice matters more as the map becomes sparser. Existing 3D keypoint detectors usually define saliency by semantics, repeatability, reconstruction or descriptor matchability. None of these definitions asks whether a point will actually be detected in an image, and as a result most of the points they select are not detected again in images. In this paper, we define 3D saliency as image detectability: the response of a 2D interest-point detector at a surface point, aggregated over all views in which the point is visible. We propose DetField, a continuous field over 3D space that takes a point cloud as input and predicts detectability at any location around it. The supervision is the response of a 2D detector, back-projected from images onto the point cloud. Multi-scale curvature invariants are passed to the decoder at every query point, bypassing the voxel pooling of the encoder. In a localization benchmark that isolates the choice of 3D points, DetField outperforms Harris-3D and five learned 3D keypoint methods on objects and on real indoor scenes. On unseen rooms, it improves localization success by 7.4 points over Harris-3D, the strongest baseline. On objects, it also leads under a 2D detector not used in training. On sparse maps, it stays ahead of Harris-3D on both objects and real scenes.

items.title: A Simple Yet Effective Agent for Open-World Aerial Object Search
items.summary: Open-world aerial object search methods often rely on persistent spatial maps, learned world models, or task-specific policy training. To examine how far a minimal, training-free design can go, we introduce SimpleUAV, an agent built around a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM). SimpleUAV separates current-view target assessment from history-conditioned action selection, combining fresh candidate evidence with lightweight search context. Local geometry converts visual selections into bounded straight-line movements, depth-based checks halt blocked segments, and measured execution feedback guides subsequent decisions. This closed loop sustains search without persistent spatial maps or task-specific training. SimpleUAV achieves 41.61% Success Rate (SR) on UAV-ON and 11.98% on AerialDojo-200K, compared with 23.80% and 3.20% for the strongest prior baselines, respectively. With limited benchmark-specific adaptation, the same core agent transfers to aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) on TravelUAV, improving Full SR by at least 19.66% across all three splits under L1 assistance. These results establish a strong baseline for evaluating when additional architectural complexity benefits aerial search.

items.title: Out of Sight, Not Out of Clues: Can Video LLMs Guess from Partial Evidence?
items.summary: In real-world applications like egocentric recording, visual accessibility, and surveillance review, visual evidence for Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) is often only partially captured. A reliable model should match its response to the evidence: answering when sufficient, guessing from visible clues when partial, and abstaining when absent. Yet existing benchmarks enforce a binary answerable-or-unanswerable split, leaving partial evidence unmeasured and obscuring whether failures arise from missing evidence or misjudging sufficiency. We introduce ClueProbe, a diagnostic benchmark to (1) separate perceiving evidence from judging sufficiency, and (2) validate our diagnosis via targeted fine-tuning. ClueProbe comprises 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, alongside controlled perturbations altering wording or visual input. Evaluating 10 open-source and proprietary Video LLMs reveals that failures stem from judgment rather than perception: models perceive the evidence yet lack graded sufficiency awareness, answering or refusing outright while rarely guessing from partial clues. Targeted fine-tuning shows that this reflects missing supervision rather than insufficient capacity: supervising the guess level lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/suat-llm/ClueProbe.

items.title: FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images
items.summary: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.

items.title: A Calibration-Referenced Protocol for Measuring Decision Stability under Reference Bank Compression
items.summary: Reference banks used for industrial image inspection can be compressed to fit a deployment budget, but the resulting anomaly decisions depend on both the compressed scores and the operating threshold. We present a four-step protocol that compares compression methods at matched deployment sizes, establishes a reference distribution from 200 recalibrations, evaluates disagreement against two calibration benchmarks, and measures changes by distance from the full-bank threshold. With WideResNet-50, budget-matched product quantization (PQ) at the 10% budget has the lowest decision disagreement among five matched methods, including int8 scalar quantization, on VisA and MVTec AD at both operating levels. Int8 scalar quantization gives lower disagreement than PQ at the other four budgets. On MVTec AD at the lower operating level, PQ meets the calibration median in 34/39 cells and the upper quantile in 39/39 cells. Category-equally weighted image-level AUROC loss at this budget ranges from 0.0003 to 0.0037 across the evaluated configurations. On VisA at the 1% budget and a 1% operating level, disagreement reaches 28.12% (95% CI 23.25--33.58%) among near-threshold anomalies and 1.30% (0.79--2.14%) across the normal holdout. The 10% budget-matched PQ setting retains the lowest disagreement among four compared methods with ResNet-18, with clean reference banks, and when thresholds are estimated from normal-directory probes. The protocol connects deployment size to a calibration-referenced decision measure and identifies the evaluation populations most informative for inspection.

items.title: An Image Detectability Field as a Viewpoint Utility for 2D-3D Localization in Sparse Maps
items.summary: In 2D-3D localization, a camera estimates its pose by matching an image to a 3D map. A camera held in a hand or mounted on a robot can often choose its viewpoint before it takes the image. In this work, we ask whether an image detectability field is a useful viewpoint utility when the planner reads only the geometry of the map. The field can be queried at any 3D point near a surface. From the local geometry around the point, it predicts how likely a 2D image detector is to fire at the projection of the point. We use the trained field as it is, without fine-tuning it for view selection. A fixed SuperPoint and EPnP-RANSAC localizer then estimates the pose from the chosen view. We answer in two settings, each with a test registered before the runs. On synthetic ShapeNet objects with sparse point maps, summing the field over the visible landmarks beats counting them by +2.0 points of localization success rate (object-clustered 95% interval [+0.7, +3.2]). It also beats summing Harris-3D ranks by +2.2 [+0.8, +3.5]. On real indoor scenes from SceneFun3D, our adaptation of the learned view scorer LWL falls below counting on the test rooms. We therefore add the field to a learned per-landmark planner. On the test rooms with sparse maps whose landmarks the field also selects, the planner with the field beats the same planner without it by +1.8 points. It beats the planner with Harris-3D or curvature in its place by +1.0 and +0.8 points. All three room-clustered intervals lie above zero. In both settings, the field helps in sparse maps and is on par with Harris-3D in dense maps.

items.title: Benefit of Structured Representations: When Equivariance Helps in Image Classification
items.summary: Equivariant neural networks promise improved representation learning through structural guarantees. However, mainstream vision encoders rarely incorporate equivariance for most geometric symmetries. Images are a particularly interesting modality with many such symmetries and extensive datasets from which to learn this structure. In this work, we investigate when vision encoders benefit from geometric inductive biases. We study the discrete rotation group of quarter-turns (C4) which acts losslessly without interpolation or boundary artifacts. Combined with image classification as a controlled invariant objective, this allows for a principled empirical investigation into the role of structural guarantees. We introduce ConvNeXt-C4 as a rotation equivariant ConvNeXt with dimension-equivalent yet orientation-structured representations. Training from scratch, our experiments show, that the C4 variant outperforms its base model across all tasks while operating with 6x fewer parameters and 1.6x fewer FLOPs. Its performance advantage increases log-linearly with decreasing training set size, with pre-training providing a similar improvement across both model variants. Analyzing the classifier head reveals that orientation information from the representations' structure is actively used, improving performance by 4.90% across all datasets. Our results highlight the sample-efficiency benefits of equivariance and the value of retained orientation information, motivating further investigation beyond image classification. Code is available at https://github.com/hlzl/equivariant-convnext.

items.title: Spe3DUp: Faithful Trajectory Distillation for Fast Image-to-3D Generation
items.summary: Recent 3D generative models can produce high-quality meshes with complex structures and fine geometric details, with broad applications in games, film, and digital design. However, high-quality generation typically relies on long multi-step sampling processes that repeatedly evaluate large networks, leading to long inference times. At the same time, reference-driven tasks such as game-asset reconstruction and product digitization demand close correspondence to the input image: generated geometry must faithfully reconstruct the specific reference object. Acceleration must therefore reduce sampling computation while preserving the model's ability to reconstruct that object. To enable fast and faithful 3D generation, we introduce Spe3DUp, a coarse-to-fine framework based on Faithful Trajectory Distillation (FTD). FTD directly supervises few-step students with the teacher's input-conditioned denoising trajectories to preserve its generation behavior. We apply FTD separately to coarse geometry generation and geometric refinement, compressing both sampling processes while maintaining correspondence to the reference input. We further accelerate the complete mesh-generation pipeline with efficient geometry decoding and parallel remeshing. Experiments show that Spe3DUp maintains geometric quality and input correspondence close to those of the teacher, accelerates the coarse and refinement DiTs by 10.0x and 19.9x, respectively, and achieves a 7.7x end-to-end speedup over the original teacher pipeline.

items.title: Non-Linear Motion from Two Frames: Cubic Hermite Trajectories for Video Frame Interpolation
items.summary: Two-frame video frame interpolation commonly resamples endpoint optical flow by the query time, which selects a constant-velocity straight-line path even though the same endpoint displacement is compatible with many intermediate trajectories. We present HermiteVFI, which replaces independent query-time motion prediction with one explicit continuous trajectory per pixel. The measured endpoint displacement fixes the two trajectory positions, while two latent endpoint derivatives learned from the frame pair control the interior path. A cubic Hermite curve is the minimum-degree polynomial that can independently satisfy these two position and two derivative boundary quantities. Its residual form contains linear motion exactly, structurally preserves the measured displacement endpoints for any network output, and has coefficients that are predicted once per frame pair and evaluated in closed form at arbitrary t. We further show that one interior query time gives a rank-deficient constraint on the two free trajectory coefficients, whereas any two distinct interior times are full rank at the representation level, motivating multi-time supervision. Appearance-derived directional cues help infer the latent derivatives that endpoint displacement alone cannot identify. On X4K1000FPS, SNU-FILM, and Vimeo90K-Septuplet, the largest gains occur for difficult non-uniform motion and high interpolation ratios. The amortization applies to trajectory-coefficient prediction; downstream reversal, refinement, and synthesis remain query dependent.

items.title: The Same Tests, the Same Ring: VegaML in the Decision-Model Ring
items.summary: I ran VegaML through the same battery of tests as Jev, Laya, and pplx, at its creator’s request. Fitting its 4B reader looks like an upgrade for held-out pairs, and a step backward for the production queue my analysts actually review. On the 5,063 pairs my analysts reviewed from a client’s production queue, fitting VegaML’s 4B reader cut recall from 98% to 73% and precision from 24% to 21%, on a queue where 25% of pairs are true matches. On 1,000 held-out pairs from a second client, the same fit raised precision from 47% to 76% and cut recall from 85% to 71%. Against the three fine-tuned Laya seeds on those held-out pairs, its recall is 14 to 23 points higher (all three intervals exclude zero) and its precision 4 to 7 points lower in point estimates (one of the three precision intervals excludes zero). Which population I evaluate on decides whether the fit looks like an upgrade. What a match is Here are two records from a client’s corrugated-sheet catalog (Part 1’s published example, descriptions only): > `275B 32.2500 X 36.0000 122.65 MSF` > `275B 32.2500 X 36.0000 122.18 MSF` Same board grade, same sheet dimensions. The last number differs, and it is followed by MSF: thousand square feet. That is how much was bought, not what was bought. These two records are the same product: MATCH. Now these two, from the same review: > `4X6 1 MIL CLEAR` (poly bag) > `4X6 4 MIL CLEAR` (poly bag) Also nearly identical, and also differing by one number. This time the number is the bag’s thickness, and the records are different products: NONMATCH. The third answer is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, the abstention, which routes the pair to a person. Recall counts an abstained true match as a miss; precision, the share of MATCH calls that are correct, never sees an abstention. The question I care about in production is how many wrong automatic calls stand for a given amount of analyst review. As a benchmark illustration on the gold set, fitting the 4B reader cut the wrong automatic calls from about 291 to about 133 per 1,000 pairs, and the referrals to a person from 342 to zero (A7). The production review book is where that picture changes. The comment Nandakishor M, creator of Laya and CEO of Embedding Space, commented on Part 4 via my LinkedIn reshare: “You should try vegaml.” I replied that I would, and this is the work. Every subject in this series gets the same battery: the populations, rubrics, and protocol that Jev ( Part 1 ), Laya ( Part 2 and Part 3 ), and pplx ( Part 4 ) ran. The ring and the fine-tuning claim rule were frozen on 2026–11–13, before any score or fit report was read. A data-sufficiency check after the ring found two gaps against the pplx battery, the ensemble comparisons, and five missing rubric rungs; both were pre-registered on 2026–11–19 as an extension and closed. Every number below is from my data and my runs. Where the evidence doesn’t close a question, I say so. Which model is in the ring Four subjects of one VegaML snapshot: `nandakishorm/vega-U` pinned at `4d2050287982ca7a7bb0c22fd19a389f5f94474e`, loaded through `vegaml` 0.16.1, served on one RTX 5090 with `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`. No API key, no bill. https://medium.com/media/44c4824230ab45204b29f7e7fbd34eac/href Unlike Part 4’s pplx, this is a production candidate. Part 1 set the rule: production auditors run locally, because the data cannot leave my hardware. VegaML clears it. The fitted heads were trained on the same 11,010 human-reviewed pairs that Part 2’s fine-tuned Laya and two of my three production auditors were trained on, with the 51 rows that overlap the gold set removed before training, and on the same question: rubric `match_rubric_v007` with ruleset `client_item_rules_v006`. A separate 1,258-row validation split never enters the fit. Vega’s fit is a cross-validated supervised head, not a stochastic loop, so there is one fit per reader and no seed replicates. Cross-validated accuracy was 0.918 (0.8B) and 0.925 (4B). One discrepancy, reported as-is: `vegaml.calibrate` reports validation accuracy of 0.253 and 0.228, far from the fits’ cross-validated 0.918 and 0.925, while its calibration-error pass improved (0.325 to 0.249; 0.342 to 0.119). Both reported accuracies sit near the training split’s 26% match share. I have not traced the cause, and neither number is used below: every result in this report is scored out-of-sample on the ring’s labeled populations. Keeping a local model honest A local model can’t be swapped behind an API alias, but a snapshot can be re-pulled, and a package can drift, and a multi-day run is exactly the window for it. What held it: one pinned snapshot, served offline; sha256-verified inputs byte-identical to the Parts 1 to 4 runs; canaries before and after each series with pre-registered gates; and a strict verifier on every run. Across 84 runs and 1,621,712 scored decisions: 0 non-OK, all 14 canary comparisons at agreement 1.000, and a maximum per-pair score difference of `8.7e-08`. Two deviations are recorded in A7, not argued: the execution order, and a driver-keying bug that killed one run, fixed and re-run clean. The served model did not change during either series. Read this before the numbers: the zero-shot legs almost always escalate VegaML’s engine answers a pair itself only when it clears the pipeline’s unchanged 0.90/0.90 confidence bar (BYPASS_LLM); otherwise it hands the pair to the language-model head (ESCALATE_LLM). Escalation is about which part of the model answers, not whether a person sees the pair. On the second client’s pair set 0 (n 18,637, rubric v007), the routing is: https://medium.com/media/3d37a496e617217ab4d7f44d49c8271d/href The 48 zero-shot ring runs escalated every pair, and the 20 ladder runs escalated 299,999 of 300,000. The 0.8B zero-shot engine probabilities sit at 0.334 to 0.538; the fitted head is what clears the bar. So the zero-shot rows below are the language-model head’s readout, not engine decisions, and every zero-shot-versus-fitted or vega-versus-pplx comparison crosses routing regimes. The two zero-shot legs are not even one kind of baseline. At v007, the 0.8B head calls almost everything MATCH (18,635 of 18,637 on set 0; precision 0.416 on the gold set, about the set’s 41% match rate). The 4B head abstains instead, on 18.6% of set 0 and 34.2% of the gold set. The zero-shot rows are the language-model head’s numbers, wearing the engine’s name. What the fit bought on held-out pairs The cleanest test is the second client’s test sets 1 and 2: 1,000 labeled pairs, 469 matches, design-weighted, out-of-sample for every subject, and the basis of the pre-registered claim. Fitted minus the same reader’s zero-shot leg at v007, with paired bootstrap 95% intervals (seed 20261013, 1,000 draws): https://medium.com/media/4258894b8aefd16d2476d9f2f102243a/href The fit moves the operating point: much more precision, some recall given back, and decisive accuracy up 21 and 29 points (ΔDA +0.213 [+0.176, +0.247] and +0.289 [+0.246, +0.336]). The comparison the comment was really about is fitted against fitted. Part 2’s fine-tuned Laya was trained on the same 11,010 pairs with the same rubric, at three seeds, and scored on the same test sets. The 4B fit minus each Laya seed: https://medium.com/media/7ec3882c500bfb5f19c1b2a8521b0313/href The 4B fit gives up 4 to 7 points of precision (significant against one seed of three) for 14 to 23 points of recall (significant against all three). The 0.8B fit sits further toward recall: 18 to 22 points less precise than the Laya seeds, with 22 to 31 points more recall, all significant (A2). Against the hosted deciders, the 4B fit is 5.4 points less precise than pplx rv007 (ΔP −0.054 [−0.096, −0.009]), level with Jev rv007 (−0.033 [−0.079, +0.015]), and 16 to 20 points ahead of both on recall. On held-out pairs, the 4B fit is a recall-leaning sibling of fine-tuned Laya: a few points less precise, a lot more recall. The production review book The book is 5,063 pairs from two of the production client’s link runs: the pairs the production auditors accepted, which my analysts then reviewed. They labeled 1,242 as matches and rejected 3,821. Every number here is conditional on that acceptance step, and a subject that calls every pair MATCH scores precision 0.245, the book’s match rate. “Rejections caught” is the share of the 3,821 rejected pairs a subject calls NONMATCH: https://medium.com/media/c15befff5f5a1a1a28bcd1873e005ef4/href The zero-shot legs are the call-everything-MATCH subject: precision at the match rate and recall near 1.000. The zero-shot readers caught one of 3,821 rejections with 0.8B and none with 4B. The fitted legs decide every pair on the book, and their NONMATCH calls run the wrong way. The 0.8B fit calls NONMATCH on 34.5% of the true matches and on 8.9% of the rejections; the 4B fit on 26.9% of the matches and 11.7% of the rejections. A reader who said NONMATCH at random, at the same rate, would hit both groups equally. These hit a larger share of the matches than of the rejections, which is why their precision (0.190, 0.212) falls below the book’s 0.245. In counts, the rejections still win (for the 4B fit, 448 correct rejections against 334 wrongly rejected matches), because the queue holds three non-matches for every match; the rates are inverted. On this reviewed queue, a true match was about 2.3 times as likely as a true non-match to get NONMATCH from the fitted 4B reader (26.9% against 11.7%); the 0.8B reader showed the same pattern, 34.5% against 8.9%. Among the other deciders, Laya base catches three-quarters of the rejections, and Jev and pplx almost none. Two cautions on what this comparison crosses. The test sets are the second client’s labeled holdout; the book is the production client’s auditor-accepted subset. The sign change from holdout to book crosses both client and selection, so it can’t be put on analyst selection alone. And the ring’s re-run majority vote calls all 5,063 book pairs MATCH; the count of its MATCH calls outside the book is unavailable here. A8 carries estimates for all 26,342 candidates; the notes I have do not specify the size, selection, or weights of the labeled draw outside the book, so I treat those estimates as indicative and do not lean on them. For the record, on that frame the 4B fit’s recall falls from 0.982 to 0.460, and its precision rises from 0.264 to 0.403. The claim: one frozen rule, split by metric The ring pre-registration, frozen 2026–11–13, states the claim as an improvement: a fitted subject “claims an improvement over like-for-like” (the same reader’s zero-shot leg at v007) if its paired delta sits beyond a 5-point band on one side of zero on both the second client’s test sets 1 to 2, and the production review book, and its trained head is used on every population. The fit pre-registration adds that a subject clearing the band on only one of the two is reported as inconsistent, and it lists the book’s metrics as precision, recall, and rejections caught. Neither document says which metric decides. The verdict depends on it: https://medium.com/media/7e96ec309900a87458b9d59ed8bdcc0f/href I scored the last row after the fact, from the existing predictions (post hoc, not pre-registered; A7): the design-weighted share of true non-matches a subject explicitly calls NONMATCH, with abstentions counted as not caught. Paired deltas: 0.8B +0.570 [+0.527, +0.613] on the test sets and +0.089 [+0.080, +0.098] on the book; 4B +0.806 [+0.772, +0.841] and +0.117 [+0.107, +0.127]. Every interval sits wholly beyond the band. Almost all of each delta comes from the fitted head: on the test sets the zero-shot readers call no true non-match NONMATCH (the 4B reader abstains on 21% of them instead), and on the book the zero-shot readers caught one of 3,821 rejections with 0.8B and none with 4B. Both readers cleared the five-point band on explicit rejection of true non-matches in both populations. I scored this comparison after examining the other outcomes, so it does not establish the pre-registered improvement claim: counting it now would be choosing the metric after seeing the results, which the pre-registration’s own no-post-hoc-selection clause rules out. For the registered metrics, the rule is inconsistent on two and not met on one; I do not claim an improvement. The rejection metric also measures only one side of a trade: the fitted head says NONMATCH where the zero-shot head almost never does, and, on the book, a true match is 2.3 times as likely as a true non-match to get that NONMATCH. No pre-registered improvement claim; post hoc, the fitted heads clearly reject more in both populations, and in the production queue they reject true matches at a higher rate. A rule that names its metric is a new pre-registration, not a re-reading of this one. Against the local auditors My production pipeline runs a vote of three local auditors: two QLoRA fine-tunes (Qwen2.5 and SmolLM3, trained on the same 11,010 pairs as the Vega fit) and SFT phi4 on an older, smaller training set. The majority vote accepts a pair when at least two say MATCH. On the pooled 2,000-pair holdout (all four of the second client’s sets, design-weighted, 865 matches): https://medium.com/media/efe968e2a22eab158517e15d028f848e/href The 4B fit minus each reference, paired: https://medium.com/media/416c59f4a351d99da7e9fb3baeac4a63/href The 4B fit is within noise of SmolLM3 on all three metrics. Against phi4 it is 8.6 points behind on recall, a significant gap; on precision and decisive accuracy the intervals include zero. Against the vote it is level on precision and 8.4 points behind on recall, a deficit whose practical size depends on the cost of a missed link. Its errors also overlap the existing deciders’ (Yule Q +0.54 to +0.69 against the three auditors, the three Laya seeds, Jev, and pplx; A4), consistent with shared training data and a shared rubric. On the vote’s own errors, it gets 50.0% of the majority’s false positives and 44.2% of its false negatives right (A4). Whether adding it to the vote would help depends on the voting rule and on the correct calls it would overturn, and I have not evaluated a four-member vote. The 4B fit is a candidate auditor at SmolLM3’s level, not a replacement for the vote. The 0.8B fit is 9 to 16 points less precise than every reference, all significant. On the gold set (n 20,000, the production client’s labeled pair pool from Part 1, 8,253 true matches), the fits sit mid-table: 4B P 0.860 / R 0.809 and 0.8B P 0.850 / R 0.599, against Jev rv007 at 0.981 / 0.922, pplx rv007 at 0.971 / 0.954, and Qwen2.5 SFT at 0.974 / 0.837 (A3). Read that table with its case mix in mind: 6,193 of the 8,253 true matches are MSF pairs, a subset that is nearly all positive, where every subject scores precision near 1.000. The spread occurs across the 13,787 non-MSF rows (14.9% match rate), with the 4B fit at P 0.578 and the 0.8B fit at 0.632, compared to Jev at 0.906 and pplx at 0.877. By pair slice (A5), the weakest for every vega subject is “part numbers on both sides, none shared” (n 235): the 4B fit’s precision is 0.361 there, against 0.677 for Jev and 0.719 for fine-tuned Laya . The rubric ladder, briefly Part 4 ran pplx on seven rubric conditions (the v1 base and the six-rung ladder rv002 to rv007) on the gold set and the 10k dev sample. The Vega ring had two of those seven (v1 and rv007) plus the original v0. The extension ran the five missing rungs on the two zero-shot readers, 20 runs. The fitted heads answer their trained question (v007) and have no ladder. The full tables are A9 to A11. The 0.8B reader buys recall as the ladder climbs: 0.307 at v1 to 0.998 at rv005, with one dip at rv004 (0.878, below rv003’s 0.929), while precision slides from 0.503 to 0.416. The dip falls on a rule change, not a wobble: rv004 is base plus the pallet rule only, and rv005 re-adds the MSF and service-run rules (Part 1 documents the ladder). The 4B reader is not monotone: rv002 to rv004 cost it recall (0.442, 0.243, 0.159) against 0.800 at v1), and precision; then rv005 recovers recall above v1 (0.896; 0.920 at rv006) at v1-level precision. That recovery is an observed rung transition; isolating the MSF rule’s own contribution would require that the rule be varied alone. One caution: rv005 and rv006 are different rubrics (23, 6, 490, and 38 verdict flips across the four reader-population cells); the 0.8B leg’s near-identical P and R on the two is flips canceling, not identity. At the same rung, for byte-identical inputs, pplx maintains precision between 0.82 and 0.98 across both populations. Vega’s zero-shot precision runs 0.24 to 0.71 (0.35 to 0.56 on the gold set). The 0.8B reader out-recalls pplx from rv003 on the gold set, at precision deficits of 0.48 to 0.56; the 4B reader is behind pplx on recall at every rung on both populations. The rubric moves vega’s zero-shot operating point as much as the reader does, and no rung brings its precision near pplx’s. Label noise Part 3’s re-labels, a second labeler’s 484 re-adjudications and 496 consensus pairs, move the vega subjects’ precision in the same direction they moved the established deciders, by less: +0.017 and +0.050 for the 0.8B and 4B fits (neither significant), +0.039 and +0.038 for the zero-shot legs (both significant), against +0.071 for pplx and +0.083 for Jev. The 0.8B fit’s recall drops 0.053 [−0.089, −0.018] on the second labeler’s labels. The large gaps in this report (the zero-shot precision deficit, the fit’s recall give-back, the direction of the fit’s errors on the book) are far outside these shifts. The small-ensemble deltas are reported as not significant on their own paired intervals, not due to relabeling. The book’s 5,063 analyst labels are not re-adjudicated here. Ways this work could have misled me One domain, one snapshot, one GPU. Industrial product matching, one pinned snapshot, one machine. Canary determinism is within the series, not across machines. A different domain, snapshot, or VegaML version could move every number here, including the routing rates. The zero-shot legs almost always escalate. Every zero-shot-versus-fitted and vega-versus-pplx comparison crosses routing regimes, and I have not decomposed that. The claim rule doesn’t name its metric. The split verdict is the honest reading of the rule as frozen; a different frozen metric would have given a single answer, and choosing one now would be a re-reading. The rejection row is post hoc. It was scored from existing predictions after the other three rows had been read, and its book interval is stratified by label rather than by the book’s own strata (A7). It clears the band, but it does not establish the pre-registered improvement claim. About 2,000 labeled holdout pairs. Enough for the large gaps, not for the small ones: the ensemble deltas, the slices, and the 10k sample (202 labeled rows, 48 positives) rest on a few dozen matches each. One fit per reader. No seed replicates, so the fit’s own spread is unmeasured. Laya showed 9 points of test-set recall across three seeds in Part 2; a gap smaller than that is as much a statement about unmeasured uncertainty as about Vega. Shared training data, shared rubric, shared errors. The fits, fine-tuned Laya, and two of the three auditors learned from the same 11,010 pairs and read the same rubric. The 4B fit’s error overlap with them may be partly that. A selected review book. The production rejections are among the pairs my auditors had already accepted and scored at the benchmark’s operating point. They say what a second model does after the auditors say yes, not how it would behave on every production pair. The calibrate readout. The validation accuracies of 0.253 and 0.228 are untraced. They are not used, but until they are explained, the fit’s own validation report is not evidence for or against it. What it cost, and what’s next API charges: $0. The served model is the local snapshot, offline. Local GPU (one RTX 5090): 64 ring runs in 51.0 hours of wall time (about 139 ms wall and 131 ms of active compute per decision, including a 1.95-hour incident gap), and 20 ladder runs in 11 hours 22 minutes, both inside their pre-registered gates. Human: no new labeling. The holdout and its re-labels come from Parts 1 to 3; the book’s labels are my analysts’ own decisions on that queue. The next legs, in order: 1. The production split, counted. MATCH, NONMATCH, and undecided on the reviewer-rejected pairs at the pipeline’s actual routing thresholds, for the fitted legs. 2. Calibration. The ring’s own calibration check on the fitted head’s probabilities, and a trace of the `calibrate` accuracy readout. 3. A metric-named claim rule. A new pre-registration, if a clean fine-tuning claim for vega is wanted. 4. The Studio head-to-head. VegaML ships a Studio that fits a model from a company description (per its documentation; I have not run it). That is a different test from the fitted-versus-fitted comparison above, which, by design, shares training data. 5. Cross-machine. A second machine or VegaML version, to take the canary from within the series to across deployments. Where that leaves deployment. On held-out pairs, the 4B fit is a credible recall-leaning auditor at SmolLM3’s level, 4 to 7 points behind fine-tuned Laya on precision in point estimates. On the production queue, as fitted, a true match is about 2.3 times as likely as a true non-match to get its NONMATCH, so I would not route on it there. It does not replace the vote (recall 0.725 against 0.809), and its errors overlap the deciders already in the ring. Legs 1 and 2 gate any routing decision. Context reading: VegaML on GitHub · vega-U on Hugging Face · Laya on GitHub Appendix The method notes and the tables the main text summarizes. It is optional; the main text carries the argument. A1. Per-rubric quality on the labeled populations Precision and recall per rubric version on the human-labeled subset of each population, per subject leg. Base rubric is v1; the ladder runs rv002 to rv007, with rv007 the top; v0 is the original rubric. False omission, the last column, is the share of the subject’s NONMATCH calls that are true matches (Part 4’s definition of the false-omission rate); its intervals are Wilson intervals over the NONMATCH-call denominator, so a small denominator makes the interval wide by construction (the 4B zero-shot leg’s 0.000 [0, 0.793] on gold20k v007 is 0 of 1: the leg makes exactly one NONMATCH call on that run, and it is correct). The second client’s set 0 to 3 populations carry no population-level human labels (their labeling sheets are empty), so they are not in this table; their quality is measured on the adjudicated holdout, A2. The 10k rows are the labeled slice (n 202, 48 positives), so their point estimates are indicative. https://medium.com/media/6e7f1acb99d0e8494fcc233d8dc870cc/href A2. The 2,000-pair holdout, all four sets and the test sets Sets 0 to 3, 2,000 labeled pairs, 865 matches. Sets 0 and 3 were the development sets for Laya’s checkpoint selection in Part 2; sets 1 and 2 are the test sets, 1,000 labeled pairs, 469 matches, and they are the out-of-sample basis of the fine-tuning claim. P = MATCH-call precision, R = recall on true matches, DA = decisive accuracy on decided pairs. The MATCH call counts are design-weighted population totals: the holdout is a weighted sample of the second client’s pair population. The vega rows below are the ring’s pooled-holdout convention (the 2,000 labeled pairs, design weights); the pplx-versus-Jev deltas on these tables are in Part 4’s A2. All four sets, design-weighted: https://medium.com/media/2e18f8c111b4ac69a0c46170694acf5a/href Paired deltas on all four sets (vega rows; 95% CIs): https://medium.com/media/6cc4de8db6ab263348cac18731073035/href The test sets (1 to 2), the claim basis: https://medium.com/media/353ff2760f08c139d20d35a6b4b755f1/href Paired deltas on the test sets (vega rows; 95% CIs): https://medium.com/media/ab4cb25c11c115463cc3e70cb856f2b3/href A3. The 20k gold-labeled set, against the auditors The “all” rows of the gold auditor analysis with the vega references added (n 20,000, 8,253 true matches; P = MATCH-call precision, R = recall, false omission = the share of NONMATCH calls that are true matches, Part 4’s definition, DA = decisive accuracy on decided pairs, undecided = abstained pairs). The MSF, non-MSF, and UIC-only subset splits are in the frozen report; the case-mix discussion is in the auditors section. https://medium.com/media/54f06bed763a37c04b4ad9d0245ab88b/href A4. Error diversity, holdout, top rubric The 2,000-pair pool, rubric v007. Double fault is the share of the pool on which both subjects call MATCH on a pair that is not a true match; Yule Q and κ on the pair-level verdicts. The cross pairs between the established deciders are in Part 4’s A4. https://medium.com/media/1f5c2cf815a4bb3e753417bab5c27a56/href How each subject resolves the majority vote’s errors (M3: at least 2 of the 3 auditors say ACCEPT): https://medium.com/media/050d5f95d78e4dcbce13096c30704413/href A5. Gap slices, holdout, design-weighted, top rubric Point precision by pair slice on the 2,000 labeled pairs (design-weighted, rubric v007). n and matches are the design-weighted slice pair and match counts; the Laya and Jev recall columns are in the frozen report. The Laya column is the mean of the three fine-tuned Laya seeds (its all-pairs value, 0.802, is the mean of A2’s three seed rows). https://medium.com/media/18777f226a1b83b7c3c24859faeafa5c/href A6. Label noise, fully paired Absolute levels (P on the 2,000-pair pool, R on true matches) against my labels, a second labeler’s 484 re-adjudications, and the 496 consensus pairs. ΔP/ΔR = the re-adjudicated (or consensus) level minus my labels, with 95% CIs; the consensus deltas are against the 496-pair levels. Same convention as Part 3’s A6 and Part 4’s A6, which is not A2’s: levels here differ slightly from A2’s (the 4B fit is 0.732 / 0.772 here against 0.720 / 0.725 in A2), so compare within this table. https://medium.com/media/669e2626595c0ae06be6d90991a424a0/href A7. Method notes Model and pin. One pinned `nandakishorm/vega-U` snapshot at `4d2050287982ca7a7bb0c22fd19a389f5f94474e` (manifest sha256 verified, snapshot sha matches the commit), `vegaml` 0.16.1 (torch 2.15.0, transformers 5.23.0), served locally by `serve_vega.py` on 127.0.0.1:8100, `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`. No API key. A local production candidate (Part 1’s rule), unlike Part 4’s hosted pplx. Subjects and training data. `vega 0p8b zs` and `vega 4b zs`: the zero-shot readers (backbones `Qwen3.5–0.8B` / `Qwen3.5–4B`), engine readout. `vega 0p8b ft` and `vega 4b ft`: the `sft_enhanced` fitted policy heads, one fit per reader (cross-validated supervised head, no seed replicates).
