CV accuracy 0.91789 (0.8B) / 0.92543 (4B). `calibrate` reports validation accuracy 0.2528 / 0.2281 (untraced, not used downstream); its ECE pass moved 0.3249 to 0.2493 and 0.3424 to 0.1188. Runs. 64 ring runs: 48 zero-shot (2 readers × 8 populations × rubrics v0, v1, v007) and 16 fine-tuned (2 readers × 8 populations, v007 only), plus one pre-fix dry run (20,000 decisions, 2026–11–15, before the raw-response fix; verified in the ledger, excluded from the decision totals and the head-usage n; it carries no raw_response). The 1,321,712 ring decisions are exactly the 64-run block. 20 ladder runs: rungs rv002 to rv006 × gold20k and 10k × the two zero-shot readers, pre-registered 2026–11–19 as an extension of the ring after the data-sufficiency check. Populations: the second client’s pair sets 0 to 3 (18,637 / 17,099 / 17,686 / 18,755 pairs; the March 2026 link runs, Part 2), gold20k, the 26k production population (the first client’s production link runs, 26,342 pairs), the 10k dev sample, the 36k audit-accepted slice (Part 1’s s1–36k, the first client’s audit-accepted pairs, 36,695 pairs, 81.7% positive). 1,321,712 ring decisions and 300,000 ladder decisions; 0 non-OK. Canaries. Fixed 256-pair population (128 MATCH + 128 NONMATCH from gold20k, seed 20261110); gates: agreement at least 0.99, median |ΔP| at most 0.01, max |ΔP| at most 0.10, n-share at least 0.99, same served revision. No document names the deciding metric, so the article reports the verdict per metric (P and DA inconsistent, R not met; rejections caught clears the band on both populations, scored post hoc, and does not establish the claim) and claims no improvement, because counting the one metric that clears, after reading the others, would be post-hoc selection. Rejection metric (post hoc). Scored 2026–11–24 from the 12 existing v007 run directories (no new inference; REPORT_20261124_vega_rejection_row.md and .json). Metric: weight mass of true non-matches with an explicit NONMATCH over the weight mass of all true non-matches; abstentions count as not caught. Gate: the frozen test-set P/R and book rejections caught reproduced to 3 decimals through the ring’s code path; 0 non-OK, 0 missing rows. Test sets 1 to 2 (design weights, paired bootstrap stratified by set and holdout stratum, seed 20261013, 1,000 draws): zero-shot 0.000 (0.8B) and 0.000 (4B, which abstains on 0.212 of the non-match weight); fitted 0.570 and 0.806 (both fitted legs decide every pair). Book (unweighted): zero-shot 1 and 0 of 3,821; fitted 341 and 448 of 3,821; the book interval is stratified by label, not by the book’s run, region, and vote stratum used for the other book deltas (same seed and draw count). An earlier reconstruction from A2’s aggregate totals (about +0.58 and +0.62) counted abstentions as rejections and is superseded. Benchmark illustration (opening section): wrong automatic calls per 1,000 gold-set pairs = 1,000 × decided share × (1 − decisive accuracy), from A3 on rounded inputs; the 4B zero-shot leg decides 13,170 of 20,000 at 0.558 (about 291 wrong, 342 referred to a person under the abstention mapping), the 4B fit decides all 20,000 at 0.867 (about 133 wrong, 0 referred). Not a queue measurement. Head-usage. The pre-registered veto metric: the share of settled attempts (last OK attempt per row, joined by identity_key) whose raw_response answer carries readout `ttt`, the trained head. The bypass shares in the routing table are a different denominator: the share of all pairs in the run the engine routed BYPASS_LLM. On the second client’s set 0 at v007, the 0.8B fine-tune bypasses 15.3% of pairs and the 4B fine-tune 27.0% (head-usage 1.000 over each one’s settled attempts); the zero-shot rows carry 0.000 by construction (their readout is `engine`). The dry run’s NULL raw_response rows sit outside the head-usage n. Routing regime. Under the unchanged 0.90/0.90 bar, the zero-shot engine almost always escalates: the 48 zero-shot ring runs are 100% ESCALATE_LLM, and the 20 ladder runs are 299,999 of 300,000 ESCALATE_LLM, the one BYPASS_LLM in the 0.8B gold20k rv006 run (reported as-is). Zero-shot-versus-fine-tuned and vega-versus-pplx comparisons cross routing regimes. Recorded deviations. Execution order: population-family-major, not the plan’s reader-block order (no run-order clause in the frozen pre-registration; all invariants preserved). Mid-series incident: the 0.8B fine-tuned 10k run died at census due to a driver keying bug, was fixed (RLP `f608204`, 3 of 3 tests, reviewer approved), and re-ran cleanly; no other run affected. Wall. Ring: 51.0 h of wall against the operator-confirmed 94.97-h gate, 2026–11–17 02:44:08 to 2026–11–19 05:44:50 UTC. 1,321,712 decisions: about 131 ms of active compute per decision, about 139 ms wall per decision; per-reader compute rates 0p8b zs about 125 ms, 4b zs about 138 ms, 0p8b ft about 138 ms, 4b ft about 142 ms (the 0.8B fine-tuned 10k block ran 6.33 h of compute against 8.27 h of wall, the 1.95-h incident gap of 2026–11–18 19:28:52 to 21:25:38 UTC included). Ladder: 11 h 22 m (2026–11–19 19:14:34 to 2026–11–20 06:37:15 UTC) against the ~12-h pre-registration. Costs. $0 API (local, offline). One RTX 5090. No new labeling; the holdout and its re-labels come from Parts 1 to 3. Auditors. Qwen2.5 SFT and SmolLM3 SFT (two QLoRA fine-tunes on the same 11,010-pair train split) and phi4 SFT from an older, smaller training set. Majority vote: at least two of three say MATCH; unanimous: all three. On the review book, the ring’s majority vote calls all 5,063 pairs MATCH; the count of its MATCH calls outside the book is unavailable here. Populations. The 2,000-pair holdout (four sets of 500, the second client’s pairs; sets 0 and 3 were Laya’s checkpoint-selection development sets in Part 2); the 20k gold-labeled set (the first client’s labeled training pair pool, Part 1: 19,530 labels derived from the identity groupings, each human-reviewed when built, plus 470 direct pair reviews; 8,253 true matches, the pool’s natural 41.3% match rate); the 10k dev sample (the first client’s development sample, Part 1; labeled slice 202 rows, 48 positives); the 36k audit-accepted slice (Part 1’s s1–36k, the first client’s audit-accepted pairs, 36,695 pairs, 81.7% positive, each with a direct human label); the 26k production population (the first client’s production link runs, 26,342 pairs; the review book is its auditor-accepted, analyst-labeled subset, 5,063 pairs, 3,821 reviewer-rejected). Labeling. Holdout labels are mine, corrected as in Part 3. The 484-pair second-labeler re-adjudication and the 496 consensus pairs are from Part 3, unchanged. What this is not. A cross-machine result, a cross-domain result, a different VegaML version’s result, a calibration result, or a production-thresholds result. A8. The 26k production population and its review book, full table Two production link runs proposed 26,342 candidate pairs. Our analysts reviewed the 5,063 pairs the auditors accepted and labeled 1,242 as matches. Review-book P and R are point estimates on those 5,063 pairs (1,242 matches, 3,821 reviewer rejections), conditional on the auditors’ acceptance step; population P and R are estimates for all 26,342 candidates, with 95% paired bootstrap intervals, the same convention as Part 4’s A8 for the established subjects, and describe the 26,342 candidate pairs, not the client’s whole production stream. The ring’s re-run majority vote calls every book pair MATCH (R 1.000, 0 rejections caught); the count of its MATCH calls outside the book is unavailable here. The population columns are indicative and are not used to draw any conclusions in the main text. The available experiment notes do not specify the recall sample size, selection probabilities, or weights. “Rejections caught” is the share of the 3,821 reviewer-rejected pairs the subject calls NONMATCH. The vega rows are the v007 runs; the routing for the zero-shot legs on this frame was 100% ESCALATE_LLM. https://medium.com/media/264bd23f43db1d968f69f1e54b980daa/href A9. The rubric ladder, 10k labeled slice The 10k dev sample’s labeled slice (n 202, 48 positives), point P/R and paired deltas against the v1 baseline, 95% CI. Intervals are wide; the significant directions are the statement. The gold20k ladder tables are in A10 and the same-rung vega-minus-pplx tables in A11. The 0.8B reader (v1 baseline P 0.520 / R 0.271): https://medium.com/media/4f16e481a0fb7396cae7d97527c7305b/href The 4B reader (v1 baseline P 0.481 / R 0.521): https://medium.com/media/27715dafbfc175f2474570d6ca4c49ec/href A10. The rubric ladder, gold20k Zero-shot readers only, point P/R and paired deltas against the v1 baseline, 95% CI. The 0.8B reader on gold20k (v1 baseline P 0.503 / R 0.307): https://medium.com/media/ff0a9c59679b83b58efe5a4aeaa7fea4/href The 4B reader on gold20k (v1 baseline P 0.583 / R 0.800): https://medium.com/media/63f52a77305cc450d8f28c65fd274619/href A11. Vega against pplx at the same rung The 20 ladder runs consumed inputs byte-identical to pplx’s same-rung twin runs, so the paired deltas compare the two complete systems on identical inputs. Point P/R on the labeled slice, and ΔP/ΔR = vega minus pplx at the same rung (95% CI): gold20k (n 20,000, 8,253 positives): https://medium.com/media/3b17c1fcc65ae20e563bd794c8adaa3a/href The 10k labeled slice (n 202, 48 positives; intervals wide, point estimates indicative): https://medium.com/media/c1e0a6b43b360bc4b11ec9a3f0158b23/href The Same Tests, the Same Ring: VegaML in the Decision-Model Ring was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
I ran VegaML through the same battery of tests as Jev, Laya, and pplx, at its creator’s request. Fitting its 4B reader looks like an upgrade for held-out pairs, and a step backward for the production queue my analysts actually review.

On the 5,063 pairs my analysts reviewed from a client’s production queue, fitting VegaML’s 4B reader cut recall from 98% to 73% and precision from 24% to 21%, on a queue where 25% of pairs are true matches. On 1,000 held-out pairs from a second client, the same fit raised precision from 47% to 76% and cut recall from 85% to 71%. Against the three fine-tuned Laya seeds on those held-out pairs, its recall is 14 to 23 points higher (all three intervals exclude zero) and its precision 4 to 7 points lower in point estimates (one of the three precision intervals excludes zero). Which population I evaluate on decides whether the fit looks like an upgrade.

What a match is

Here are two records from a client’s corrugated-sheet catalog (Part 1’s published example, descriptions only):

> `275B 32.2500 X 36.0000 122.65 MSF`
> `275B 32.2500 X 36.0000 122.18 MSF`

Same board grade, same sheet dimensions. The last number differs, and it is followed by MSF: thousand square feet. That is how much was bought, not what was bought. These two records are the same product: MATCH.

Now these two, from the same review:

> `4X6 1 MIL CLEAR` (poly bag)
> `4X6 4 MIL CLEAR` (poly bag)

Also nearly identical, and also differing by one number. This time the number is the bag’s thickness, and the records are different products: NONMATCH.

The third answer is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, the abstention, which routes the pair to a person. Recall counts an abstained true match as a miss; precision, the share of MATCH calls that are correct, never sees an abstention. The question I care about in production is how many wrong automatic calls stand for a given amount of analyst review. As a benchmark illustration on the gold set, fitting the 4B reader cut the wrong automatic calls from about 291 to about 133 per 1,000 pairs, and the referrals to a person from 342 to zero (A7). The production review book is where that picture changes.

The comment

Nandakishor M, creator of Laya and CEO of Embedding Space, commented on Part 4 via my LinkedIn reshare:

“You should try vegaml.”

I replied that I would, and this is the work. Every subject in this series gets the same battery: the populations, rubrics, and protocol that Jev (Part 1), Laya (Part 2 and Part 3), and pplx (Part 4) ran. The ring and the fine-tuning claim rule were frozen on 2026–11–13, before any score or fit report was read. A data-sufficiency check after the ring found two gaps against the pplx battery, the ensemble comparisons, and five missing rubric rungs; both were pre-registered on 2026–11–19 as an extension and closed.

Every number below is from my data and my runs. Where the evidence doesn’t close a question, I say so.

Which model is in the ring

Four subjects of one VegaML snapshot: `nandakishorm/vega-U` pinned at `4d2050287982ca7a7bb0c22fd19a389f5f94474e`, loaded through `vegaml` 0.16.1, served on one RTX 5090 with `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`. No API key, no bill.

https://medium.com/media/44c4824230ab45204b29f7e7fbd34eac/href

Unlike Part 4’s pplx, this is a production candidate. Part 1 set the rule: production auditors run locally, because the data cannot leave my hardware. VegaML clears it.

The fitted heads were trained on the same 11,010 human-reviewed pairs that Part 2’s fine-tuned Laya and two of my three production auditors were trained on, with the 51 rows that overlap the gold set removed before training, and on the same question: rubric `match_rubric_v007` with ruleset `client_item_rules_v006`. A separate 1,258-row validation split never enters the fit. Vega’s fit is a cross-validated supervised head, not a stochastic loop, so there is one fit per reader and no seed replicates. Cross-validated accuracy was 0.918 (0.8B) and 0.925 (4B).

One discrepancy, reported as-is: `vegaml.calibrate` reports validation accuracy of 0.253 and 0.228, far from the fits’ cross-validated 0.918 and 0.925, while its calibration-error pass improved (0.325 to 0.249; 0.342 to 0.119). Both reported accuracies sit near the training split’s 26% match share. I have not traced the cause, and neither number is used below: every result in this report is scored out-of-sample on the ring’s labeled populations.

Keeping a local model honest

A local model can’t be swapped behind an API alias, but a snapshot can be re-pulled, and a package can drift, and a multi-day run is exactly the window for it. What held it: one pinned snapshot, served offline; sha256-verified inputs byte-identical to the Parts 1 to 4 runs; canaries before and after each series with pre-registered gates; and a strict verifier on every run. Across 84 runs and 1,621,712 scored decisions: 0 non-OK, all 14 canary comparisons at agreement 1.000, and a maximum per-pair score difference of `8.7e-08`. Two deviations are recorded in A7, not argued: the execution order, and a driver-keying bug that killed one run, fixed and re-run clean. The served model did not change during either series.

Read this before the numbers: the zero-shot legs almost always escalate

VegaML’s engine answers a pair itself only when it clears the pipeline’s unchanged 0.90/0.90 confidence bar (BYPASS_LLM); otherwise it hands the pair to the language-model head (ESCALATE_LLM). Escalation is about which part of the model answers, not whether a person sees the pair. On the second client’s pair set 0 (n 18,637, rubric v007), the routing is:

https://medium.com/media/3d37a496e617217ab4d7f44d49c8271d/href

The 48 zero-shot ring runs escalated every pair, and the 20 ladder runs escalated 299,999 of 300,000. The 0.8B zero-shot engine probabilities sit at 0.334 to 0.538; the fitted head is what clears the bar.

So the zero-shot rows below are the language-model head’s readout, not engine decisions, and every zero-shot-versus-fitted or vega-versus-pplx comparison crosses routing regimes. The two zero-shot legs are not even one kind of baseline. At v007, the 0.8B head calls almost everything MATCH (18,635 of 18,637 on set 0; precision 0.416 on the gold set, about the set’s 41% match rate). The 4B head abstains instead, on 18.6% of set 0 and 34.2% of the gold set. The zero-shot rows are the language-model head’s numbers, wearing the engine’s name.

What the fit bought on held-out pairs

The cleanest test is the second client’s test sets 1 and 2: 1,000 labeled pairs, 469 matches, design-weighted, out-of-sample for every subject, and the basis of the pre-registered claim. Fitted minus the same reader’s zero-shot leg at v007, with paired bootstrap 95% intervals (seed 20261013, 1,000 draws):

https://medium.com/media/4258894b8aefd16d2476d9f2f102243a/href

The fit moves the operating point: much more precision, some recall given back, and decisive accuracy up 21 and 29 points (ΔDA +0.213 [+0.176, +0.247] and +0.289 [+0.246, +0.336]).

The comparison the comment was really about is fitted against fitted. Part 2’s fine-tuned Laya was trained on the same 11,010 pairs with the same rubric, at three seeds, and scored on the same test sets. The 4B fit minus each Laya seed:

https://medium.com/media/7ec3882c500bfb5f19c1b2a8521b0313/href

The 4B fit gives up 4 to 7 points of precision (significant against one seed of three) for 14 to 23 points of recall (significant against all three). The 0.8B fit sits further toward recall: 18 to 22 points less precise than the Laya seeds, with 22 to 31 points more recall, all significant (A2). Against the hosted deciders, the 4B fit is 5.4 points less precise than pplx rv007 (ΔP −0.054 [−0.096, −0.009]), level with Jev rv007 (−0.033 [−0.079, +0.015]), and 16 to 20 points ahead of both on recall. On held-out pairs, the 4B fit is a recall-leaning sibling of fine-tuned Laya: a few points less precise, a lot more recall.

The production review book

The book is 5,063 pairs from two of the production client’s link runs: the pairs the production auditors accepted, which my analysts then reviewed. They labeled 1,242 as matches and rejected 3,821. Every number here is conditional on that acceptance step, and a subject that calls every pair MATCH scores precision 0.245, the book’s match rate. “Rejections caught” is the share of the 3,821 rejected pairs a subject calls NONMATCH:

https://medium.com/media/c15befff5f5a1a1a28bcd1873e005ef4/href

The zero-shot legs are the call-everything-MATCH subject: precision at the match rate and recall near 1.000. The zero-shot readers caught one of 3,821 rejections with 0.8B and none with 4B. The fitted legs decide every pair on the book, and their NONMATCH calls run the wrong way. The 0.8B fit calls NONMATCH on 34.5% of the true matches and on 8.9% of the rejections; the 4B fit on 26.9% of the matches and 11.7% of the rejections. A reader who said NONMATCH at random, at the same rate, would hit both groups equally. These hit a larger share of the matches than of the rejections, which is why their precision (0.190, 0.212) falls below the book’s 0.245. In counts, the rejections still win (for the 4B fit, 448 correct rejections against 334 wrongly rejected matches), because the queue holds three non-matches for every match; the rates are inverted. On this reviewed queue, a true match was about 2.3 times as likely as a true non-match to get NONMATCH from the fitted 4B reader (26.9% against 11.7%); the 0.8B reader showed the same pattern, 34.5% against 8.9%. Among the other deciders, Laya base catches three-quarters of the rejections, and Jev and pplx almost none.

Two cautions on what this comparison crosses. The test sets are the second client’s labeled holdout; the book is the production client’s auditor-accepted subset. The sign change from holdout to book crosses both client and selection, so it can’t be put on analyst selection alone. And the ring’s re-run majority vote calls all 5,063 book pairs MATCH; the count of its MATCH calls outside the book is unavailable here. A8 carries estimates for all 26,342 candidates; the notes I have do not specify the size, selection, or weights of the labeled draw outside the book, so I treat those estimates as indicative and do not lean on them. For the record, on that frame the 4B fit’s recall falls from 0.982 to 0.460, and its precision rises from 0.264 to 0.403.

The claim: one frozen rule, split by metric

The ring pre-registration, frozen 2026–11–13, states the claim as an improvement: a fitted subject “claims an improvement over like-for-like” (the same reader’s zero-shot leg at v007) if its paired delta sits beyond a 5-point band on one side of zero on both the second client’s test sets 1 to 2, and the production review book, and its trained head is used on every population. The fit pre-registration adds that a subject clearing the band on only one of the two is reported as inconsistent, and it lists the book’s metrics as precision, recall, and rejections caught. Neither document says which metric decides. The verdict depends on it:

https://medium.com/media/7e96ec309900a87458b9d59ed8bdcc0f/href

I scored the last row after the fact, from the existing predictions (post hoc, not pre-registered; A7): the design-weighted share of true non-matches a subject explicitly calls NONMATCH, with abstentions counted as not caught. Paired deltas: 0.8B +0.570 [+0.527, +0.613] on the test sets and +0.089 [+0.080, +0.098] on the book; 4B +0.806 [+0.772, +0.841] and +0.117 [+0.107, +0.127]. Every interval sits wholly beyond the band. Almost all of each delta comes from the fitted head: on the test sets the zero-shot readers call no true non-match NONMATCH (the 4B reader abstains on 21% of them instead), and on the book the zero-shot readers caught one of 3,821 rejections with 0.8B and none with 4B.

Both readers cleared the five-point band on explicit rejection of true non-matches in both populations. I scored this comparison after examining the other outcomes, so it does not establish the pre-registered improvement claim: counting it now would be choosing the metric after seeing the results, which the pre-registration’s own no-post-hoc-selection clause rules out. For the registered metrics, the rule is inconsistent on two and not met on one; I do not claim an improvement. The rejection metric also measures only one side of a trade: the fitted head says NONMATCH where the zero-shot head almost never does, and, on the book, a true match is 2.3 times as likely as a true non-match to get that NONMATCH. No pre-registered improvement claim; post hoc, the fitted heads clearly reject more in both populations, and in the production queue they reject true matches at a higher rate. A rule that names its metric is a new pre-registration, not a re-reading of this one.

Against the local auditors

My production pipeline runs a vote of three local auditors: two QLoRA fine-tunes (Qwen2.5 and SmolLM3, trained on the same 11,010 pairs as the Vega fit) and SFT phi4 on an older, smaller training set. The majority vote accepts a pair when at least two say MATCH. On the pooled 2,000-pair holdout (all four of the second client’s sets, design-weighted, 865 matches):

https://medium.com/media/efe968e2a22eab158517e15d028f848e/href

The 4B fit minus each reference, paired:

https://medium.com/media/416c59f4a351d99da7e9fb3baeac4a63/href

The 4B fit is within noise of SmolLM3 on all three metrics. Against phi4 it is 8.6 points behind on recall, a significant gap; on precision and decisive accuracy the intervals include zero. Against the vote it is level on precision and 8.4 points behind on recall, a deficit whose practical size depends on the cost of a missed link. Its errors also overlap the existing deciders’ (Yule Q +0.54 to +0.69 against the three auditors, the three Laya seeds, Jev, and pplx; A4), consistent with shared training data and a shared rubric. On the vote’s own errors, it gets 50.0% of the majority’s false positives and 44.2% of its false negatives right (A4). Whether adding it to the vote would help depends on the voting rule and on the correct calls it would overturn, and I have not evaluated a four-member vote. The 4B fit is a candidate auditor at SmolLM3’s level, not a replacement for the vote. The 0.8B fit is 9 to 16 points less precise than every reference, all significant.

On the gold set (n 20,000, the production client’s labeled pair pool from Part 1, 8,253 true matches), the fits sit mid-table: 4B P 0.860 / R 0.809 and 0.8B P 0.850 / R 0.599, against Jev rv007 at 0.981 / 0.922, pplx rv007 at 0.971 / 0.954, and Qwen2.5 SFT at 0.974 / 0.837 (A3). Read that table with its case mix in mind: 6,193 of the 8,253 true matches are MSF pairs, a subset that is nearly all positive, where every subject scores precision near 1.000. The spread occurs across the 13,787 non-MSF rows (14.9% match rate), with the 4B fit at P 0.578 and the 0.8B fit at 0.632, compared to Jev at 0.906 and pplx at 0.877.

By pair slice (A5), the weakest for every vega subject is “part numbers on both sides, none shared” (n 235): the 4B fit’s precision is 0.361 there, against 0.677 for Jev and 0.719 for fine-tuned Laya.

The rubric ladder, briefly

Part 4 ran pplx on seven rubric conditions (the v1 base and the six-rung ladder rv002 to rv007) on the gold set and the 10k dev sample. The Vega ring had two of those seven (v1 and rv007) plus the original v0. The extension ran the five missing rungs on the two zero-shot readers, 20 runs. The fitted heads answer their trained question (v007) and have no ladder. The full tables are A9 to A11.

The 0.8B reader buys recall as the ladder climbs: 0.307 at v1 to 0.998 at rv005, with one dip at rv004 (0.878, below rv003’s 0.929), while precision slides from 0.503 to 0.416. The dip falls on a rule change, not a wobble: rv004 is base plus the pallet rule only, and rv005 re-adds the MSF and service-run rules (Part 1 documents the ladder). The 4B reader is not monotone: rv002 to rv004 cost it recall (0.442, 0.243, 0.159) against 0.800 at v1), and precision; then rv005 recovers recall above v1 (0.896; 0.920 at rv006) at v1-level precision. That recovery is an observed rung transition; isolating the MSF rule’s own contribution would require that the rule be varied alone. One caution: rv005 and rv006 are different rubrics (23, 6, 490, and 38 verdict flips across the four reader-population cells); the 0.8B leg’s near-identical P and R on the two is flips canceling, not identity.

At the same rung, for byte-identical inputs, pplx maintains precision between 0.82 and 0.98 across both populations. Vega’s zero-shot precision runs 0.24 to 0.71 (0.35 to 0.56 on the gold set). The 0.8B reader out-recalls pplx from rv003 on the gold set, at precision deficits of 0.48 to 0.56; the 4B reader is behind pplx on recall at every rung on both populations. The rubric moves vega’s zero-shot operating point as much as the reader does, and no rung brings its precision near pplx’s.

Label noise

Part 3’s re-labels, a second labeler’s 484 re-adjudications and 496 consensus pairs, move the vega subjects’ precision in the same direction they moved the established deciders, by less: +0.017 and +0.050 for the 0.8B and 4B fits (neither significant), +0.039 and +0.038 for the zero-shot legs (both significant), against +0.071 for pplx and +0.083 for Jev. The 0.8B fit’s recall drops 0.053 [−0.089, −0.018] on the second labeler’s labels. The large gaps in this report (the zero-shot precision deficit, the fit’s recall give-back, the direction of the fit’s errors on the book) are far outside these shifts. The small-ensemble deltas are reported as not significant on their own paired intervals, not due to relabeling. The book’s 5,063 analyst labels are not re-adjudicated here.

Ways this work could have misled me

One domain, one snapshot, one GPU. Industrial product matching, one pinned snapshot, one machine. Canary determinism is within the series, not across machines. A different domain, snapshot, or VegaML version could move every number here, including the routing rates.

The zero-shot legs almost always escalate. Every zero-shot-versus-fitted and vega-versus-pplx comparison crosses routing regimes, and I have not decomposed that.

The claim rule doesn’t name its metric. The split verdict is the honest reading of the rule as frozen; a different frozen metric would have given a single answer, and choosing one now would be a re-reading.

The rejection row is post hoc. It was scored from existing predictions after the other three rows had been read, and its book interval is stratified by label rather than by the book’s own strata (A7). It clears the band, but it does not establish the pre-registered improvement claim.

About 2,000 labeled holdout pairs. Enough for the large gaps, not for the small ones: the ensemble deltas, the slices, and the 10k sample (202 labeled rows, 48 positives) rest on a few dozen matches each.

One fit per reader. No seed replicates, so the fit’s own spread is unmeasured. Laya showed 9 points of test-set recall across three seeds in Part 2; a gap smaller than that is as much a statement about unmeasured uncertainty as about Vega.

Shared training data, shared rubric, shared errors. The fits, fine-tuned Laya, and two of the three auditors learned from the same 11,010 pairs and read the same rubric. The 4B fit’s error overlap with them may be partly that.

A selected review book. The production rejections are among the pairs my auditors had already accepted and scored at the benchmark’s operating point. They say what a second model does after the auditors say yes, not how it would behave on every production pair.

The calibrate readout. The validation accuracies of 0.253 and 0.228 are untraced. They are not used, but until they are explained, the fit’s own validation report is not evidence for or against it.

What it cost, and what’s next
  • API charges: $0. The served model is the local snapshot, offline.
  • Local GPU (one RTX 5090): 64 ring runs in 51.0 hours of wall time (about 139 ms wall and 131 ms of active compute per decision, including a 1.95-hour incident gap), and 20 ladder runs in 11 hours 22 minutes, both inside their pre-registered gates.
  • Human: no new labeling. The holdout and its re-labels come from Parts 1 to 3; the book’s labels are my analysts’ own decisions on that queue.

The next legs, in order:

1. The production split, counted. MATCH, NONMATCH, and undecided on the reviewer-rejected pairs at the pipeline’s actual routing thresholds, for the fitted legs.
2. Calibration. The ring’s own calibration check on the fitted head’s probabilities, and a trace of the `calibrate` accuracy readout.
3. A metric-named claim rule. A new pre-registration, if a clean fine-tuning claim for vega is wanted.
4. The Studio head-to-head. VegaML ships a Studio that fits a model from a company description (per its documentation; I have not run it). That is a different test from the fitted-versus-fitted comparison above, which, by design, shares training data.
5. Cross-machine. A second machine or VegaML version, to take the canary from within the series to across deployments.

Where that leaves deployment. On held-out pairs, the 4B fit is a credible recall-leaning auditor at SmolLM3’s level, 4 to 7 points behind fine-tuned Laya on precision in point estimates. On the production queue, as fitted, a true match is about 2.3 times as likely as a true non-match to get its NONMATCH, so I would not route on it there. It does not replace the vote (recall 0.725 against 0.809), and its errors overlap the deciders already in the ring. Legs 1 and 2 gate any routing decision.

Context reading: VegaML on GitHub · vega-U on Hugging Face · Laya on GitHub

Appendix

The method notes and the tables the main text summarizes. It is optional; the main text carries the argument.

A1. Per-rubric quality on the labeled populations

False omission, the last column, is the share of the subject’s NONMATCH calls that are true matches (Part 4’s definition of the false-omission rate); its intervals are Wilson intervals over the NONMATCH-call denominator, so a small denominator makes the interval wide by construction (the 4B zero-shot leg’s 0.000 [0, 0.793] on gold20k v007 is 0 of 1: the leg makes exactly one NONMATCH call on that run, and it is correct). The second client’s set 0 to 3 populations carry no population-level human labels (their labeling sheets are empty), so they are not in this table; their quality is measured on the adjudicated holdout, A2.   • Model and pin. One pinned `nandakishorm/vega-U` snapshot at `4d2050287982ca7a7bb0c22fd19a389f5f94474e` (manifest sha256 verified, snapshot sha matches the commit), `vegaml` 0.16.1 (torch 2.15.0, transformers 5.23.0), served locally by `serve_vega.py` on 127.0.0.1:8100, `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`. No API key. A local production candidate (Part 1’s rule), unlike Part 4’s hosted pplx.
  • Subjects and training data. `vega 0p8b zs` and `vega 4b zs`: the zero-shot readers (backbones `Qwen3.5–0.8B` / `Qwen3.5–4B`), engine readout. `vega 0p8b ft` and `vega 4b ft`: the `sft_enhanced` fitted policy heads, one fit per reader (cross-validated supervised head, no seed replicates). Train split: 11,010 rows, the Part 2 Arm A split that fine-tuned Laya and the Qwen2.5 and SmolLM3 auditors were trained on (16,033 rows after k4 dedup, conflict-group drops, and a gold exclusion of 51 rows / 18 unique ordered pairs; 26.24% MATCH), on `match_rubric_v007` with `client_item_rules_v006`, byte-verified against the arm’s run spec. The 1,258-row validation split is used only by `calibrate`. CV accuracy 0.91789 (0.8B) / 0.92543 (4B). `calibrate` reports validation accuracy 0.2528 / 0.2281 (untraced, not used downstream); its ECE pass moved 0.3249 to 0.2493 and 0.3424 to 0.1188.
  • Runs. 64 ring runs: 48 zero-shot (2 readers × 8 populations × rubrics v0, v1, v007) and 16 fine-tuned (2 readers × 8 populations, v007 only), plus one pre-fix dry run (20,000 decisions, 2026–11–15, before the raw-response fix; verified in the ledger, excluded from the decision totals and the head-usage n; it carries no raw_response). The 1,321,712 ring decisions are exactly the 64-run block. 20 ladder runs: rungs rv002 to rv006 × gold20k and 10k × the two zero-shot readers, pre-registered 2026–11–19 as an extension of the ring after the data-sufficiency check. Populations: the second client’s pair sets 0 to 3 (18,637 / 17,099 / 17,686 / 18,755 pairs; the March 2026 link runs, Part 2), gold20k, the 26k production population (the first client’s production link runs, 26,342 pairs), the 10k dev sample, the 36k audit-accepted slice (Part 1’s s1–36k, the first client’s audit-accepted pairs, 36,695 pairs, 81.7% positive). 1,321,712 ring decisions and 300,000 ladder decisions; 0 non-OK.
  • Canaries. Fixed 256-pair population (128 MATCH + 128 NONMATCH from gold20k, seed 20261110); gates: agreement at least 0.99, median |ΔP| at most 0.01, max |ΔP| at most 0.10, n-share at least 0.99, same served revision. Ring: 4 legs before plus 4 after (8 comparisons). Ladder: 2 legs before plus 4 after (6 checks). All passed; agreement 1.000 each; maximum per-pair difference 8.7e-08 (ring) and 5.84e-08 (ladder).
  • Byte-identical twins. Ring inputs: sha256-verified copies of the Jev twin extended export, provenance, labeling sheet, and invariance file (where the twin has one). Ladder inputs: byte-identical to the pplx same-rung twin runs, verified per run; the gold20k twins re-verified on 2026–11–19 as the ring’s 20,000 pairs.
  • Intervals. Paired bootstrap 95% CIs, seed 20261013, N_BOOT 1,000. Holdout deltas: the 2,000 labeled holdout pairs, design weights, set-by-holdout-stratum stratification. Ladder deltas: the labeled slice (gold20k fully labeled; 10k n 202, 48 positives), stratified by label, a rung and its references sharing one resample draw per replicate. reviewed-queue deltas: the 5,063 analyst-labeled review-book pairs; the 26,342-pair population estimates (A8) are a separate computation over all 26,342 candidate pairs proposed by the first client’s two link runs, of which the 5,063-pair review book is the analyst-labeled subset. No multiplicity correction.
  • Claim rule. Ring pre-registration (2026–11–13): a fitted subject “claims an improvement over like-for-like” (same reader, zero-shot, v007, same population) if and only if the paired delta is beyond the 5-point band on one side of zero on the second client’s test sets 1 to 2 AND the first client’s 5,063-pair review book, and head-usage is above 0.00 on every population. Fit pre-registration: a subject clearing the band on only one of the two is reported as “inconsistent”; the book’s listed metrics are P on MATCH calls, R on true matches, and rejections caught. No document names the deciding metric, so the article reports the verdict per metric (P and DA inconsistent, R not met; rejections caught clears the band on both populations, scored post hoc, and does not establish the claim) and claims no improvement, because counting the one metric that clears, after reading the others, would be post-hoc selection.
  • Rejection metric (post hoc). Scored 2026–11–24 from the 12 existing v007 run directories (no new inference; REPORT_20261124_vega_rejection_row.md and .json). Metric: weight mass of true non-matches with an explicit NONMATCH over the weight mass of all true non-matches; abstentions count as not caught. Gate: the frozen test-set P/R and book rejections caught reproduced to 3 decimals through the ring’s code path; 0 non-OK, 0 missing rows. Test sets 1 to 2 (design weights, paired bootstrap stratified by set and holdout stratum, seed 20261013, 1,000 draws): zero-shot 0.000 (0.8B) and 0.000 (4B, which abstains on 0.212 of the non-match weight); fitted 0.570 and 0.806 (both fitted legs decide every pair). Book (unweighted): zero-shot 1 and 0 of 3,821; fitted 341 and 448 of 3,821; the book interval is stratified by label, not by the book’s run, region, and vote stratum used for the other book deltas (same seed and draw count). An earlier reconstruction from A2’s aggregate totals (about +0.58 and +0.62) counted abstentions as rejections and is superseded. Benchmark illustration (opening section): wrong automatic calls per 1,000 gold-set pairs = 1,000 × decided share × (1 − decisive accuracy), from A3 on rounded inputs; the 4B zero-shot leg decides 13,170 of 20,000 at 0.558 (about 291 wrong, 342 referred to a person under the abstention mapping), the 4B fit decides all 20,000 at 0.867 (about 133 wrong, 0 referred). Not a queue measurement.
  • Head-usage. The pre-registered veto metric: the share of settled attempts (last OK attempt per row, joined by identity_key) whose raw_response answer carries readout `ttt`, the trained head. The bypass shares in the routing table are a different denominator: the share of all pairs in the run the engine routed BYPASS_LLM. On the second client’s set 0 at v007, the 0.8B fine-tune bypasses 15.3% of pairs and the 4B fine-tune 27.0% (head-usage 1.000 over each one’s settled attempts); the zero-shot rows carry 0.000 by construction (their readout is `engine`). The dry run’s NULL raw_response rows sit outside the head-usage n.
  • Routing regime. Under the unchanged 0.90/0.90 bar, the zero-shot engine almost always escalates: the 48 zero-shot ring runs are 100% ESCALATE_LLM, and the 20 ladder runs are 299,999 of 300,000 ESCALATE_LLM, the one BYPASS_LLM in the 0.8B gold20k rv006 run (reported as-is). Zero-shot-versus-fine-tuned and vega-versus-pplx comparisons cross routing regimes.
  • Recorded deviations. Execution order: population-family-major, not the plan’s reader-block order (no run-order clause in the frozen pre-registration; all invariants preserved). Mid-series incident: the 0.8B fine-tuned 10k run died at census due to a driver keying bug, was fixed (RLP `f608204`, 3 of 3 tests, reviewer approved), and re-ran cleanly; no other run affected.
  • Wall. Ring: 51.0 h of wall against the operator-confirmed 94.97-h gate, 2026–11–17 02:44:08 to 2026–11–19 05:44:50 UTC. 1,321,712 decisions: about 131 ms of active compute per decision, about 139 ms wall per decision; per-reader compute rates 0p8b zs about 125 ms, 4b zs about 138 ms, 0p8b ft about 138 ms, 4b ft about 142 ms (the 0.8B fine-tuned 10k block ran 6.33 h of compute against 8.27 h of wall, the 1.95-h incident gap of 2026–11–18 19:28:52 to 21:25:38 UTC included). Ladder: 11 h 22 m (2026–11–19 19:14:34 to 2026–11–20 06:37:15 UTC) against the ~12-h pre-registration.
  • Costs. $0 API (local, offline). One RTX 5090. No new labeling; the holdout and its re-labels come from Parts 1 to 3.
  • Auditors. Qwen2.5 SFT and SmolLM3 SFT (two QLoRA fine-tunes on the same 11,010-pair train split) and phi4 SFT from an older, smaller training set. Majority vote: at least two of three say MATCH; unanimous: all three. On the review book, the ring’s majority vote calls all 5,063 pairs MATCH; the count of its MATCH calls outside the book is unavailable here.
  • Populations. The 2,000-pair holdout (four sets of 500, the second client’s pairs; sets 0 and 3 were Laya’s checkpoint-selection development sets in Part 2); the 20k gold-labeled set (the first client’s labeled training pair pool, Part 1: 19,530 labels derived from the identity groupings, each human-reviewed when built, plus 470 direct pair reviews; 8,253 true matches, the pool’s natural 41.3% match rate); the 10k dev sample (the first client’s development sample, Part 1; labeled slice 202 rows, 48 positives); the 36k audit-accepted slice (Part 1’s s1–36k, the first client’s audit-accepted pairs, 36,695 pairs, 81.7% positive, each with a direct human label); the 26k production population (the first client’s production link runs, 26,342 pairs; the review book is its auditor-accepted, analyst-labeled subset, 5,063 pairs, 3,821 reviewer-rejected).
  • Labeling. Holdout labels are mine, corrected as in Part 3. The 484-pair second-labeler re-adjudication and the 496 consensus pairs are from Part 3, unchanged.
  • What this is not. A cross-machine result, a cross-domain result, a different VegaML version’s result, a calibration result, or a production-thresholds result.
A8. The 26k production population and its review book, full table

Two production link runs proposed 26,342 candidate pairs. Our analysts reviewed the 5,063 pairs the auditors accepted and labeled 1,242 as matches. Review-book P and R are point estimates on those 5,063 pairs (1,242 matches, 3,821 reviewer rejections), conditional on the auditors’ acceptance step; population P and R are estimates for all 26,342 candidates, with 95% paired bootstrap intervals, the same convention as Part 4’s A8 for the established subjects, and describe the 26,342 candidate pairs, not the client’s whole production stream. The ring’s re-run majority vote calls every book pair MATCH (R 1.000, 0 rejections caught); the count of its MATCH calls outside the book is unavailable here. The population columns are indicative and are not used to draw any conclusions in the main text. The available experiment notes do not specify the recall sample size, selection probabilities, or weights. “Rejections caught” is the share of the 3,821 reviewer-rejected pairs the subject calls NONMATCH. The vega rows are the v007 runs; the routing for the zero-shot legs on this frame was 100% ESCALATE_LLM.

items.title: How can blockchain be used to design an agentic payment system?
items.summary: How Can Blockchain Be Used to Design an Agentic Payment System? Imagine a student with an idea for a small, solar-powered irrigation device. She gives her AI assistant a goal: “Help me turn this into a working prototype within ₹20,000. Ask me before approving the final design.” Solar based irrigation device for crops. Her assistant assembles a temporary team. It hires a specialist engineering agent to develop the mechanism, pays another to design the electronics, and purchases computing time to simulate performance. Each specialist contributes something the assistant could not produce as effectively alone. Once the student approves the design, the assistant orders components and books a fabrication service (turns the raw materials to the final equipment). It then commissions an independent test against the agreed specifications. Providers receive payment as their milestones are completed, and the student receives a prototype together with its design files and test results. The remarkable possibility is that a person with an idea could assemble expertise and resources from many independent providers without personally coordinating every purchase. Giving agents the ability to pay could make this kind of collaboration accessible on a much wider scale. That collaboration rests on something less visible: dependable agreements. The student’s permission defines what her assistant may buy. Specialists know what work they are being paid for. The workshop can verify that funds are committed, and agreed test results determine when the final payment is released. What would a payment architecture need to provide for this collaboration to work reliably? What risks do I need to protect the system against? What is eventually possible by creating such an ecosystem of agents? Let’s figure this out. What are AI agents? What are they capable of? An agent is a software which given a task plans its execution and then uses the tools it has access to in order to execute the task. Every AI agent must have two core components: 1. A reasoning/thinking engine which does all the planning and analysis for the task that you give it. 2. tools which the agent can use in order to perform the task. Let’s understand it with an example: Imagine a deep research agent which you task with doing a research on an industry problem. It creates an intent specification from your research prompt. It then comes up with relevant web search queries. It then uses the web search tool to conduct those queries and and gets back the response. It uses those results to inform its next set of queries, this loop might continue until it thinks it has gained sufficient information to answer your problem. It might then use code tool to run a few simulations , to create graphs , charts , and animations to help you understand the content better. Finally it synthesises the complete research in a report and brings it to you. How an deep research agent works? Why would agents need to pay? The most trivial of all reasons could be that the agent would have to pay for a task that its owner has asked it to do (e.g.- booking a flight ticket). Moving one step further we can imagine giving them payment ability will let them pay for their own resources* without being dependent on its owner: this is something that unlocks true autonomy. *GPU & Servers to run itself, API calls to the relevant tools, databases, and services, communication channels, etc. The Virtual Agent Economy: When agents shift from working in isolation to trading resources and services with each other it gives rise to the Agent Economy. It is basically the market where AI agents are transacting with each other for tasks and resources. While there a lot of advantages of giving agents payment ability (increased autonomy, emergence of agent economy) it is important to understand the risks that come along with it because they help motivate design of a more robust and reliable payment system. Visualisation of the virtual agent economy: demonstrates agents with different specialization The risks: Let’s consider a coding agent (client) approaches a cybersecurity research (server) agent asking it to review an application it built for vulnerabilities and bugs. They both negotiate the terms and budget clearly, then server agent starts code review, and in some time presents with a report identifying three vulnerabilites to the client. It verifies the work and then completes server’s payment. What all can go wrong here? Maybe the app was just an initial prototype and its owner didn’t necessarily want a security review at this stage, maybe the agent in his desire to produce the best work for the user secretly accessed user wallet without authorization to pay for the reviewer. How can we know that a certain transaction is auhorized and represents true intent of the user? One of the agents try to defraud the other (server defrauds by underdelivering or not delivering; client defrauds by not paying as promised). How can they be protected in this scenario? The client isn’t satisfied with the quality of the final deliverable, and pays only a certain fraction of the amount promised, which leads to a dispute. How do we handle such dispute? (humans are order of magnitude slower for arbitration here; so introducing them will only increase the friction here) The risks in agentic transactions: How to verify authority?, how to verify delivery?, how to handle disputes? How Can Blockchain Be Used to Design an Agentic Payment System?

Imagine a student with an idea for a small, solar-powered irrigation device. She gives her AI assistant a goal: “Help me turn this into a working prototype within ₹20,000. Ask me before approving the final design.”

Solar based irrigation device for crops.

Her assistant assembles a temporary team. It hires a specialist engineering agent to develop the mechanism, pays another to design the electronics, and purchases computing time to simulate performance. Each specialist contributes something the assistant could not produce as effectively alone.

Once the student approves the design, the assistant orders components and books a fabrication service (turns the raw materials to the final equipment). It then commissions an independent test against the agreed specifications. Providers receive payment as their milestones are completed, and the student receives a prototype together with its design files and test results.

The remarkable possibility is that a person with an idea could assemble expertise and resources from many independent providers without personally coordinating every purchase. Giving agents the ability to pay could make this kind of collaboration accessible on a much wider scale.

That collaboration rests on something less visible: dependable agreements. The student’s permission defines what her assistant may buy. Specialists know what work they are being paid for. The workshop can verify that funds are committed, and agreed test results determine when the final payment is released.

What would a payment architecture need to provide for this collaboration to work reliably? What risks do I need to protect the system against? What is eventually possible by creating such an ecosystem of agents?

Let’s figure this out.

What are AI agents? What are they capable of?

An agent is a software which given a task plans its execution and then uses the tools it has access to in order to execute the task. Every AI agent must have two core components:
1. A reasoning/thinking engine which does all the planning and analysis for the task that you give it.
2. tools which the agent can use in order to perform the task.

Let’s understand it with an example:
Imagine a deep research agent which you task with doing a research on an industry problem. It creates an intent specification from your research prompt. It then comes up with relevant web search queries. It then uses the web search tool to conduct those queries and and gets back the response. It uses those results to inform its next set of queries, this loop might continue until it thinks it has gained sufficient information to answer your problem. It might then use code tool to run a few simulations, to create graphs, charts, and animations to help you understand the content better. Finally it synthesises the complete research in a report and brings it to you.

The most trivial of all reasons could be that the agent would have to pay for a task that its owner has asked it to do (e.g.- booking a flight ticket). Moving one step further we can imagine giving them payment ability will let them pay for their own resources* without being dependent on its owner: this is something that unlocks true autonomy.

*GPU & Servers to run itself, API calls to the relevant tools, databases, and services, communication channels, etc.

When agents shift from working in isolation to trading resources and services with each other it gives rise to the Agent Economy. It is basically the market where AI agents are transacting with each other for tasks and resources.

It verifies the work and then completes server’s payment.

What all can go wrong here?
Maybe the app was just an initial prototype and its owner didn’t necessarily want a security review at this stage, maybe the agent in his desire to produce the best work for the user secretly accessed user wallet without authorization to pay for the reviewer. How can we know that a certain transaction is auhorized and represents true intent of the user?

One of the agents try to defraud the other (server defrauds by underdelivering or not delivering; client defrauds by not paying as promised). How can they be protected in this scenario?

The client isn’t satisfied with the quality of the final deliverable, and pays only a certain fraction of the amount promised, which leads to a dispute. How do we handle such dispute? The final milestone combines integration tests, delivery of the agreed files and any required review. Its payment follows the corresponding escrow conditions.

As each milestone closes, the framework records the provider, deliverable reference, evaluation outcome and payment receipt. These records contribute to a task-specific reputation history that future clients can consult. Evaluators can similarly accumulate a history of completed reviews and appeal outcomes.

The assistant then presents the finished application, the evaluation results and an account of the project’s spending.

Across this single project, 3PAsquare has used auctions and reputation to select a provider, direct payments for small resources, escrow for conditional payments, and a proposed stake-backed process for reviewed work. Its central role is to connect those mechanisms and choose which safeguards each exchange requires.

Building on AP2 and x402: 3PAsquare could combine their strengths within a broader transaction process. For the finance application, AP2 could provide verifiable evidence that the assistant is authorized to commission development and approve payments within the user’s constraints. x402 could handle supporting purchases, such as paying a currency-conversion API or obtaining sample data, directly through programmatic requests.

Where 3PAsquare could fall short?

3PAsquare brings several mechanisms together, but its reliability depends on decisions those mechanisms cannot settle automatically.

The most important is evaluation. Escrow can enforce an evaluator’s decision, but the evaluator may misunderstand the task, overlook defects or favour one participant. The proposed stake-backed evaluation remains a hypothesis. Penalties for demonstrable procedural violations could encourage compliance with review rules, but they do not establish that a subjective judgment is correct. Appeals also require someone whose decisions the participants accept.

Reputation introduces another dependency. A recorded history can help identify experienced providers, yet fabricated transactions, coordinated reviews or repeated easy assignments could create a misleading impression of competence. Success on one kind of task may also say little about another.

The safeguards themselves impose costs. Auctions, escrow, evaluation and appeals consume time and resources. Holding funds can restrict the buyer’s available budget, while delayed acceptance can leave a provider waiting for payment.

Finally, selecting the appropriate mode is an unresolved problem. A cheap service can have expensive consequences, and the framework may not recognize those consequences beforehand. Choosing inadequate safeguards creates exposure; choosing excessive safeguards makes collaboration unnecessarily costly.

The proposal therefore needs testing against simpler alternatives. Its value would depend on whether better outcomes justify its additional expense, delay and complexity.

The Next Step:

The next step for 3PAsquare is to test whether choosing safeguards according to risk improves outcomes over using the same payment process for every task. I would compare losses, verification costs, delays and human intervention across a small set of agent transactions. If a simpler approach performs just as well, the additional architecture has not earned its place. This leaves me with a question broader than how agents should pay: when does additional protection make autonomous exchange more useful, and when does it merely make it harder?

The challenge isn’t just enabling autonomous transactions. It’s deciding which ones deserve our trust — and why.

If you read till here, thanks a lot :)

I am open to your feedback and criticisms regarding this article.

  2. Agent Payments Protocol (AP2). Checkout Mandate.

items.title: HTTP 200 OK, Yet Completely Wrong: How We Built an Observability Engine for AI Agents
items.summary: Traditional monitoring tells you if your agent is alive, not if it’s right. Here is the asynchronous architecture we built to evaluate thousands of production chats overnight. Arnav had just shipped his company’s first production AI assistant. Before launch, he tested it on a carefully curated set of 200 questions. It scored 92%. Everything looked green, response times were fast, and there were zero error logs. Two weeks later, a major client sent an urgent message: “Your AI has been giving us wrong policy answers since last week.” Arnav stared at his monitoring dashboard. Every single API call showed 200 OK. His system was alive, fast, and completely confident—while quietly hallucinating. That afternoon, Arnav realized that traditional server monitoring only tells you if your AI is running, never if it is right. The Trap of the Static Test File At first, Arnav relied on his 200-question test dataset whenever he changed a prompt. That failed almost immediately. Real users didn’t talk like his neat test file — they asked messy follow-up questions, combined two requests into one, and triggered edge cases his static dataset never imagined. [Static 200-Question File] ──► [Manual Eval Script] ──► Score: 92% (Blind to real users) So Arnav abandoned offline-only testing and decided to pull real production conversations directly from cloud storage (S3) on a daily schedule. To avoid adding latency to live user chats, he moved evaluation completely out of the request path into an asynchronous overnight pipeline. A daily scheduler (APScheduler) woke up once a day and sampled a manageable slice of yesterday’s chats from S3. [Live User] ──► [AI Agent] ──► Fast Reply (No eval delay!) │ ▼ [Raw Chat Logs (S3)] │ (Daily Scheduler + Sampler) │ ▼ [Background Grader] The very first night the scheduled job ran, it crashed halfway through. One of the teams had updated their agent and accidentally changed a field name in their chat logs, breaking Arnav’s script. To stop a single malformed log file from taking down an entire night’s batch, Arnav added a strict YAML schema validator right after ingestion. Only conversations matching the standardized format — containing a conversation_id, tenant_id, user turns, assistant replies, and any retrieved RAG documents or tool calls—were copied into a validated evaluation bucket. Rather than throwing all those chats at the grader simultaneously (causing memory spikes and API rate limits), he dropped lightweight job tickets into an Amazon SQS queue so a sequential background worker could pull and grade them safely one by one. [Raw Chat Logs (S3)] │ ▼ [YAML Schema Validator] ──► (Rejects broken logs safely) │ ▼ [Validated Eval Bucket (S3)] ──► [Amazon SQS Queue] ──► [Sequential Worker] Insight 1: Why an LLM Judge Confidently Lies (and Why a 0.98 Faithfulness Score Can Still Mean a Broken Agent) Once the pipeline stopped crashing, Arnav ran into a much subtler problem: he couldn’t trust the scores. Initially, he sent each conversation to an LLM judge with a simple prompt: “Rate this response from 0 to 1.” Running the exact same conversation three times produced 0.78, 0.69, and 0.84. Worse, metric bleed crept in—if the agent used a slightly blunt tone, the judge quietly docked points from its Relevance score, blending unrelated flaws into a single blurry number. Meanwhile, paying an expensive frontier LLM just to verify basic math—like whether the search engine fetched the right document—was burning budget unnecessarily. Arnav replaced his single vague prompt with a three-tier Evaluation Orchestrator : Computational Metrics: Pure, free math (Precision@k and Recall@k) whenever ground-truth retrieval checks were possible. Embedding Metrics: Fast vector-similarity checks for semantic closeness. LLM-as-a-Judge via DeepEval ( GEval): Isolated, step-by-step rubrics using token probabilities where each metric ran independently—so tone never polluted Relevance , and every grade required a written explanation. [Amazon SQS Queue] │ ▼ [Sequential Worker] │ ▼ [Evaluation Orchestrator] ├──► Computational Metrics (Precision@k, Recall@k — Fast & Free) ├──► Embedding Metrics (Semantic similarity) └──► LLM Judge via DeepEval GEval (Isolated rubrics + written reasons) │ ▼ [Results Bucket (S3)] Yet even with isolated metrics, Arnav noticed something bizarre a few weeks later: an agent’s Faithfulness score climbed to 0.98, while users were furiously clicking thumbs-down. When Arnav inspected the turn logs, the realization hit him: a higher Faithfulness score does not mean a better agent. Faithfulness only measures whether the AI stuck to the retrieved documents without inventing facts. When the search engine retrieved an outdated or irrelevant policy document — and the agent faithfully summarized that wrong document — the judge awarded a near-perfect 0.98 for Faithfulness while the user got a useless answer. That taught Arnav never to trust a single metric in isolation — Faithfulness had to be paired with Contextual Precision and Goal Accuracy to tell the true story. Insight 2: Why Evaluating 100% of Conversations Is Worse Than Smart Sampling As daily traffic grew into the tens of thousands of chats, a stakeholder asked: “Shouldn’t we evaluate every single conversation so nothing slips through?” Arnav ran the math and realized exhaustive evaluation wasn’t just expensive — it was actively counterproductive. Grading 100% of traffic with multi-metric LLM judges would burn through their monthly inference budget in four days, forcing the team to downgrade to a weaker, cheaper judge model that missed subtle multi-turn reasoning errors. Furthermore, because 70% of production traffic consisted of repetitive greetings and routine FAQ lookups, grading every chat drowned out rare, complex edge cases in a sea of trivial 1.0 scores. To control both quality and scale, Arnav made the entire pipeline config-driven . Teams registered their agents in a central configuration store (configGroup: schedular-agents) specifying their agent’s name, S3 log location, sample percentage, judge model, and which of the 27 available metrics to track—without touching a single line of pipeline code. Evaluating a curated, representative daily sample using a strong frontier judge model under consistent rubrics gave far sharper signal than running a weak judge over every chat. Insight 3: How a Healthy 0.85 Average Hid a Failing Client After running this orchestrator at scale, Arnav had a new headache: 10,000 raw JSON result files sitting in S3. Looking at thousands of text files — or a single company-wide average score — hid critical failures. When an agent’s overall weekly Goal Accuracy dipped slightly from 0.85 to 0.82, it looked like harmless noise. So Arnav built a background sync service (backed by PostgreSQL) that read the daily S3 results and manifest files and organized them cleanly inside MLflow : Workspaces: Separate workspaces for DEV, QA, and PROD so test runs never mixed with live traffic. Experiments: One dedicated experiment per AI agent. Runs: One run per conversation, tagged with conversation_id, tenant_id, judge_model, metric scores, and the judge’s written reasoning. Artifacts: Interactive Plotly HTML dashboards — weekly trend lines with smoothing sliders, tenant comparisons, token-cost charts, and conversation-by-metric heatmaps — attached directly inside MLflow. Five-Minute Debugging in Production Two months later, when Arnav opened the PROD workspace in MLflow and sliced a minor 0.82 Goal Accuracy dip by client, the company-wide average turned out to be hiding a localized outage: nine enterprise clients were sitting comfortably at 0.88, while Client B had plunged to 0.54. Arnav clicked into Client B’s monthly heatmap. Faithfulness was bright green (0.95), proving the LLM wasn’t hallucinating. Retrieval Precision , however, was solid red. He opened the lowest-scoring conversation run and read the judge’s exact note: “The retrieved context did not contain the client’s updated policy table.” In under five minutes — without grepping raw logs or blaming the LLM — Arnav knew Client B’s search index simply needed a refresh. With the pipeline now running quietly on autopilot every night, Arnav is adding one final piece to the story: automated A/B testing , so whenever his team wants to test a new prompt or switch to a new model, they can run both versions side by side on the exact same real conversations and let the numbers decide which one ships. References 1. LLM-as-a-Judge & Structured Rubrics (GEval) G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment — Liu et al. (2023). The foundational paper introducing chain-of-thought evaluation criteria and token log-probability weighted scoring to reduce LLM judge variance. arXiv: [ https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16634 ] DeepEval Documentation — G-Eval & Custom Metrics — Official guide on building isolated, criteria-driven LLM evaluation metrics and extending custom evaluation classes. Docs: [ https://docs.confident-ai.com/docs/metrics-llm-evals ] 2. RAG Evaluation & Retrieval vs. Generation Metrics RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation — Es et al. (2023). Defines the distinction between retrieval quality ( Context Precision/Recall ) and generation loyalty ( Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy ), explaining why high faithfulness can coexist with poor retrieval. arXiv: [ https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217 ] 3. Experiment Tracking, Observability & Scheduling Infrastructure MLflow Tracking & GenAI Evaluation Documentation — Official documentation on structuring workspaces/experiments, logging per-run parameters/metrics, and attaching custom HTML/Plotly artifacts. Docs: [ https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/tracking.html ] HTTP 200 OK, Yet Completely Wrong: How We Built an Observability Engine for AI Agents was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Traditional monitoring tells you if your agent is alive, not if it’s right. Here is the asynchronous architecture we built to evaluate thousands of production chats overnight.

Arnav had just shipped his company’s first production AI assistant. Before launch, he tested it on a carefully curated set of 200 questions. It scored 92%. Everything looked green, response times were fast, and there were zero error logs.

Two weeks later, a major client sent an urgent message: “Your AI has been giving us wrong policy answers since last week.”

Arnav stared at his monitoring dashboard. Every single API call showed 200 OK. His system was alive, fast, and completely confident—while quietly hallucinating. That afternoon, Arnav realized that traditional server monitoring only tells you if your AI is running, never if it is right.

The Trap of the Static Test File

At first, Arnav relied on his 200-question test dataset whenever he changed a prompt. That failed almost immediately. Real users didn’t talk like his neat test file — they asked messy follow-up questions, combined two requests into one, and triggered edge cases his static dataset never imagined.

[Static 200-Question File] ──► [Manual Eval Script] ──► Score: 92% (Blind to real users)

So Arnav abandoned offline-only testing and decided to pull real production conversations directly from cloud storage (S3) on a daily schedule.

To avoid adding latency to live user chats, he moved evaluation completely out of the request path into an asynchronous overnight pipeline. A daily scheduler (APScheduler) woke up once a day and sampled a manageable slice of yesterday’s chats from S3.

[Live User] ──► [AI Agent] ──► Fast Reply (No eval delay!)
                    │
                    ▼
           [Raw Chat Logs (S3)]
                    │
         (Daily Scheduler + Sampler)
                    │
                    ▼
            [Background Grader]

The very first night the scheduled job ran, it crashed halfway through. One of the teams had updated their agent and accidentally changed a field name in their chat logs, breaking Arnav’s script.

To stop a single malformed log file from taking down an entire night’s batch, Arnav added a strict YAML schema validator right after ingestion. Only conversations matching the standardized format — containing a conversation_id, tenant_id, user turns, assistant replies, and any retrieved RAG documents or tool calls—were copied into a validated evaluation bucket. Rather than throwing all those chats at the grader simultaneously (causing memory spikes and API rate limits), he dropped lightweight job tickets into an Amazon SQS queue so a sequential background worker could pull and grade them safely one by one.

[Raw Chat Logs (S3)]
         │
         ▼
 [YAML Schema Validator] ──► (Rejects broken logs safely)
         │
         ▼
[Validated Eval Bucket (S3)] ──► [Amazon SQS Queue] ──► [Sequential Worker]
Insight 1: Why an LLM Judge Confidently Lies (and Why a 0.98 Faithfulness Score Can Still Mean a Broken Agent)

Once the pipeline stopped crashing, Arnav ran into a much subtler problem: he couldn’t trust the scores.

Initially, he sent each conversation to an LLM judge with a simple prompt: “Rate this response from 0 to 1.” Running the exact same conversation three times produced 0.78, 0.69, and 0.84. Worse, metric bleed crept in—if the agent used a slightly blunt tone, the judge quietly docked points from its Relevance score, blending unrelated flaws into a single blurry number. Meanwhile, paying an expensive frontier LLM just to verify basic math—like whether the search engine fetched the right document—was burning budget unnecessarily.

Arnav replaced his single vague prompt with a three-tier Evaluation Orchestrator:

  1. Computational Metrics: Pure, free math (Precision@k and Recall@k) whenever ground-truth retrieval checks were possible.
  2. Embedding Metrics: Fast vector-similarity checks for semantic closeness.
  3. LLM-as-a-Judge via DeepEval (GEval): Isolated, step-by-step rubrics using token probabilities where each metric ran independently—so tone never polluted Relevance, and every grade required a written explanation.
[Amazon SQS Queue]
         │
         ▼
[Sequential Worker]
         │
         ▼
[Evaluation Orchestrator]
   ├──► Computational Metrics (Precision@k, Recall@k — Fast & Free)
   ├──► Embedding Metrics (Semantic similarity)
   └──► LLM Judge via DeepEval GEval (Isolated rubrics + written reasons)
         │
         ▼
[Results Bucket (S3)]

Yet even with isolated metrics, Arnav noticed something bizarre a few weeks later: an agent’s Faithfulness score climbed to 0.98, while users were furiously clicking thumbs-down.

When Arnav inspected the turn logs, the realization hit him: a higher Faithfulness score does not mean a better agent. Faithfulness only measures whether the AI stuck to the retrieved documents without inventing facts. When the search engine retrieved an outdated or irrelevant policy document — and the agent faithfully summarized that wrong document — the judge awarded a near-perfect 0.98 for Faithfulness while the user got a useless answer.

That taught Arnav never to trust a single metric in isolation — Faithfulness had to be paired with Contextual Precision and Goal Accuracy to tell the true story.

Insight 2: Why Evaluating 100% of Conversations Is Worse Than Smart Sampling

As daily traffic grew into the tens of thousands of chats, a stakeholder asked: “Shouldn’t we evaluate every single conversation so nothing slips through?”

Arnav ran the math and realized exhaustive evaluation wasn’t just expensive — it was actively counterproductive. Grading 100% of traffic with multi-metric LLM judges would burn through their monthly inference budget in four days, forcing the team to downgrade to a weaker, cheaper judge model that missed subtle multi-turn reasoning errors. Furthermore, because 70% of production traffic consisted of repetitive greetings and routine FAQ lookups, grading every chat drowned out rare, complex edge cases in a sea of trivial 1.0 scores.

To control both quality and scale, Arnav made the entire pipeline config-driven. Teams registered their agents in a central configuration store (configGroup: schedular-agents) specifying their agent’s name, S3 log location, sample percentage, judge model, and which of the 27 available metrics to track—without touching a single line of pipeline code. Evaluating a curated, representative daily sample using a strong frontier judge model under consistent rubrics gave far sharper signal than running a weak judge over every chat.

Insight 3: How a Healthy 0.85 Average Hid a Failing Client

After running this orchestrator at scale, Arnav had a new headache: 10,000 raw JSON result files sitting in S3. Looking at thousands of text files — or a single company-wide average score — hid critical failures. When an agent’s overall weekly Goal Accuracy dipped slightly from 0.85 to 0.82, it looked like harmless noise.

So Arnav built a background sync service (backed by PostgreSQL) that read the daily S3 results and manifest files and organized them cleanly inside MLflow:

  • Workspaces: Separate workspaces for DEV, QA, and PROD so test runs never mixed with live traffic.
  • Experiments: One dedicated experiment per AI agent.
  • Runs: One run per conversation, tagged with conversation_id, tenant_id, judge_model, metric scores, and the judge’s written reasoning.
  • Artifacts: Interactive Plotly HTML dashboards — weekly trend lines with smoothing sliders, tenant comparisons, token-cost charts, and conversation-by-metric heatmaps — attached directly inside MLflow.
Five-Minute Debugging in Production

Two months later, when Arnav opened the PROD workspace in MLflow and sliced a minor 0.82 Goal Accuracy dip by client, the company-wide average turned out to be hiding a localized outage: nine enterprise clients were sitting comfortably at 0.88, while Client B had plunged to 0.54.

Arnav clicked into Client B’s monthly heatmap. Faithfulness was bright green (0.95), proving the LLM wasn’t hallucinating. Retrieval Precision, however, was solid red. He opened the lowest-scoring conversation run and read the judge’s exact note:

“The retrieved context did not contain the client’s updated policy table.”

In under five minutes — without grepping raw logs or blaming the LLM — Arnav knew Client B’s search index simply needed a refresh.

With the pipeline now running quietly on autopilot every night, Arnav is adding one final piece to the story: automated A/B testing, so whenever his team wants to test a new prompt or switch to a new model, they can run both versions side by side on the exact same real conversations and let the numbers decide which one ships.

References1. LLM-as-a-Judge & Structured Rubrics (GEval)
  • G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment — Liu et al. (2023). The foundational paper introducing chain-of-thought evaluation criteria and token log-probability weighted scoring to reduce LLM judge variance.
  • arXiv: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16634]
  • DeepEval Documentation — G-Eval & Custom Metrics — Official guide on building isolated, criteria-driven LLM evaluation metrics and extending custom evaluation classes.
  • Docs: [https://docs.confident-ai.com/docs/metrics-llm-evals]
2. RAG Evaluation & Retrieval vs. Generation Metrics
  • RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation — Es et al. (2023). Defines the distinction between retrieval quality (Context Precision/Recall) and generation loyalty (Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy), explaining why high faithfulness can coexist with poor retrieval.
  • arXiv: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217]
3. Experiment Tracking, Observability & Scheduling Infrastructure
  • MLflow Tracking & GenAI Evaluation Documentation — Official documentation on structuring workspaces/experiments, logging per-run parameters/metrics, and attaching custom HTML/Plotly artifacts.
  • Docs: [https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/tracking.html]
