items.title: WhatsApp, Claude and Cursor Quietly Ate 60 GB of My Mac. Here’s Where It Hides.
items.summary: My Mac was down to 17 GB. The heaviest things on it weren’t junk. They were conversations. 170.81 GB of System Data, and no ⓘ to look inside. My MacBook got down to 17 GB free this week. Storage settings had the answer, sort of: System Data, 170.81 GB. Every other row has a little ⓘ you can click to see what’s inside. System Data doesn’t. Photos, for comparison: 20 MB. I should admit something first: I build a Mac storage app. So the obvious move would be to tell you to buy it. Instead I went looking for the junk myself, the way I’d tell a friend to. I didn’t find much junk. The three heaviest things on my Mac were a messaging app, an AI app and a code editor, and the biggest of them is the one thing on this machine I’d never want a cleaner to touch. That changed how I think about cleanup. “System Data” isn’t junk. It’s four kinds of files sharing one grey bar. Some your Mac frees by itself, some rebuild on their own, some come back only if you download them again, and one pile never comes back at all. Size tells you nothing about which is which. What is System Data on a Mac? It’s the leftovers bucket. Anything your Mac can’t file under Apps, Documents, Photos and the rest ends up there: temporary files, logs, the search index, app data that doesn’t fit a neat label. So “is System Data safe to delete?” has no single answer. It’s like asking whether it’s safe to clear out the garage. Mostly, yes. Not the box with the passports. What I found when I looked You can see the biggest folders yourself. Open Terminal (it’s in Applications → Utilities), paste this line, and press Return. It only looks; it doesn’t change anything: du -sh ~/Library/* 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -8 The biggest folders on my Mac. The top one was WhatsApp. Here’s what the top of my list turned out to be. 42 GB: WhatsApp. Years of photos, videos and voice notes from my chats, all stored on the Mac. 7.8 GB: one single file in my code editor. It’s where the app keeps its saved state, and as far as I can tell that includes my AI chat history. One file, bigger than a lot of people’s entire photo library. 12 GB: a whole mini computer inside the Claude app. The app keeps a small virtual machine to run code in. Most of it can probably be downloaded again. But one of its files is called “session data”, and I’m not deleting anything with that name until I know what’s in it. The real junk was smaller and scattered: about 17 GB of leftovers from building apps, temporary files and old downloads, spread across folders most people never open. Size is the wrong question Most storage tools start the same way: sort by size and show you the biggest thing first. On my Mac that puts 42 GB of WhatsApp at the very top. It’s the biggest item by far and the least replaceable. All the real junk put together adds up to less than half of it. So the useful question isn’t “what’s biggest?” It’s “what happens if this disappears?” The four piles Every file on your Mac answers that question in one of four ways. It frees itself. Your Mac quietly hands this space back when it needs room. You rarely have to do anything. It rebuilds. Temporary files your Mac can recreate from what’s already there. Delete them and the only cost is a slower first launch. It downloads again. Safe to delete, but it only comes back over the internet. Fine at home, painful on a slow connection. It never comes back. Chat photos you haven’t backed up. iPhone backups. That one file in Downloads you’ll need next Tuesday. Nothing recreates these. Nearly every “a cleaner wrecked my Mac” story I’ve read comes down to pile 3 or pile 4 being treated like pile 2. What to try first (no app needed) Look first. System Settings → General → Storage. Click the ⓘ next to each category and see what’s actually there. Check your chat apps. WhatsApp has its own storage screen: Settings → Storage and Data → Manage Storage. It lists your chats by size, so you can clear old videos from one group without touching the rest. Telegram and Messages have similar settings. Empty the Trash. It sounds obvious, but files in the Trash still take up space until you empty it. Old iPhone backups. In Finder, click your iPhone, then Manage Backups. Delete only the ones you’re sure you don’t need. If you write code, that’s where the easy wins are. Xcode’s build folder (~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData) rebuilds itself, and brew cleanup and npm cache verify deal with old downloads. Mine had about 12 GB here I could clear tonight. items.summary_html:
My Mac was down to 17 GB. The heaviest things on it weren’t junk. They were conversations.170.81 GB of System Data, and no ⓘ to look inside.

My MacBook got down to 17 GB free this week. Storage settings had the answer, sort of: System Data, 170.81 GB. Every other row has a little ⓘ you can click to see what’s inside. System Data doesn’t. Photos, for comparison: 20 MB.

I should admit something first: I build a Mac storage app. So the obvious move would be to tell you to buy it. Instead I went looking for the junk myself, the way I’d tell a friend to.

I didn’t find much junk. The three heaviest things on my Mac were a messaging app, an AI app and a code editor, and the biggest of them is the one thing on this machine I’d never want a cleaner to touch.

That changed how I think about cleanup. “System Data” isn’t junk. It’s four kinds of files sharing one grey bar. Some your Mac frees by itself, some rebuild on their own, some come back only if you download them again, and one pile never comes back at all. Size tells you nothing about which is which.

What is System Data on a Mac?

It’s the leftovers bucket. Anything your Mac can’t file under Apps, Documents, Photos and the rest ends up there: temporary files, logs, the search index, app data that doesn’t fit a neat label.

So “is System Data safe to delete?” has no single answer. It’s like asking whether it’s safe to clear out the garage. Mostly, yes. Not the box with the passports.

What I found when I looked

You can see the biggest folders yourself. Open Terminal (it’s in Applications → Utilities), paste this line, and press Return. It only looks; it doesn’t change anything:

du -sh ~/Library/* 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -8
The biggest folders on my Mac. The top one was WhatsApp.

Here’s what the top of my list turned out to be.

42 GB: WhatsApp. Years of photos, videos and voice notes from my chats, all stored on the Mac.

7.8 GB: one single file in my code editor. It’s where the app keeps its saved state, and as far as I can tell that includes my AI chat history. One file, bigger than a lot of people’s entire photo library.

12 GB: a whole mini computer inside the Claude app. The app keeps a small virtual machine to run code in. Most of it can probably be downloaded again. But one of its files is called “session data”, and I’m not deleting anything with that name until I know what’s in it.

The real junk was smaller and scattered: about 17 GB of leftovers from building apps, temporary files and old downloads, spread across folders most people never open.

Size is the wrong question

Most storage tools start the same way: sort by size and show you the biggest thing first.

On my Mac that puts 42 GB of WhatsApp at the very top. It’s the biggest item by far and the least replaceable. All the real junk put together adds up to less than half of it.

So the useful question isn’t “what’s biggest?” It’s “what happens if this disappears?”

The four piles

Every file on your Mac answers that question in one of four ways.

It frees itself. Your Mac quietly hands this space back when it needs room. You rarely have to do anything.

It rebuilds. Temporary files your Mac can recreate from what’s already there. Delete them and the only cost is a slower first launch.

It downloads again. Safe to delete, but it only comes back over the internet. Fine at home, painful on a slow connection.

It never comes back. Chat photos you haven’t backed up. iPhone backups. That one file in Downloads you’ll need next Tuesday. Nothing recreates these.

Nearly every “a cleaner wrecked my Mac” story I’ve read comes down to pile 3 or pile 4 being treated like pile 2.

What to try first (no app needed)

Look first. System Settings → General → Storage. Click the ⓘ next to each category and see what’s actually there.

Check your chat apps. WhatsApp has its own storage screen: Settings → Storage and Data → Manage Storage. It lists your chats by size, so you can clear old videos from one group without touching the rest. Telegram and Messages have similar settings.

Empty the Trash. It sounds obvious, but files in the Trash still take up space until you empty it.

Old iPhone backups. In Finder, click your iPhone, then Manage Backups. Delete only the ones you’re sure you don’t need.

If you write code, that’s where the easy wins are. Xcode’s build folder (~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData) rebuilds itself, and brew cleanup and npm cache verify deal with old downloads. Mine had about 12 GB here I could clear tonight.

So, is a Mac cleaner worth it?

For most people, no. If the steps above get you comfortable again, stop there.

It’s worth it if you keep running into folders with names you don’t recognise and don’t want to Google them at midnight. Or if deleting things with no undo makes your stomach drop a little.

What it’s never worth: a big “12 GB cleaned!” number with no list behind it, things ticked for you in advance, or a subscription for something you’ll open twice a year.

Why I built one anyway

Because I kept being the person staring at folder names I half recognised, wondering which pile they were in.

Most tools tell you how big something is. I wanted one that tells you what it is and what happens if it’s gone. So I built Clean House. It draws your Mac as a little house you walk through room by room, instead of a wall of red warnings. Every item has a “Why?” that says in plain English what it is and whether it comes back. Nothing is deleted for real: it goes to the Trash, and you can undo it.

It’s a one-time $6.99 at launch ($9.99 after), and the first 5 GB are free.

Clean House shows your Mac as a house, room by room.Before anything moves, every item says whether it rebuilds or downloads again.

If the steps above were enough, you don’t need it, and I mean that. If they weren’t, it’s here.

Quick answers

Is it safe to delete System Data on a Mac?
Not as one block. Some of it frees itself or rebuilds. Backups and chat media don’t come back. Ask what happens if each thing disappears, then decide.

Why does System Data keep growing?
Usually temporary files, the search index, and apps that store a lot locally, like chat and AI apps. Check again after big macOS updates.

Do Macs need a cleaner at all?
Not to stay healthy. macOS has built-in malware protection, and most cleanup is a few steps you can do yourself. A tool helps you see what’s there and gives you an undo. That’s it.

How many GB should System Data be?
There’s no normal number. Apple doesn’t publish one, and it depends on the apps you use. Mine was 170 GB and most of it wasn’t junk. Look closer when it’s bigger than your free space, or keeps growing every week.

Why is my System Data 200 GB?
Usually a few big owners, not thousands of junk files. On my Mac it was WhatsApp (42 GB), a virtual machine inside the Claude app (12 GB) and one Cursor file (7.8 GB). The actual junk was about 17 GB.

What’s the heaviest thing on your Mac? I’m curious how many turn out to be conversations too.

I’m Shiva. I make small, pay-once Mac apps, including Clean House.

items.title: LLM vs. LRM: Which AI Should You Pay For?
items.summary: Have you ever asked an AI a hard question and watched it pause for a long moment before replying? Maybe you saw a little “thinking…” message, and you wondered what on earth was going on in there. That pause is the whole story of large reasoning models , or LRMs. They are one of the biggest shifts in AI in recent years, and the idea behind them is surprisingly human: slow down before you answer. In this post, I’ll explain what LRMs are, how they’re trained, why they cost more, and how to decide when the extra thinking is worth it. First, a quick refresher on LLMs You probably know the basics. A large language model, or LLM, predicts the next token in a sequence. A token is a small chunk of text. Given your prompt, it picks the most likely next token, then the next, then the next, and the result reads like human writing. This works wonderfully for many tasks. Ask for a fun social media post or a friendly email, and that fast, reflex-like response is usually perfect. But now imagine asking something harder: “Debug this messy stack trace.” “Trace money through four different shell companies.” A quick reflex isn’t enough. You’d want someone to pause, test ideas, and double-check their work. So what makes a model a “reasoning” model? An LRM still produces text one token at a time. The difference is what happens before the final answer. Reasoning models are language models that reflect on a problem before generating an answer. They sketch a plan, weigh options, check calculations, and sometimes test ideas along the way. Only then do they write the response you see. Think of a student in a classroom. A reasoning model is like a student who takes time to understand the question, splits it into manageable steps, and details the solution process instead of rushing to write the answer. That internal “chain of thought” lets the model try a hypothesis, drop a dead end, and land on a reasoned answer instead of just following a statistically likely pattern. Here’s a quick comparison: LLM (fast reflex) LRM (thinks first) How it answers Predicts the next words straight away Plans, checks, then answers Best at Writing, summaries, simple Q&A Multi-step logic, math, tricky debugging Speed Fast Slower Cost Lower Higher Prompting May need tricks like “think step by step” Usually needs less prompt coaching How do you teach a model to think? This part fascinated me. It happens in stages. Stage 1: Pre-training, learning about the world An LRM usually starts as an existing LLM. In pre-training, it reads billions of web pages, books, and code repositories. That gives it language skills and broad knowledge, like a student who has read a very big library. Stage 2: Reasoning-focused tuning, learning to show its work Next comes specialized training. The model is shown curated problems, such as logic puzzles, multi-step math, and tricky coding tasks, along with full step-by-step solutions. It learns a pattern: take the problem, make a plan, carry out the steps, and reach a solution. It’s learning to show its work. Stage 3: Reinforcement learning, learning from feedback Then the model is let loose on fresh problems of its own, and it learns through reinforcement learning , which is basically trial and error with rewards. The rewards can come from several places: Human feedback, where people rate steps up or down (this is called RLHF). Process reward models, smaller models that judge whether each step of a reasoning chain is good or bad. Checkable outcomes, such as whether a math answer is right or whether code passes tests. That last one is important. The research behind DeepSeek-R1 found something remarkable. DeepSeek-R1 uses large-scale reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable outcomes, and DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained with reinforcement learning directly from a base model, with no supervised warm start. In other words, useful reasoning habits like reflecting and trying alternatives can emerge from rewards alone. As that training progresses, the model generates more tokens, which means more “thinking time,” and behaviors such as reflection and exploring alternative approaches appear. Other methods: distillation There’s another popular technique called distillation. A large “teacher” model solves problems and writes out its reasoning. Then a smaller or newer model is trained on those reasoning traces. If the teacher can think through a puzzle, that path becomes training material for the student. It works well. Distilled models such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B maintain strong performance on reasoning benchmarks. One note of caution: researchers have found that small models sometimes copy the look of long reasoning without truly understanding it, which can lead to overthinking. So distillation helps, but it isn’t magic. The result of all this training is a model that can plan, verify, and explain. And that finally makes it possible to untangle those shell-company cash flows. Thinking time: how long should the model think? Training is only half the picture. The other half is inference time , sometimes called test-time compute. That’s what happens each time you ask a question. Different questions can get different amounts of thinking: “Debug my stack trace” might get a large thinking budget. “Write a nice caption” gets a quick pass. During longer thinking, a model may do several things: Run multiple chains of thought and vote on the best one. Backtrack with a search when it hits a dead end. Call outside tools, like a calculator, a database, or a code sandbox, for spot checks. This idea is more important than it first seems. A key insight from OpenAI’s o1 was that performance improved as test-time compute increased, which simply means the more tokens a model generates, the better its response tends to be. It changed how people think about progress. Instead of only making models bigger, you can also let them think longer. The price of thinking I want to be honest about the downside, because it’s real. Every extra pass, self-check, or search branch costs: More compute, which means more GPU time, memory, and energy. Higher bills, since you pay for those extra tokens. More waiting, because replies come slower. So the question becomes: is the boost in accuracy worth the cost? It depends on the problem. For a hard bug that has cost you hours, a minute of thinking is a bargain. For a quick social post, it’s wasted money and time. The pros and cons, side by side What LRMs do well Complex reasoning. They shine on multi-step logic, planning, and abstract problems. Better decisions. Because they can verify and deliberate internally, answers tend to be more nuanced and often more accurate. Less prompt hackery. You don’t need magic phrases like “let’s think step by step,” because the model already does it. Where they struggle Higher cost. More VRAM, more energy, and a bigger cloud invoice. Higher latency. Slower replies while the model works things through. Overkill for simple tasks. A regular LLM or a smaller model can be the better choice. There’s a small joy in all this, too. Reading a model’s thinking steps as it works can be oddly entertaining, a little like watching someone solve a puzzle out loud. Not everyone feels that way, but I do. A simple way to choose If you’re unsure which to use, try this quick guide: Is the task simple or creative? Writing, summarizing, rephrasing, brainstorming: use a regular LLM. Does it need several steps of logic? Math, planning, tricky code, analysis: try an LRM. Is speed more important than depth? Start with a faster model, and escalate only if it fails. Is cost a concern at scale? Use reasoning models only where accuracy really pays off. Can you check the answer easily? If yes, a cheaper model with a retry may be enough. A good habit is to match the effort to the stakes. You wouldn’t call a specialist for a paper cut, and you wouldn’t skip one for something serious. A small caution about “reading the thinking” It’s tempting to treat the visible reasoning as a perfect window into the model’s mind. It’s helpful, but be a little careful. The displayed steps can be a useful guide, yet they aren’t always a flawless explanation of how the model reached its answer. Use them as clues, and still verify important results yourself. AI models used to just spill out words as fast as they could predict them. Now many of them stop to think, and the most capable models on many benchmarks tend to be the reasoning ones. That doesn’t mean thinking is always better. It means we have a new choice: speed or depth, cheap or careful. The best builders and users will be the ones who know when to pick each. So next time you see that pause before an answer, you’ll know what’s happening. Somewhere in there, a model is making a plan, weighing options, and double-checking its work. Isn’t that a little bit wonderful? items.summary_html:
Have you ever asked an AI a hard question and watched it pause for a long moment before replying? Maybe you saw a little “thinking…” message, and you wondered what on earth was going on in there.

That pause is the whole story of large reasoning models, or LRMs. They are one of the biggest shifts in AI in recent years, and the idea behind them is surprisingly human: slow down before you answer.

In this post, I’ll explain what LRMs are, how they’re trained, why they cost more, and how to decide when the extra thinking is worth it.

First, a quick refresher on LLMs

You probably know the basics. A large language model, or LLM, predicts the next token in a sequence. A token is a small chunk of text. Given your prompt, it picks the most likely next token, then the next, then the next, and the result reads like human writing.

This works wonderfully for many tasks. Ask for a fun social media post or a friendly email, and that fast, reflex-like response is usually perfect.

But now imagine asking something harder:

  • “Debug this messy stack trace.”
  • “Trace money through four different shell companies.”

A quick reflex isn’t enough. You’d want someone to pause, test ideas, and double-check their work.

So what makes a model a “reasoning” model?

An LRM still produces text one token at a time. The difference is what happens before the final answer. Reasoning models are language models that reflect on a problem before generating an answer. They sketch a plan, weigh options, check calculations, and sometimes test ideas along the way. Only then do they write the response you see.

Think of a student in a classroom. A reasoning model is like a student who takes time to understand the question, splits it into manageable steps, and details the solution process instead of rushing to write the answer.

That internal “chain of thought” lets the model try a hypothesis, drop a dead end, and land on a reasoned answer instead of just following a statistically likely pattern.

Here’s a quick comparison:

LLM (fast reflex) LRM (thinks first) How it answers Predicts the next words straight away Plans, checks, then answers Best at Writing, summaries, simple Q&A Multi-step logic, math, tricky debugging Speed Fast Slower Cost Lower Higher Prompting May need tricks like “think step by step” Usually needs less prompt coaching

How do you teach a model to think?

This part fascinated me. It happens in stages.

Stage 1: Pre-training, learning about the world

An LRM usually starts as an existing LLM. In pre-training, it reads billions of web pages, books, and code repositories. That gives it language skills and broad knowledge, like a student who has read a very big library.

Stage 2: Reasoning-focused tuning, learning to show its work

Next comes specialized training. The model is shown curated problems, such as logic puzzles, multi-step math, and tricky coding tasks, along with full step-by-step solutions. It learns a pattern: take the problem, make a plan, carry out the steps, and reach a solution. It’s learning to show its work.

Stage 3: Reinforcement learning, learning from feedback

Then the model is let loose on fresh problems of its own, and it learns through reinforcement learning, which is basically trial and error with rewards. The rewards can come from several places:

  • Human feedback, where people rate steps up or down (this is called RLHF).
  • Process reward models, smaller models that judge whether each step of a reasoning chain is good or bad.
  • Checkable outcomes, such as whether a math answer is right or whether code passes tests.

That last one is important. The research behind DeepSeek-R1 found something remarkable. DeepSeek-R1 uses large-scale reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable outcomes, and DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained with reinforcement learning directly from a base model, with no supervised warm start. In other words, useful reasoning habits like reflecting and trying alternatives can emerge from rewards alone. As that training progresses, the model generates more tokens, which means more “thinking time,” and behaviors such as reflection and exploring alternative approaches appear.

Other methods: distillation

There’s another popular technique called distillation. A large “teacher” model solves problems and writes out its reasoning. Then a smaller or newer model is trained on those reasoning traces. If the teacher can think through a puzzle, that path becomes training material for the student.

It works well. Distilled models such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B maintain strong performance on reasoning benchmarks. One note of caution: researchers have found that small models sometimes copy the look of long reasoning without truly understanding it, which can lead to overthinking. So distillation helps, but it isn’t magic.

The result of all this training is a model that can plan, verify, and explain. And that finally makes it possible to untangle those shell-company cash flows.

Thinking time: how long should the model think?

Training is only half the picture. The other half is inference time, sometimes called test-time compute. That’s what happens each time you ask a question.

Different questions can get different amounts of thinking:

  • “Debug my stack trace” might get a large thinking budget.
  • “Write a nice caption” gets a quick pass.

During longer thinking, a model may do several things:

  • Run multiple chains of thought and vote on the best one.
  • Backtrack with a search when it hits a dead end.
  • Call outside tools, like a calculator, a database, or a code sandbox, for spot checks.

This idea is more important than it first seems. A key insight from OpenAI’s o1 was that performance improved as test-time compute increased, which simply means the more tokens a model generates, the better its response tends to be. It changed how people think about progress. Instead of only making models bigger, you can also let them think longer.

The price of thinking

I want to be honest about the downside, because it’s real. Every extra pass, self-check, or search branch costs:

  • More compute, which means more GPU time, memory, and energy.
  • Higher bills, since you pay for those extra tokens.
  • More waiting, because replies come slower.

So the question becomes: is the boost in accuracy worth the cost? It depends on the problem. For a hard bug that has cost you hours, a minute of thinking is a bargain. For a quick social post, it’s wasted money and time.

The pros and cons, side by side

What LRMs do well

  • Complex reasoning. They shine on multi-step logic, planning, and abstract problems.
  • Better decisions. Because they can verify and deliberate internally, answers tend to be more nuanced and often more accurate.
  • Less prompt hackery. You don’t need magic phrases like “let’s think step by step,” because the model already does it.

Where they struggle

  • Higher cost. More VRAM, more energy, and a bigger cloud invoice.
  • Higher latency. Slower replies while the model works things through.
  • Overkill for simple tasks. A regular LLM or a smaller model can be the better choice.

There’s a small joy in all this, too. Reading a model’s thinking steps as it works can be oddly entertaining, a little like watching someone solve a puzzle out loud. Not everyone feels that way, but I do.

A simple way to choose

If you’re unsure which to use, try this quick guide:

  1. Is the task simple or creative? Writing, summarizing, rephrasing, brainstorming: use a regular LLM.
  2. Does it need several steps of logic? Math, planning, tricky code, analysis: try an LRM.
  3. Is speed more important than depth? Start with a faster model, and escalate only if it fails.
  4. Is cost a concern at scale? Use reasoning models only where accuracy really pays off.
  5. Can you check the answer easily? If yes, a cheaper model with a retry may be enough.

A good habit is to match the effort to the stakes. You wouldn’t call a specialist for a paper cut, and you wouldn’t skip one for something serious.

A small caution about “reading the thinking”

It’s tempting to treat the visible reasoning as a perfect window into the model’s mind. It’s helpful, but be a little careful. The displayed steps can be a useful guide, yet they aren’t always a flawless explanation of how the model reached its answer. Use them as clues, and still verify important results yourself.

AI models used to just spill out words as fast as they could predict them. Now many of them stop to think, and the most capable models on many benchmarks tend to be the reasoning ones.

That doesn’t mean thinking is always better. It means we have a new choice: speed or depth, cheap or careful. The best builders and users will be the ones who know when to pick each.

So next time you see that pause before an answer, you’ll know what’s happening. Somewhere in there, a model is making a plan, weighing options, and double-checking its work. Isn’t that a little bit wonderful?
